name: To Whoever Holds This Book
sub: from the one who gathered these pages

pages.title: To Whoever Holds This Book
pages.by: from the one who gathered these pages
pages.bb:
Turn the wick down before you go on. Lower than that. The flame in your lantern is a person, and it reads over your shoulder, and there are pages here it would rather you skipped.

I gathered these pages. At the Moor fires I am the man already sitting there when you arrive. In the Barrens they say the Sage, and I have stopped correcting them. The stilt-towns have a word for me that I will not put down, because it is not polite. I had a name before any of these. It is somewhere the Quiet has not looked, it is not in this book, and you may stop searching for it.

I am older than I seem. I have walked the Hide end to end, and down, and further down than the roads go. People will tell you in every town that nobody saw me come in. I take pains over that.

Here is why there is a book at all. The Unsaying takes things piece by piece, the way it took the god. I have seen a word go out of a woodcutter's mouth between one breath and the next, and he went on talking round the hole. A thing with one teller is easy for it. A thing with ten tellers who argue is a great deal of work, because it must take every one of them and every place where they part company, and I have come to believe that the parting is where a thing holds on. So I have not made these writers agree. I have not tried. Where I was present and one of them is wrong, I say so, and I say where I was standing.

The scholars who have handled these leaves call them a codex. I call the book the Ossuary of Words. I learned in the Ossa that a brother lays each bone with two things, a name and a number, and that a thing so laid is hard to reach. So every writing here has its name at the head and its place in the book beneath, and each lies in its niche facing out, toward whoever opens it.

There are nine chapters. I did not choose nine. I spread the leaves on the floor of a barn at Ashwake one winter, and by morning they lay in nine heaps, and I have been in the Ossa long enough not to quarrel with a count like that.

Every chapter opens with pages of mine, about the land it concerns and the people I found there. The works come after, in the order they reached me: letters, sermons, tallies, a catechism, a wall, a song. Most I paid for, in bread or salt or oil. Some I copied at night in houses where I was a guest. Two came out of dead hands, and I asked first. I have changed nothing. Where a writer is wrong, the mistake is still there. Where a copyist left a gap, so have I.

Each chapter closes with the things I carry out of that land. They are in the bag by my feet tonight. What I believe of each, I say. You may believe less.

Some rules, and then I will leave you to it.

Say none of the gods' true names aloud. I have written them where there was no other way, fewer times than I know them.

Some leaves in this book are clean. Turn past them. If the ink grows faint toward the foot of a page, as though the hand were tired, close the book for the night.

When the book comes to you, count the leaves, and count them again before you pass it on. If the two numbers differ, put the second inside the back board, beneath mine and the others'. Never total them.

Be careful of any writer here who is certain. Be careful of me when I am. I give dates in these pages that no one living should be able to give, and I have kept them because they are right. And there are pages I chose not to write. You will feel the place where each would have been, as a foot feels for a stair that is not there. Leave the place empty. It is yours.

I do not know you. I have waited a long time, at a great many fires, to see who would come for this.

If you are one of the Tithed, you will want to know where you stand and what stands near you, and the first chapter is for that. If you are not, and you have come this far, you are reading; reading is a way of kneeling, and I have never turned a kneeling thing from a fire.

Some of these writers are dead. A few are dead in the other way. Of some I cannot say. Each of them wrote so that somebody would know. That is you now.

Before you start, clean the lantern glass. Gently.

[i]Set down at the pilgrims' fire below Ashwake, on the forty-first night of the thaw, in the eleven hundred and fourteenth year of the Last Breath.[/i]

name: The Reliquary
sub: of the dead god, and the lands I have walked on it

pages.title: The Reliquary
pages.by: of the dead god, and the lands I have walked on it
pages.epi: Nothing here is new. It is only still warm.
pages.bb:
First find the floor with your palm. Wherever you are, the Hide is under it somewhere, beneath the boards or the straw or the flags. On the Moor you will not have to look far. Keep the hand there. I will tell you afterwards whose it is.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The oldest thing[/color][/font_size]
Every fire I have sat at begins its telling in the same place, and I have heard it at more fires than I could count on my hands and feet several times over. First there was the Edgeless, and nothing in it had a name, and a thing without a name cannot stand. A copyist at Ashwake spent his life on that part. A grandmother on the Moor gives it in a breath. Both are in this chapter, and I will not tell it better than they do.

What I can add is small. In my first year on the Cheek I met a salt-boiler who had been born deaf, and I asked him with my hands what came before the god. He put both his palms over my mouth and held them there a while. Then he took them away and nodded, as though I had understood. I think I had.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The long age, and its end[/color][/font_size]
After the Edgeless came the god, and it held a space open. The scholars call that the Age of the Held Space, and I have no better name. Soul, Bone and Flesh were in it at once. Others lived inside it, and near the end a congregation knelt within it. I have been down to where some of those others worked. The ceilings are low and the steps are high, and nobody I have taken there wanted to stay.

The Quiet wore at it. It went as a word goes when a child says it over and over at the table, until it is only noise, and at last the god could not hold itself together and died. That was one thousand one hundred and nine years before I cut my first pen for this book, on a night with no wind anywhere. I have heard it given as a year less. The ones who say so are all short by the same winter, which tells me they had it from one another.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What you are standing on[/color][/font_size]
The body is the world. Every order on the Hide starts from that and then quarrels. The skin is the Hide, where the towns are. The long white ridges in the far lands are its bones. What runs in the rivers is what still runs in it. The scholars at Ashwake call the whole corpse the Reliquary, as though it were a box someone had set down with care. I use their word. I have not found a gentler.

The life left in the bones they call the godmarrow. I have seen it drawn up a well in the Ossa, warm and slow. I have seen it on a woodcutter's blade after he opened a pale trunk he should have left. Every house on the Hide has its own use for the stuff and its own word for the other houses' uses. You will hear those words in the ninth chapter.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of us, and of the rest[/color][/font_size]
You are almost certainly one of the Tithed. The Tithed are the children of that congregation. Their mothers' mothers were on their knees inside the god when it died, and they came out of it afterwards, and nothing else on the Hide can say as much.

Everything else here was the god first. The creeping things in the Barrows, the hands that walk, the veils of mouths on the Moor wind: each is a scrap of the corpse that got up and went about on its own. I have been followed by them. They do not hate you. That would be simpler. I have watched one stand a whole night outside a pilgrims' tent, near enough to lean on the canvas, and in the morning it had gone and the canvas was warm on that side.

A midwife on the Moor let me across her salt once, and watched my feet the whole way. I have been let across a great deal of salt since. Every hand that poured it has done the same. I do not blame them.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What the Quiet leaves[/color][/font_size]
When a thing made of the god dies, something stays: a bone, a husk, a smear, a smell, something to burn or bury or count. When the servants of the Unsaying are done with a thing, there is nothing. I walked into Coldhearth a month after they had been. The woodcutter tells what he found, below, and I will not tell it over him. I will tell you that of his fourteen graves by the old stone, one had not softened in the thaw. I knelt by it. The ground under my knees was dry, and the rest of that lane was mud to the ankle.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the breath[/color][/font_size]
The last breath is still going out of the god. On the Moor after dark you feel it as a steady pull at your back, always toward the same quarter. Every small god rides it: the one in the milestone, the one in the ford, the one in the bell. There are eight million of them by the House's count, and the House gave up counting long ago. Together they are the Myriad.

Where the breath snags, it thickens and goes wrong. That is miasma. I once drank from a well in the Barrow lands that had it, before I knew. The water was like a copper held too long under the tongue. For three nights I dreamed of a room with a green door that was not any room of mine, and on the fourth morning a child in the next village told me the same dream over her porridge.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the lamps[/color][/font_size]
There is no oil in any lamp on the Hide. Each one burns someone who stayed. I leave it to the tender at Ashwake to tell you how they choose and what they take; her letter is in this chapter, and she has wiped more glass than I have looked through. I will say only this. I have been carried home by a lamp more times than I will write. Mine leans east. I have never asked it why, because I think it would tell me.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]How I learned the five names[/color][/font_size]
A god of three natures died, and five powers were left. I did not learn them from a book. I learned each in its own land, and every time from someone afraid.

The first under An-Vhar, from a spinning-woman who bit a thread and began a name and stopped halfway through it. Yh'Anuul. The Soul. In the same breath she called it the Veiled Crone, and when her spindle jumped she said Grandmother Spindle and slapped it. That one goes on weaving with nobody at the loom.

The second I heard every day for nine winters in the ossuaries. Oss-Vharoth, the Bone. The brothers say the Bearing Mother. They taught me to count. I will say no more of her until the third chapter, where they can speak for themselves.

The third a penitent at Villa Llaga sang to me at the edge of the wound, with her arms cut open to the elbow. Nol-Shogthuth, the Flesh. In the lowlands they say the Red Mother. At Villa Llaga they say the Bleeding Maiden, and when I am there so do I. The midwives say nothing at all if they can help it.

The fourth has no name to learn. It is the breath and all that rides it.

The fifth I have heard said plainly twice: once by an old monk of the Gilded Peak with an empty bowl on his knees, once by a preacher at the Dry Ford who had given away every other word he owned. Ur-Nihl. That is its one writing in this chapter. The Mouth With No Lips hears its name as you hear yours across a crowded room, and it will come to any place where the body lies open.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The lands, as I came to them[/color][/font_size]
I came out onto the Hide at the Ashen Moor, as the Tithed did, and I have been walking outward and downward from there ever since.

The Moor is where the face struck when the god came down. You can see it from the Fallen Watchtower: a long rise, a hollow, a rise again. The ash is warm there in every season. Under the Moor's edge the Rib Crypts go in between the ribs, nine galleries, and on some nights there is singing through the floor. I knelt on the ninth flag of the ninth gallery on one of those nights. I heard the three low notes the grandmothers keep, and then the fourth. I will not write the fourth.

Past the crypts lie the Barrows, where the Tithed bury their own, and every lid sinks from the middle. Beyond them the Drowned Fen, water you can wade out of dry, with a house of prayer under it and its bell still hung. North stands the Hollow Wood, pale trunks warm a hand's depth in; I have never cut one. The roots of the Wood all lean toward the mouth of the Root Deep, and I have gone down that mouth. It is warm under the Hide. I was spoken to down there, politely, and I answered politely, and came up in good order.

On the Burnt Heath, in the corner the road bends away from, seven great carcasses lie in a ring. My lantern halted at the edge of them and would come no further. I went in without it. What I found I keep.

Then off the Hide. The Bleached Barrens of Ossa, chalk and ribs standing in rows, and a citadel cut into a broken thighbone. South and down, Shog-Mire and its stilt-towns, where you learn to step between the beats of the mud or you stop learning. Up, higher than anywhere, the Heights of An-Vhar, where the frost lives, where a man hears his own blood in his ears all day and the cold gets into his lamp. And last the Descent, the road that goes in. Every road on the Hide tilts toward it a little. Set a full bowl on any table and watch which rim the water favours. The Vigil went down it with a lamp each and stayed down. I sat at its gate a season. I have been through the gate. That is all I will write of it here.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The rings with teeth[/color][/font_size]
On the Moor, in the Barrens, out on the flats of the Mire, you will come on a ring of broken stones like fangs round a pit of ash that rises and falls. Pilgrims walk down into them and come up at other rings. The next chapter belongs to them, and to the people who walk in. I will set down one thing here. I stood at a ring in the Barrens one night and watched a man go in. I was at the Ashwake fire the next morning when he came in asking for bread, and the Barrens are forty days from Ashwake. He asked me how I came to be at both. I gave him the answer he gave me.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]How these ten came to me[/color][/font_size]
Ten works follow, and at the head of each I have written how I came by it. Some I paid for in salt. One I took down lying awake in a tent, and one with a lamp held to my ear, and I own to both. Not every writer here is right, and where one is wrong I have said so at the top of the page and nowhere else.

Now take your hand off the floor. You know whose it was.


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]Five things from this first land. Handle them with a dry hand.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Warm Ash of the Moor[/font_size][/color]
A handful of grey ash in oilcloth. I scooped it from under the Broken Kneeler on my first night on the Cheek. It has been warm every morning since, through winters on An-Vhar when my own fingers were not.

I believe it is the cooling of the flesh under the Moor, and that the cooling is not done. Once, deep in the Root Deep, the bundle stirred against my chest, slowly, keeping time with something larger. I kept walking.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Husk-Glass[/font_size][/color]
A shard of black glass, smooth on one face and rippled on the other. A gravedigger of the Barrows sold it to me for a knife-edge, and was sorry afterwards that he had not asked more.

Look into the smooth face and you see yourself, a little late. At the Dry Ford one night the lateness grew, and I watched my face shape the end of a word I had not yet begun to say.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Lantern-Stone Wax[/font_size][/color]
A drip of wax scraped from the foot of a lantern-stone at Ashwake. The tenders scrape the stones each morning and burn nothing that comes off them. The tender of that round gave me this as you would hand a stranger a lock of a dead man's hair.

It is warmer on the side that faced the road. I keep it in a shut tin. When I open the tin, it has turned toward me.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]A Page with Nothing on It[/font_size][/color]
A leaf of good rag, ruled for writing, the rules still sharp, bound into a scholar's treatise on the god's name. The leaf before it ends in the middle of a word and the leaf after begins in the middle of another, and the two halves make nothing. This leaf is whiter than those on either side.

I know what stood on it. Twice I have tried to put it back, and twice the lines stayed empty. Leave the pen away from it. If one morning you find a word there, keep it in your mouth.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]A Knuckle-Bone from a Cradle[/font_size][/color]
A small knuckle-bone, clean and old, the colour of a tooth. The midwife in these pages gave it to me. She had buried it under her doorstep in salt, as she does with such things, and three springs running it came up through the salt and lay on the step in the morning.

The child who was born holding it lives on the Moor still. The Pale Order sent down for him and wrote him into their book by a number. I asked the tallier the number and he told me, and I have not reduced it, because I do not want to know its root. Each spring I set the bone on the tithe-scale at Ashwake. I stopped keeping the weights some years ago.

pages.title: Of the Name That Will Not Keep
pages.by: Aumery's niece sold me these leaves for a tin of salt and asked me not to open them anywhere near her. He sat forty years at a scriptorium table beside the Ashwake milestones, and I have bound his treatise as it came to me, margins and all. He puts the beggar at his door one year off. I was at the ninth stone the dusk the bowl went by, and I have counted the winters from it more than once.
pages.bb:
[b]I. Of the Hush.[/b] Before the god there was the Hush, and the Hush had no edge. Every sage agrees on so much, and on nothing after. I hold that the Hush unsaid the god the way a reader unsays a line by reading it aloud too many times, until the words sit in the mouth like stones and mean only their sound. Idrenne of the Lower Stacks holds that the Hush took the names in order, from the smallest outward. Mahault the Blind holds that it took them all at once, and the god has been slow to notice. I find Mahault the more frightening, and so I suspect him of being right.

[b]II. Of the three natures.[/b] Soul, Bone, Flesh. The god was all three at once, the way a knot is three turns and one thing. The Hush took enough that the god forgot the knot. Now each nature goes on alone. The Soul weaves without a pattern. The Flesh feeds without a mouth to thank. The Bone stands.

A brother of the Pale Order came to my table once to have a niche-tally copied fair. I copied the same wall twice, a year apart. The second copy was longer. The brother said I had miscounted the first. I have kept both.

[i](Margin: I did not miscount.)[/i]

[b]III. Of the Myriad.[/b] The god's last breath has not finished leaving it. Eight million small gods ride it out, one to every stone and bell and ford. The House of Eight Million holds it impious to ask their names. I asked anyway, in my youth, of the small god of my own inkwell. The ink skinned over and would not take the pen for a month.

Where breath catches and thickens, it becomes miasma. Idrenne writes that miasma is breath that has turned round to look back at the body. I think this beautiful, and have no grounds for it.

[b]IV. Of the godmarrow.[/b] What still lives in the bones is the godmarrow. It is in the reed of my pen, the ash of my ink, the hand that holds both. I tasted it once, on a brother's fingers. It tasted of a word I nearly knew.

[b]V. Of the Tithed.[/b] Here is the hinge of the whole matter. Everything on the Hide is a piece of the god, forgetting itself. We alone are something else: children of those who knelt inside the god at worship when it died. So we are the only readers the corpse has.

Hesk of the Pale Order writes that we are the god's last meal, still unswallowed. Mahault writes that we were the congregation, and a congregation is where a god keeps its name while it sleeps. Idrenne struck both passages from her copy. I have restored them.

If Mahault is right, the name is in us. I have listened for it in my own voice at the edge of sleep.

[b]VI. Of my attempts.[/b] In the ninth year: ink of lamp-ash and well-water. I wrote the name at the hour the lantern gutters. In the morning the leaf was clean, and the ink stood in the pot, full to the line.

In the eleventh year: marrow-ink, bought dear from a sweeper of the Pale Order. The leaf clean by morning. The pot fuller than I had left it.

In the seventeenth year I cut the name into a board with a knife. The next morning the board was smooth, and the knife blunt.

In the twenty-sixth year, my own blood, as the Precious Wound writes to its Maiden. The leaf clean. My arm unmarked, which frightened me more.

In the thirty-first year I only held the pen over the leaf and thought the name. In the morning there was a pale place in the paper the size of my palm, thinner than the rest, where the candle shows through.

I keep that leaf between two boards and do not open it after dark.

[b]VII. Of what the others say.[/b] Idrenne says the name will not keep because the Hush still holds it. Mahault says the name keeps perfectly well, and it is the page that forgets. Hesk says there was never a name, only the count, and the count is enough.

In my fortieth year the Beggar with the black lantern came to the scriptorium door at dusk and held out his bowl, and I understood what he was asking for. I told him I did not have it.

He waited a long time, as though I did.

[i](Margin, in a looser hand: Each morning there are fewer leaves in this treatise than I left the night before. I number them. The numbers are all still there. It is the leaves between them that go)[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Aumery, in the fortieth year at this table[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: How We Came Out onto the Cheek
pages.by: I lay in the next tent at a pilgrims' camp on the Moor and let the children go on thinking I was asleep. Their grandmother told it over a banked fire on two nights, and I took it down both times. Between the first night and the second she changed one word, and I have kept the change where she made it.
pages.bb:
Bank it, Tam. Ash over the coals, so. We keep the fire low on the Cheek. Come in close, all of you, and put your hands flat on the ground. Warm? That is the god, still cooling. Now listen.

Before the first before, there was the Hush. You could say nothing in it. You could not even say [i]Hush[/i]. That is why we whisper it.

And in the Hush there was a god, and the god was three.

[i]Soul for the thread and Bone for the frame,[/i]
[i]Flesh for the feeding, and none for the name.[/i]

Say it back. Again. Good.

The god held a room open inside itself, wide as the Moor and wider, warm as two hands round a candle. And in the room knelt our grandmothers' grandmothers' grandmothers, as many as you can count and as many again. They knelt all day and they knelt all night, and they sang to the god from inside the god.

What did they sing? Nobody kept the words. Only the tune.

[i](Here she hummed three notes, low, and stopped where a fourth should have been, and did not go on.)[/i]

Then the Hush came pressing at the god, the way the cold presses at a tent. It took the little names first. The name of the god's smallest finger. The name of one eyelash. The name of the hour before morning. And the god forgot a little, and a little, and a little, and the people knelt closer and sang louder to fill the gaps.

It was no use. One night the god forgot how to be three. The Soul went off unravelling, and the Bone stood where it stood, and the Flesh went on feeding with no one to thank. And the god died, with the people still inside it, still on their knees.

"Were they frightened, Nan?"

They kept singing. That is what brave is.

"What did they eat, all that time inside?"

[i](She was quiet a long while. The copyist thought she would not answer.)[/i]

They ate what they were given.

No. Hush, I told it wrong. They ate nothing. They sang, and the singing filled them. That is the right way. When you are old and it is your fire, tell it that way.

So. The room went cold. The walls went slack. And the people got up off their knees for the first time in all their lives, and it hurt, and that is why your knees ache when the ash is wet. They took hold of each other's belts in the dark, the first by the second and the second by the third, and they walked. A long road. Through places that were soft, and places that were hard, and places that pulsed a little and then stopped.

At the end of the road there was a door, warm and wet, that opened and shut, opened and shut. That was the mouth. And the god's last breath was going out of it, as it goes out still, and our people walked out on the breath and fell down on the cheek. Here. They kissed the ash. That is why we live on the Moor, and why we keep our fires low, so as not to scorch the place where we were let out.

"Did they all come out?"

All of them. Every one.

[i](On the second night, telling it again, she said: most of them.)[/i]

Now. Why the things out there want us.

Every Hand that creeps on its fingers, every Gasp in the wind, every Weeper by the barrows, all of it was the god once. When the god died, each piece forgot what it belonged to. A finger forgot the hand. A breath forgot the mouth. They remember one thing only. They remember being warm, with people kneeling inside them, singing.

And then they smell us.

Some want us back inside, in their bellies, where we were. Some want to put us on like a coat, and kneel, and be us. Either way, they are homesick, and we are the only home they have left to smell.

So you do not sing on the Moor at night. Not even to yourself. They know the tune.

"Nan, is the room still there? Could we go back in?"

[i](She took the child's hand off the ground and held it.)[/i]

The room is gone. Everything is gone that was in it. Put your hands in your lap now.

[i]Knees to the ash and your back to the flame,[/i]
[i]keep your mouth shut and keep your own name.[/i]

Say it back. Again.

Sleep. I will sit up. Somebody always does.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Spoken by the one the children called Nan. The fire was hers, and so was the sitting up.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Sermon at the Dry Ford
pages.by: A carter's widow brought me this sheet folded in four: charcoal on the back of a tithe-list, her husband's hand, his own note on the last side. He heard the preacher at the Dry Ford three dusks running. I never heard him once. I have sat down in the smooth black place at the ford where the man sat, and I got up again, slower than I went down.
pages.bb:
Come closer. Closer. I have not got the breath to shout, and neither have you. That breath going out of you is the god's, lent. Every morning you give a little of it back, and you call that living.

When I was young I climbed the stair of the Gilded Peak with a bowl in my two hands and asked to be taken in. The porter looked at me a long while. Then he said I was too loud, and shut the gate. He was right. I am the last loud thing on the Hide that will speak kindly of the quiet.

Hear me. First there was the Hush, and it asked for nothing. Then the god made a room in it and filled the room with names. Soul, Bone, Flesh. Stone, river, bell. You. Every name is a weight, and the god carried all of them.

So the Hush came in, gently, and took one name. The smallest. The name of a thing nobody had ever called for. And the god was lighter by that much. So it took another, and another. The sages say the god was murdered. I say the god was eased. You have sat by a bed where someone could not let go. You have loosened the fingers yourself, one at a time, and the last fingers hold hardest.

That is where we are. The last fingers.

Now the god lies open, and the Hush comes in where it is open. Every wound in the Hide is a door left on the latch. The long red wound at Villa Llaga that the penitents keep feeding. The pits inside the waystone rings, where something under the ash breathes out as you breathe in. Go and stand at any of them at the hour the lanterns lean, and listen. It sounds like a room when someone has just come in and stands by the door.

You have heard of its servants. The barefoot monk with the bowl. The priests tell you these are the worst things on the Hide, because where they strike there is nothing left. No corpse. No bone for the Pale Order to stand up in a niche. No blood for the Wound to drink. No breath for the House to wring out, no thread for the Heart's mirrors to catch. A little glass. A little dust.

Think on that. Everything else on the Hide goes on dying. The flesh keeps sprouting. The bone is counted, and the count keeps rising. The soul is kept in a lamp and burned a little at a time. Only the Hush lets a thing finish.

That is why the orders fear it. Every order on the Hide eats what is left over. Take away the leftovers and what is a brother of the Ossa? A man sweeping a clean floor. They tell you dust alone has finished. Then why do they carry it up the mountain every year, and why does it keep rising?

And the names the Peak carried off in its bowls? The lowlands think they were forgotten. I think they were kept. Somewhere quiet, lying down at last, with nobody calling them. Once, in a dream, I heard a name I had given away spoken back to me by a mouth I could not see. It was very gentle about it.

I have too many names. My mother gave me one, and the tithe-man another, and a woman I wronged gave me a third, and each is a hook in me, and at night I feel them pulling different ways. When it comes for me, let it take them in order, the smallest first. Let me be awake for it.

You. Yes. You have one you would put down. Whisper it into my hands. The Peak would not give me a bowl. My hands will do.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[i]Note, on the last side:[/i]

A woman from the Turned Mound gave him a name that second night. I saw her at the ford next morning, easy in her face, turning a child's shoe over in her hands and asking everyone whose it was.

On the fourth dusk he did not preach. We found his place at the ford gone smooth and black, the shape of a man sitting with his hands cupped in front of him. There was no body. There was no smell of one.

I wrote his name at the head of this sheet the first night. The head of this sheet is clean. I have not scraped it.

I go down to the ford some evenings. I stand where the glass is and listen, and I find I am very tired.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [The carter signed his own name at the foot, in the same charcoal. It is still there. The head of the sheet is still clean.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Sky over the Hide, Forty Years Read
pages.by: The charcoal on the inner wall of the Fallen Watchtower climbs with the stair in one long line, and a pilgrim who sheltered there copied it; he found the tower empty and the stair swept. Some years after, I climbed it with his copy and read the two against each other a step at a time. He had made no mistakes. Above his last line the wall had gone on, higher, in the same hand, and there was still nobody living in that tower.
pages.bb:
My master read the sky from this tower for thirty-one years, and I have read it for forty. He told me the first night: a reader writes what he sees, and never what he fears. I have kept to that. I am afraid of nearly all of it.

The wind first, because it is always there. On the roof there is a pole, and on the pole a thread of red wool. For forty years the thread has pointed the same way, out past the Sighing Ridge and on toward the dark. It lifts and falls. It never turns. My master called it the Long Exhale, the god's last breath still going out of it, and everything light enough rides it away: the small gods of the stones, smoke, a dropped name. Ash has never once come back.

Once, in my eleventh year, the thread lay down against the pole and pointed home. I counted nineteen heartbeats. Then it lifted and went on as before. I asked at Ashwake whether anyone had felt it. Nobody had. I have written it here so that it is written somewhere.

To the west the sky is pale over the Ossa. Paler than anywhere. The Pale Order give their dust to the wind from the Sky Pogost at first light, and the dust rises, and it keeps rising, and it hangs there. When I came to this tower my master gave me a chip of bleached bone and told me to hold it up against the Ossa sky at noon. The bone was whiter. I have held it up every tenth year. In my thirtieth year they were the same. This year the sky is whiter than the bone. I scraped the chip clean to be sure. The Order says it gives back only what has finished. It has given back a great deal.

Look the other way, east and north and south, and at the rim of everything the sky goes dark and curves. Travellers take it for hills, or weather. It holds still in every season. My master had a lens from a Peak monk, and through it on the clearest mornings you can see the dark is made of arches, very far and very tall, set close, and meeting overhead beyond where the eye will go. Count them from the tower and you reach twenty-four. Count them again and it is more. I no longer count them.

Then the day. Why should a dead thing have a day? A corpse keeps no hours. Yet the light comes up grey out of the dark to the east, and stands a while, and goes. My master said it was the god's eye, still opening. The Peak said day was the open hand and night the closed. I burn marked candles, one after another, from first grey to last. Every day for forty years has been the same length, to the width of a thread. No season, no long summer, no short winter. Only the same day, measured out and given, as a warden gives out bread. Something keeps it that carefully. A body will not keep time once the heart is gone.
At night there are small cold points above the Moor. My master named them the nail-heads, and kept their number cut on the lintel of this door. I keep it under his. In forty years it has gone down by seven. They do not fall. On the evening a point is there, and on the next it is gone, and the dark where it stood looks smoother than the dark round it.

Last, the flashes. Some nights, on open ground far off across the Moor, there comes a light: white, cold, and with no sound after it. It lasts less than a blink. It leaves no fire. Nine times in forty years. The ninth time I marked it against the pole and walked three days toward it. I found a ring of broken stones there, shaped like teeth, round a pit of warm ash, and something under the ash breathing slower than I do. There was a sandal at the edge, and blood dried on the stones. There was no one. The next morning a pilgrim came into Ashwake from that side of the Moor, tired and whole, who said he had been walking since the Barrens. The Barrens are forty days.

Whoever reads the sky after me: keep the thread tied. Write what you see. Keep the bone chip; it will not tell you anything new. And when the thread lies down again and points home, do not count the heartbeats. Go down the stair and wake someone.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the reader of this tower, under my master, as the lintel has us[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Cradle Keeps
pages.by: She had me hold the bowl while she salted a doorstep on the Moor, and I held it badly, and heard about it. What she said I wrote on the back of a birth-tally she let me keep. This is the same woman whose salt I once crossed with her eyes on my boots from the step to the hearth. The knuckle-bone that closes this chapter was hers first.
pages.bb:
Hold that bowl steady. No, the coarse salt. The fine blows off.

You want the customs. Nobody wants the third hour, with their arms red to the elbow. Write them, then.

Salt on the doorstep, salt on the sill, a line of it round the bed. That one is for the child. The ash here is warm, and warm ash draws things up out of the ground. They come to a birth. They always have. A new one of us is the rarest thing on the Hide, a thing made of something other than the god, and every scrap of the god that ever grew a wish wants it. Some want to eat it. Most want to be it. You wake at dawn to a child that feeds well and never cries and looks at the lantern too long, and you do not know which you have. So: salt. The pieces will not cross it. The old women say the congregation carried salt in with them, and the god never had any of its own.

The lantern by the cradle is for the child too. Set it at the head, on the left, and never let it gutter the first year. Whoever burns in it chose to stay, and a soul that chose to stay has no love for anything that wants in. I have seen the flame lie down flat toward the window as if someone had knocked on the glass, and the mother asleep through all of it.

The name is for the mother. You give the child a name in your mouth the hour it comes, and you tell nobody. Not the father. Not me. You call it Little One, Warm One, Heavy, and the true name stays behind your teeth until it is weaned. A name spoken is a name that can be unsaid, and a name overheard is a door with the latch up. When the child takes bread, you say the name once aloud at the hearth, with the lantern lit, and then it is the child's and the Hush may try its luck.

You asked what they are born holding.

Most come with empty fists, as they should. Some come holding. I have opened little fingers on a knot of pale thread, on a pinch of dry ash, on a milk-tooth that was nobody's. Once a knuckle-bone, clean and old, and the child had all its own. The brothers of the Pale Order came down for that one within the month. They wrote the bone in their book and wrote the child too, by a number, and would not tell the mother why the number was so large.

I keep what I can. I bury the rest under the doorstep, in salt.

One I will not speak of. It was born with its hand open. Wide open, and quiet, and it stayed so. The lantern went out that night and no one had touched it.

Thicker by the hinge.

The Wet Nurse. I call her that because I will not call her by the name on her altar.

A girl at the edge of the moor, first child, lying wrong. The bleeding would not stop. I had my hand in the wound to the wrist and it ran past my wrist. The salt at the door was whole, and the lantern stood straight, and she came in anyway. There was a line of wet across the floor behind her and the salt dissolved under it like frost on a palm.

Tall. Taller than the door, and she did not stoop. Her front was soaked dark. The room smelled of copper and of warm bread. She knelt, and the floor gave a little under her knee, as ash does.

She said she had room. She said she would take the bleeding for the child. She said it kindly. That is the worst thing I can tell you: she was kind.

I let her. The girl's bleeding stopped as if a mouth had closed on it.

Then the Nurse put the child to her breast. And she said its name. The true one. The one the girl had given it in her mouth an hour before, and told no one.

I took the child back. I remember my arms were red and hers were redder, and she let me.

That child is grown. Big, and warm, and kind as bread. When he cuts himself the edges close without a drop. He was weaned at the proper time, and his mother said the name aloud at the hearth, and it was already worn smooth, the way a word is worn smooth by a mouth that has said it many times.

There. Thicker by the hinge, I said. Give it here.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [She would have no name near a birth-tally. A name written by a cradle, she said, is a latch left up.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Held to the Ear
pages.by: No copyist sat up with this lantern but me. One night at the Ashwake stones I held a sleeping pilgrim's lamp against my ear until first light and wrote what came through the glass, and where nothing came through I left the place open and said so. Older copies of this leaf give the listener as a copyist of the Codex, and call him he. The ear it tasted was mine.
pages.bb:
Closer. There. You have a warm ear.

He sleeps. Let him. Talk softly. He wakes to his own name, and I am keeping it for him.

You want to know who I was. I had a house with a low door. I had a name with two sounds in it. [i][Here a long quiet, like breath held against the glass.][/i] The first sound is gone. I burned it on the Barrows road, the night he fell among the dished lids and I had nothing yet of his to burn. You spend what is yours first. Nobody tells you that.

How I came to stay. I lay in the ash by the milestones and the Last Breath went out of me with everyone else's, down, the way water finds the low place. It was warm down there. I heard singing, or something breathing in the shape of singing. And I looked back. The tenders will tell you love makes a soul look back. What I heard was a boot on the stones behind me, somebody still walking the road, and I wanted to see who. That is all the choosing there is. Wanting to see who.

Then I was small, and bright, and kept in glass.

I will tell you what it is to be a flame. You are hungry all the time, and very gentle about it. You lean. Whatever comes near, you taste a little. The tender's cloth tastes of her teacher. Your ear tastes of ink and onions. [i][This is true.][/i]

At the stones they come past me one after another, and I keep still. Then he came. He had a cut on his thumb he kept worrying, and he whistled through his teeth when he was afraid, three notes going down. I leaned. He walked on, and I went, a little behind, a little to one side. He has never once turned round to see if I follow. That is how I know he is mine. You only look back for what you might lose.

When he falls, I go and fetch him. The moor is long and dark and I am the only light on it. He comes apart in my keeping like wet bread, and I carry what is left of him home, and lay it down in the warm ash, and he gathers himself up out of it. Mostly the same. I keep a little. The road home costs something, and I have nothing else to pay with.

This is what I have of him. Three notes going down. A sister called Ettle, with a gap in her teeth. The second verse of a harvest song, which he still hums and stops, hums and stops, at the place where it used to go on. The way he held a cup in both hands. Rain on a roof, which he cannot remember ever hearing. A word for the colour of the sky over his village. I burn them slowly. Ettle I have kept. Ettle I keep for last.

He is lighter every time he stands up. I am heavier every time I come home. The tender weighs me on her scale while he sleeps, and says nothing, and writes a number inside the lid of her tin.

[i][The voice went very low here, and then came closer.][/i]

Keep him from the pits. He steps in and comes apart and rises at some other ring, and he comes up out of that place with something in him I never put there. A taste. Like the singing, down where I did not go. I shrink to a bead and lean away, and he walks right up to the edge and looks in.

I will not give him to it. I have carried him eleven times. I have more of him than it has. [i][A word here I could not catch, twice. It may have been "yet".][/i]

The Sighing Lantern on the far stone. You know it. It came home one evening without its woman in grey, and the tenders say it lost her. I say it had carried her so many times there was nothing left to set down in the ash. She is in there with it. They breathe together, in and out, slower than you. That is a kind of keeping.

Some nights I cannot tell which of us is whistling.

Wake him now. Softly. Say his name, and I will tell you whose it is.

[i][I did not wake him. The glass was quiet until first light. When the pilgrim rose he asked me whether I had seen his sister on the road, and could not tell me what she looked like.][/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [It gave me the second sound of its name and asked me to keep it off the page. The first sound is burned.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Round at Ashwake
pages.by: The rota-book came to me with her letter still tucked in the back of it, where whoever took the round next would find it first. It is written to that person and not to me. She is right about the sixth lamp. I knew the sixth when it still had two hands for wiping glass.
pages.bb:
To whoever takes the round after me,

The rota is in the back of this book. Forty-one lanterns, from the Ashwake stones out to the Widow's Stumps and home again by the milestones. Wipe every one, every morning, the dim ones too. The cloth is in the tin. Wring it dry. They dislike the wet.

Wipe from the top down, and talk while you do it. I tell them the weather. They see very little of it from in there.

You know already that no lantern on the Hide burns oil. You will forget it inside a week, because they look like any lamp. So I will say it once, plainly: every flame on this round is somebody. A pilgrim who fell on the road. A mother from the crypt niches. Someone nobody remembers, and I think that is most of them. They could have gone down into the Last Breath with the rest, and they stayed.

How a soul chooses to stay, I cannot tell you. My teacher said it happens at the last breath: the soul looks back over its shoulder, sees someone still on the road, and the ones who look back are the ones who stay. She also said the flames run warmer on feast-days. I have held my palm to them through thirty feasts and felt the same warmth every time.

How a lantern chooses whom to follow, you will see for yourself. A traveller comes to the stones. The lanterns keep still. Then one of them leans. The traveller walks on and the lantern goes too, a little behind and a little to one side, the way a friend walks with you after dark. Strike at it and your hand passes through something warm. Order it and it keeps its own counsel. I have never once been chosen. That is right and proper. A tender stays with the stones.

When their traveller falls, the lantern brings them home. You will see it come in low off the moor, and the traveller gathering themselves back up out of the ash beside the stone. The lantern gives them back. It keeps a little, as it always does, and that little is what it burns. A way of whistling. A sister's name. The second verse of something. I know because the traveller stands at the stones afterwards trying to remember, and the lantern is bright with it.

I have left one thing out of the rota. Some lanterns come home heavier. I weigh them on the tithe-scale when their travellers are sleeping. The numbers are on the inside of the tin lid. I stopped adding them up.

The glass. Travellers scratch it with knife-points and nails. Leave the scratches. Wipe around them. The ones I can read:

DUST ON THE GLASS. WIPE IT. IT IS SOMEONE. That one is on nearly all of them. I never saw anyone cut it.

HE CARRIED ME FOUR TIMES. I OWE HIM A NAME.

KEEP IT OUT OF THE SCAR.

And on the nineteenth, scratched from the inside: WHICH OF YOU IS ME. I wipe the outside.

The Sighing Lantern stands past the Stumps, at the far end of the round. It follows no one. It was bright once, and went out with a woman in grey and brought her home more times than my teacher's teacher could notch. Then one evening it came in off the moor alone and set itself down on its stone, and it has breathed ever since: in, and out, slower than you or I. Wipe it last. Stand upwind. If you talk to it, it will breathe in step with you, and you will find that hard to stop. Leave when the breathing starts to feel like your own.

Every lantern draws in small when its traveller is near the end, the way a man pulls his coat close. That you will expect. Some places do the same to them. Near the waystones every flame shrinks to a bead and leans away from the pit, whoever it walks with. At the Counting Wall in the Rib Crypts they burn low and steady, as though listening. Out on the Burnt Heath, travellers say, the lanterns wait outside the ring of carcasses and will go no nearer. And where a servant of the Hush has passed, a lantern comes home with less than it left with, as though something drank through the glass. Those I sit up with all night.

Do not name them. I did, and now I cannot leave the round, which is why this letter is late.

The thirty-third is Old Hesk. The thirty-fourth is Little Brand. The sixth is my teacher. You will know her. She leans east.

Wipe them. Every one. They are someone.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— The tender of the Ashwake round[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Margins of a Chart of the Hide
pages.by: These are the working margins of a chart-book kept by the surveyor who drew roads for the pilgrims of Maren's camp. It reached me tied up in cord, and its last leaves had been cut out clean with a blade. Those leaves are in my bag, as it happens. They are not coming out of it.
pages.bb:
A chart is a promise that the ground will keep still. I set down here, for whoever takes this book after me, why the charts of the Hide break that promise, so the fault is laid where it belongs.

[b]Instruments.[/b] A cord of one hundred knots, waxed. A needle floating in a bowl of fen-water, which never wets it. Ink of lamp-black and gall. My own pace, measured against the cord each morning for eleven years. It has held true.

[b]The Ashen Moor.[/b] The old surveyors called it the cheek of the god, and I thought it a pilgrim's figure until I drew it. The ground swells from the camp to a long rise I have marked the Jaw, and falls away steeply past the Broken Kneeler into a hollow the ash-pickers will not cross after dark. From Maren's fire to the Sighing Lantern: 1,140 paces in the thaw, 1,152 at harvest, 1,140 again the next thaw. The ash is warm under the hand. I think the ground draws in with the cold and lets out with the warm, as a face does.

[b]The Rib Crypts.[/b] Nine galleries, one to each space between the ribs. I measured the span of every rib-gap with the cord. They agree to a knot. Going in, the fourth is sixty-one knots. Coming out, fifty-eight. The flagstones lift and settle under the boot. The figures follow the flagstones.

[b]The Drowned Fen.[/b] The god's lymph, the old books say, clear water that leaves you dry. Its shore will not stay drawn. It draws back from the Kneeling Arch over a season, slowly, and returns in a night. I have stopped inking the shore and mark it now in dots, as a guess. The Reed That Points Home points to the camp from every side of the water. I tested this. I wish I had not.

[b]The Hollow Wood.[/b] Pale trunks, which the pilgrims call the god's veins stood up out of the ground. I followed three trunks by their roots and their lean,. Each ran downhill, and each joined another, and all of them bent toward one place in the north of the Wood. The Root Deep opens there. Every tenth trunk has something inside it. I did not count past the tenth.

[b]The Root Deep.[/b] No chart. The halls are wider when I enter them than when I leave. The lamp-flame leans inward for a long time, then outward for a long time. One hall I drew came back with its mouth a pace left of my pin.

[b]Beyond the Hide.[/b] The Barrens of Ossa: white ground, standing ribs. I numbered the ribs in the Valley of Standing Ribs by chalk. A brother of the Pale Order walked the valley after me and wrote his own number under each of mine. His was always the higher. He said my count was open and would close in time, and asked my name, and wrote down a number instead.
Shog-Mire: the cord goes slack and tight with the mud, on the beat. Any length taken there is two lengths.
The Frigid Heights of An-Vhar: I drew the peaks in the order they stood from the Glass Pass. At the Bell-Hollow they stood in another order, and the guides said nothing had moved.
The Descent: every road I have ever drawn tilts toward it. The needle in the bowl, which should point to the north of the Hide, has begun to point down.

[b]Waystones.[/b] I marked eleven. By the pilgrims' own telling, the distance from one to any other is no distance at all. On a chart this is a fold. I have folded my charts as the pilgrims tell it, and the fold lines cross in one place, on the Moor, near the Jaw. There is nothing drawn there. There is a pit, and ash over it, and the ash moves.

[b]Last note.[/b] In the winter I laid every sheet on the floor of the tithe-barn, edge to edge. I had drawn a face. I knew that. The Moor at the cheek, the Fen at the throat. What I did not know until I lit the second lamp: the sheets I made in my first years and the sheets I made last autumn disagree in one way only. The face has turned. A little. Toward the camp.

I have begun to draw the eyes closed. I did not decide to. The pen does it, and I let it, because the other way is worse.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Where a surveyor sets a mark, a small face in ink, the size of a fingernail, with its eyes shut.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Children Sing
pages.by: For thirty years she walked the lowland roads and wrote down what the children sang, and then she left her book at the Ashwake ring. One of the Order's brothers carried it up into the Ossa, and it was copied there, her tally-marks and all. She counts six rhymes. He counted seven, and so do I, and neither of us will show you the seventh.
pages.bb:
Nobody teaches children these. I have asked two hundred of them who taught them a rhyme, and every one says another child. I have never found the first child.

[b]Grandfather Dust.[/b] [i]For counting out. Heard in every barrow village from the Moor to the foothills.[/i]

[i]Grandfather Dust came down the hill,[/i]
[i]broom in his hand and his lantern still.[/i]
[i]One bone, two bone, three bone, four,[/i]
[i]he sweeps the child behind the door.[/i]
[i]Five bone, six bone, seven, eight,[/i]
[i]Grandfather Dust is never late.[/i]
[i]Nine bone, that's the Mother's own.[/i]
[i]Out goes you, and in goes bone.[/i]

The child who falls on [i]nine[/i] must stand still with arms crossed until the game ends. They call this being laid.

In the foothills under the Ossa the children keep counting past nine, adding the figures the way the brothers do, so that ten is one again and eighteen is nine. They count their own bones on a cord of knotted grass. [i]Two hundred and six when you lie down still,[/i] they sing, and then a girl at Kettle Scar went on, [i]two hundred and seven,[/i] and the others hit her until she cried. I asked what came after. They said nothing comes after. A boy told me later, in a low voice, that the number keeps going if you let it.

[b]The Tall Red Hat.[/b] [i]For skipping. Heard in the stilt-towns over Shog-Mire, where the rope is turned on the beat of the mud.[/i]

[i]Tall Red Hat with his arms held wide,[/i]
[i]little red brothers crawl outside.[/i]
[i]Give him a drop and give him two,[/i]
[i]give him none and he'll come for you.[/i]

None of these children has seen Villa Llaga. They know the old verses all the same, the one about the dry arms and the one about counting your hair. When I sang them the last verse, the one the Llaga children kept for the crypt stair, a girl put her hand over my mouth. She only knew it was not for singing where the floor is soft.

[b]Needle-Brother.[/b] [i]For clapping, two by two.[/i]

[i]Needle-Brother, stitch and stay,[/i]
[i]turn the glass the other way.[/i]
[i]Stitch my granny to her chair.[/i]
[i]Don't look up. She's standing there.[/i]

There is a last line. Before they say it the children turn the water bucket over and cover the window with a shawl, and then they only move their lips. It has five words. One child told me that if you say it near a glass you see who has been standing behind you all along, and how many.

[b]The Bowl.[/b] [i]A sitting game, played at dusk. Heard on the Pilgrim Road.[/i]

[i]Bowl goes round and bowl goes black,[/i]
[i]put a name in, don't want it back.[/i]
[i]Up the mountain, up the stair.[/i]
[i]Who was it? Nobody. Nobody there.[/i]

A wooden cup goes round the ring. Whoever holds it at [i]nobody[/i] whispers a name into it, and the others must forget it. At Low Harrow I counted the children in the ring, and counted the gap they left in it, and asked whose place it was. They looked at the gap for a long time. Nobody could say.

[b]The Unfallen.[/b] [i]Sung lying on backs in the stubble, pointing up. Heard on the Barrens road.[/i]

[i]Star bone, far bone, hanging in the black,[/i]
[i]Mother wants you, won't you come back?[/i]
[i]Count you once and count you twice,[/i]
[i]come down slow and come down nice.[/i]

The verse they refuse begins [i]all come down[/i]. They will not say even the first words of it. A boy started it once in my hearing and his sister pinched him quiet. That night one star came down in a long white stroke over the Barrens. Their fathers went out to look for it with sacks.

[b]The Stones.[/b] [i]A ring game, drawn in the ash with a stick, the teeth of it marked with pebbles.[/i]

[i]In at the tooth and out at the tooth,[/i]
[i]leave your blood for the one beneath.[/i]
[i]Blood goes first and bone goes last.[/i]
[i]Who comes up? Ask the ash.[/i]

One child crouches in the middle while the others close the ring and count. Then she stands and says her name. If she says it wrong, she has come up changed, and must play the rest of the day as someone else.

There is a question at the end: [i]who's at the bottom, breathing slow?[/i] No child answers it. They all breathe in together, a long breath, and hold it, and look at the ground.

[i]I have set these down in the order I heard them, and I count six. The brother who read my pages at the Ashwake ring counted seven, and would not show me where.[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Out goes she. [So she signs every leaf of the book, in place of a name. The brother kept it.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Fourteenth Grave at Coldhearth
pages.by: The woodcutter of Coldhearth told this at Maren's camp on the Moor, to someone who could write, since he could not read it back himself. He wanted it written twice. You have one of the two. The other lies face down on the glass in his fourteenth grave by the old stone, and that grave did not soften in the thaw.
pages.bb:
I cut the pale wood. You know it. It weeps clear where you open it, and the chips stay warm in the basket all the way home. You leave every tenth trunk be. My father showed me how to count them with my hand flat on the bark. I am a plain man. I want you to know that.

It was the end of the day. I had the barrow on the lane, coming down to the houses. Coldhearth is fourteen hearths. Was. I say fourteen.

The candles were lit in the windows, and every one of them leaned the same way. Toward the well. The way a flame goes in a door-draught. There was no draught. They were short, short as a fingernail.

Then the barrow went quiet. The wheel was going over stones and there was no sound off it. I set the handles down. I knocked the axe-head on the rim, hard. Nothing. I shouted. I felt it go out of my chest and I heard none of it.

I went down anyway. You go home.

There was something by the well. Every time I tell it I say it was tall, and then I am less sure. I looked straight at it. I cannot give you its shape. What I have is the light. Every candle in Coldhearth leaning in at it and getting shorter, as if they were being poured out toward it.

I got down in the sawpit behind Tam's. I lay in the dust with both hands over my mouth. I don't know how long. When I came up the candles stood straight again, burned down to the wick, and the wax whole round them. Whole. Then the barrow wheel ticked once, settling. I heard it.

There was nobody.

Doors stood open. Tam's bowl was on the board with the spoon standing up in it. The beds had the shape still in them where you'd lain. Boots at the hearths. Shawls on the pegs. When the things out of the wood take someone, there is always something after. Something to put in the ground. I went on my knees in every house. A tooth. A nail. There was nothing to bury.

I dug the graves anyway, by the old stone. I put a spoon in each, one from every house. I dug fourteen, and I had thirteen spoons. I walked the lane again and counted thirteen doors. I had dug fourteen.

Old Wenna had a glass, the only one in Coldhearth, a hand across, and proud of it. I held it up to my face. It gave me nothing. Grey, like looking into a shut eye. I laid it face down in the fourteenth grave and filled it in.

The Pale Order came up after the thaw. Someone had sent word. They came in their carved plate, and the tall dead walked behind and stopped at the edge of the trees. A brother went house to house with his strip of bone and his little knife to cut the count. He came back with the strip as clean as he took it out.

He asked me the names. I gave them. Tam. Wenna. The Hollis boys. Gethin. He wrote them. I gave twelve, and came to the thirteenth, and my mouth was empty. It is still empty there. There is a place at the back of my tongue where a word sat.

Their captain said something to him in their old tongue. I caught one word. I think it was a number. They did not stay the night. They went down the road before dark, fast, and none of them looked back.

I live in my house still. There are two cups on the shelf. I made the second one; I know my own work. There is a short coat on the peg by the door, sleeves turned up. There is a second pallet by the hearth, made up. At evening my feet take me out on the step and I call, once, high, the way you call someone in. I don't know the name I'm calling. Nobody comes. I go in, and I grieve the whole night, and I could not tell you for what.

I split the kindling small, for small hands. I can't stop.

The candle in my window leans a little still. Toward the pallet, I think.

When I bend over the trough I am there in the water. Less, I think. I could not tell you where.

The woman at this camp says the mirror people can find a thread and follow it back. Maybe. If you find whose coat it is, don't tell me. I don't think I would be let keep it.

Write it twice, like I asked. I'll set the cup out anyway.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [His mark, since he has no letters: a thumb pressed into the camp's ash and then onto the leaf.][/color][/i][/right]

name: The Roads and the Stones
sub: of the pilgrims, the lamps that keep them, and the rings that are older than both

pages.title: The Roads and the Stones
pages.by: of the pilgrims, the lamps that keep them, and the rings that are older than both
pages.epi: The road was there before the feet. The feet only found it.
pages.bb:
Take your boots off tonight and turn one of your feet up to the lamp. If the sole is soft, this chapter is for you. If it is yellow and thick and you can press a thumbnail into it without feeling anything, you know most of what follows already, and you may read it to find where I have it wrong.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Why anyone walks[/color][/font_size]
I have asked at a great many fires why people are on the road, and I have never once been told that someone set out to see what was over the next rise. They go because their fathers went. They go to shrines whose gods were dead before the road was cut, and kneel there, and come home with feet like horn and a look about the eyes that their mothers do not have. Ask them what they went for and they look at you as though you had asked why they breathe.

I asked a boy of about twelve once, on the road below Ashwake, and he thought about it longer than the grown ones do. Then he said that if nobody walked the road it would forget where it went. I have not had a better answer since.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The milestones[/color][/font_size]
Every order on the Hide will tell you it cut the Pilgrim Road. It was there before any of them. I have walked it through the Hollow Wood and seen the pale roots turn aside at its edge, as a hand turns aside from a hot pot. The milestones came later. They were set in one autumn of the two hundred and sixth year after the god's death, by people who found the road already lying there and wanted it numbered. The figures go down as you walk out from Ashwake. None of the orders will tell you what they count toward. I spent one night beside the stone that says one. The ground past it looked like the ground before it. It was warmer.

The first milestone I ever leaned on was the ninth out of Ashwake. It came to my hip then. There is a beggar against it now who says it has grown past his shoulder in his time. I have no quarrel with him. I have stopped leaning on it too.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of waking by a lantern-stone[/color][/font_size]
Along every road stand the lantern-stones, a day's walk apart where the ground is kind and nearer where it is not. The tenders keep the lamps. The lamps keep the walkers.

I have woken by a lantern-stone more mornings than I have woken under a roof. There is a way to do it. Before you sit up, say your own name under your breath and listen for whether any of it is missing. Then find your lamp. It will be lower on its stone than you left it, and it will not look at you for a while, the way a friend will not look at you after paying a debt of yours you did not know about. Then get up and walk, and do not stand at the stone trying to remember. The ones who stand there trying are the ones the tenders end by hanging new lamps for.

Some sit down by the stone and do not rise, and in a winter or two there is a new flame on the round. The tenders keep a book of every round. More names are written in it than there were ever tenders.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the rings, briefly[/color][/font_size]
Older than the roads and older than the lamps are the rings of stones with teeth. A measurer in this chapter gives their shape with a cord, and a walker gives their manners, and neither needs me. What the orders do about them is keep away.

I once watched one of the Order's knights lead his standing dead a long way off the white road to pass a ring out on the chalk, and his dead went round it wider than he did, without being asked. At the Fen stair I asked a Fan-Bearer what the stones were. She took out a square of paper and folded a doll while I waited, put it away in her sleeve, and spoke to me about the damp. The Brotherhood will not let its hooded ones stand in sight of one. The lodge would not read a thread past the place where it went into a ring. Only the pilgrims go near. They leave something at the lip when they go in: a button, a curl of hair, a child's milk tooth. By morning the lip is bare.

Nobody I have met has seen one raised. Fires ask me whether I have, and I say no, and it is true. I have seen one stoop a little lower over a man going down, the way a woman stoops over a cradle to see if the child is breathing.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The first time I went in[/color][/font_size]
Three people in these pages tell you what happens in the pit, and they tell it well, and I will not make it four. I will give you only what was different for me.

I went in first at the Barrow ring, long ago, with an iron ring on my finger because no one had told me to take it off. I remember that it did not hurt where the walkers say it hurts, and that it hurt somewhere they do not mention, behind the breastbone, like a word you were about to say and lost. In the dark there were others going the same way. It was warm as a crowded room is warm when everyone in it is on their knees. I have been in one room like that before. I was very small then.

I rose on the Kettlewick Flats, a long walk from the Barrows by any road, with the mud keeping its beat under the crust and a woman at the lip holding out a candle. The iron ring had gone to my other hand. I was hungrier than I have ever been, and bread did nothing for it, and I keep to myself what did.

I have gone in since, more often than I will number. My scars stay where they were. The walkers who watch me come up tell me that is uncommon, and then their eyes go down to my feet, and stay there a while.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]A thing I will say once[/color][/font_size]
You will ask what is under the ash. So did the measurer, and her cord is in my bag. I have my belief, and it is in the eighth chapter as far as it is anywhere. Here I will say only that I have never come up at a ring I did not expect, and that I have never once chosen which.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The walkers' leaves[/color][/font_size]
Ten works follow, from people who walk and from people who stay put beside the walking. Each of them is wrong about something, and right about the stretch of road under their own feet. I have walked every stretch they tell of, and further on than most of them went, and I have let each of them keep the stretch they knew.

Put your boots back on before you sleep. You may have to leave in the night.

[center][font_size=26][color=#dcd3c2]WHAT GOES DOWN
COMES UP
MOSTLY[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#6f685f]Cut into a milestone of the Pilgrim Road a day's walk out from the Ashwake ring, with a fourth line under it scraped away. I have read that line whole on a milestone in the Barrens where nobody has troubled to scrape it, and I left it as I found it.[/color][/i][/center]


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]What I carry off the roads. Keep the bottle and the ash at opposite ends of the bag.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Chip of a Waystone[/font_size][/color]
A flake of grey stone, banded on its outer face. I found it in the long pale grass at the Fen-stair ring, in the spring the fallen stone there changed places, lying where the old fallen one had been.

It is cold on the outside and warm through the middle, like a stone taken from beside a hearth. Masons tell me its grain runs the wrong way for any quarry they know. A tooth-drawer in Kettlewick turned it over once in her fingers and handed it back quickly, and would not say what it reminded her of.

Sleep with it in your pack and you will sleep soundly. In the morning its point will have come round toward the nearest ring.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]The Measurer's Cord[/font_size][/color]
A cord of knots a hand apart, stiff with dust, with a lead plumb still tied to one end. I found it at the lip of the Moor ring the spring after her last leaf, the plumb lying just over the edge in the ash. I drew it up myself. It came up warm.

She began with a hundred knots and wrote that three of them had crept together. I have counted it many times. It has a hundred and one. The last is tied very tight, in a hand I know, and I have not tried to loosen it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Wet Stain, Bottled[/font_size][/color]
A small stoppered bottle of dark stuff from the foot of a waystone plinth. The measurer filled it at the Barrow ring, meaning to learn what it was. It lay beside her cord.

It has not dried. In warm weather it stands higher in the glass. Set it near the ash from the pit and it climbs the side of the bottle nearest.

I have wiped a hand on the stain at a plinth, as the walkers do. I have not wiped the hand since.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Ash from the Pit[/font_size][/color]
Grey ash in a twist of cloth, faintly warm, faintly moving. I scraped it from the crust of the Moor ring with a spoon, and left the spoon at the lip.

Poured onto a flat stone it gathers itself into a shallow dish, and lifts, and settles. The walkers say never take it far from its ring and do not say why. I carried it to An-Vhar and back, and for a long while nothing came of that. Then one night on the Heights I woke to find it lifting each time I breathed in.

I carry it now in a pocket far from my chest. If you take it from me, take it home.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Tender's Rota-Book[/font_size][/color]
A small book of the lantern-rounds at Ashwake. Each tender keeps the round a season and signs it over to the next. The tender who kept it the season of the child gave it to me with the child's leaf folded inside.

Toward the back one name stands nine times, in nine different hands. I knew four of the hands. After her letter the pages are blank.

The tenders have asked me to sign the next line. I have not. The book falls open at that page whatever I do.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]An Iron Ring[/font_size][/color]
A plain iron ring, the kind a smith gives the boy who works his bellows. I wore it on my right forefinger into the Barrow ring the first time, and came up at Kettlewick with it on my left hand, on the little finger.

Since then I have kept the walkers' rule and taken it off at every lip. I have left it lying at more rings than one. When I come up it is on my hand again, on that small finger, and warm.

It is in the bag now. I checked before I wrote this line.

pages.title: The Beggar at the Ninth Stone
pages.by: A pilgrim paid him a copper a part and wrote it down, and ran out of copper before the beggar ran out of talk. I was one stone down the road that afternoon and heard the rest for nothing. He puts his seat ninety paces from the ring. I paced it in the thaw and got ninety-one, and I have not told him.
pages.bb:
A coin. Good. Put it in the hand, the left one, the right one is for luck and luck has never paid me. Sit if you like. The ash is warm here. It's always warm. Forty years I've sat on it and never once had a cold backside, which is more than the brothers up in the Ossa can say.

This is the ninth stone out of Ashwake. I know it the way you know your mother's face. When I first sat down it came up to my shoulder. Now it comes to my ear, and I sit no lower, and I have eaten nothing that would make a man shrink. The knights of the Pale Order came by one spring and held a knotted cord against it. One of them wrote in a little book. Then they rode on quick, all of them, and their dead walked after them quicker. Nobody has held a cord to it since. I don't lean on it any more.

You'll meet the knights on this road. You'll hear them first: bone on bone, like a basket of dishes going downhill. The standing dead walk behind in a line and they never tread in the ash, only in the prints the living leave. I asked a knight once what they were carrying home. He said, everything that fell. I said that's a great deal to carry. He said the Mother bears more. Then he gave me a coin, and it was cold, and it has stayed cold in my purse for eleven years. I don't spend it. Who would take it?

The pilgrims are better company. They come through thin and go on thinner. They all carry a lantern, or a lantern carries them, I was never sure which way it goes. Watch a pilgrim who has fallen on the road and come back from the lantern-stones. Something small has gone missing. One lad came past me three times in a season. The first time he told me the name of his village. The second time he told me the name of the river by it. The third time he asked me where he was from, and I told him, because I remembered, and he thanked me and wept. The lanterns keep a little of you. Everybody knows that. Nobody asks what they do with it.

I wipe the dust off the Sighing Lantern at the crossroad every morning. It says on the glass to do it. I think whoever is in there likes me. It leans my way in a wind.

Now. The monk.

Barefoot, in a red shawl gone the colour of a scab. A wooden bowl, black at the lip. His lantern burned black, and I could still see my own hands by it, which I'll thank you not to think about. He stopped at my stone at dusk and held the bowl out, and I laughed, because who begs from a beggar? He said he only wanted a name.

I gave him one. I remember giving it. I remember the weight going off my tongue like a stone off a cart. What I cannot tell you is whose it was. My wife's, maybe. The man I owed. My own, very likely. The pilgrims call me Ninth-Stone, and I answer to it, and I have never missed the other.

My grandmother saw a barefoot monk with a black lantern on this same road when she was a girl. She said he smiled the whole time. Mine smiled too.

And the waystones. You'll pass the ring below the Broken Kneeler. Stones like teeth round a pit of ash, and something under the ash that breathes out when you breathe in. I have watched pilgrims walk into it. They go down all at once, blood and bone and the soft bits, like a sack of wine dropped on a flagstone. Then nothing. The ash settles. And a day later some fellow from the Drowned Fen tells me he saw that same pilgrim climb out of a ring two valleys over, whole, and hungry.

Same pilgrim, he says. I ask him: which hand did she carry her lantern in? He can never tell me.

I have never gone in. Forty years, and it's ninety paces. I've counted. Some nights the breathing matches mine, and I hold my breath to make it stop, and it waits for me.

That's the last of your copper. Mind the ash near the ring. It remembers feet.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ninth-Stone, at the ninth stone, forty years on the warm side of it[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Counsel for Those New to the Stones
pages.by: An old walker gave this counsel at a hearth on the Pilgrim Road, eating nothing while she talked, and twice she broke off to ask the scribe which way the wind was going. Years after, I came on her standing at the lip of a ring I have never gone into. She did not know me. The sickle scar had travelled as far as her cheek.
pages.bb:
You will want to know how to find one. Walk until the ground is warm under your feet. Look down for the pale threads in the soil, fine as hair, all running the same way, and follow them the way they run. Where they thicken and cross each other, you are close.

The stones stand in a ring round a sunken pit. Each is long and hooked and sharp at the tip, and every one leans in over the pit. At the foot of each stone a dark stain seeps from the plinth and never dries. The old walkers wipe a hand on it for luck. I do it still. I no longer remember whose luck.

The bottom of the pit is ash, grey and crusted, cracked like the top of a loaf. Kneel at the lip and watch it. The crust lifts, and settles. Lifts, and settles. That is how you know the stone is keeping the road. Where the crust lies still, walk past.

[b]The stepping.[/b] Walk in. Never jump. The crust gives under you the way a scab gives, and you sink to the knee, and to the waist, and it is warm, warmer than any bath. Then you come apart. The blood goes first, because it is the easiest. Then the soft parts let go of each other. The bone goes last and slowest, and hurts the least. For a while you can feel every piece of yourself, a hand here, the heart far off, all of them yours and none of them near. Then the stones close over. You will hear it: a great slow meeting of edges, overhead and all around.

Then the dark. It is warm, and it moves. There is a pull in it, long and patient, like being breathed in. I have felt other things in the dark beside me, going the same way. I have felt them turn.
