The knight who came for her bones read the last one, set the pot back, and left it, and a pedlar had it after; I bought the letters still in their pot. I knew Benn on the Sixth Stair. His last letter is signed with a number one higher than the Warden gave him, and he never saw it, and I never said.
pages.bb:
[b]I.[/b]

Mam,

A brother writes this for me because my letters are not good yet. He says to say all of it and he will put it down.

I am well. They took my shirt and gave me grey, but I kept the collar where you sewed BENN, and at night I feel the stitches. Tell Da I did not cry on the road. I cried at the gate.

They have given me my teacher. He is Brother Oskol, and he has been dead a long while, and I carry him. He hangs on a yoke across my shoulders in a frame of cord, every bone in its knot, and I take him up the stair in the morning and down at night. The yoke is heavy. I must learn Oskol by touch: the long bone of his left arm, the little bones of his wrist, which are the hardest. When I get one wrong the brother lays my hand on the right one and says its name twice.

His skull sits by my ear on the stair. It turns a little when the lamp goes past. The brother says that means he likes me.

Your Benn. [i](Here, in a child's hand:)[/i] BENN

[b]II.[/b]

Mother,

Three winters. I write myself now.

I have learned the Count. Every bone laid gets two things, a name the Mother hears and a number the Count keeps, because the Hush can take a name and has nothing to hold in a number.

I have learned roots. Add the figures till one stands alone. Cold Adit is forty-one households: four and one, five. An open count. I lay awake over it. Tell the headman.

I tie my cord of two hundred and six knots and tell it in the dark. Brother Oskol I can tell in the dark now too, from the yoke, without my hands. The Tallier says that is the right way round.

The brothers teach it is holier to have less. A child has more bones than a man, and they knit. So I am less holy than Oskol, who is as knit as he will ever be. I am trying to be patient.

I have stopped being homesick. I think it knitted.

The stitches in my collar are going. I have let no one mend them.

Benn

[b]III.[/b]

Mother,

At the Feast of the Laying I held a lamp for the sweepers, and at dawn the Warden gave me my number. I am nine thousand one hundred and six. Nine and one and nought and six: sixteen; seven. An open count. I will close in the niche, when my number is cut beside me. I am glad of it.

At first I turned round for Benn and nobody was there. Now I turn round for the number.

I have set Brother Oskol down. He stands on the Fourth Stair, facing up. When I pass with the lamp his skull comes round after me, further than the others. My shoulders still sit as if the yoke were on them. The brothers say they will stay so.

A thing I have not told Brother Confessor. I told Oskol every night for four years. Two hundred and six. In the third winter, two hundred and seven: a small one at the heel of the right foot, that I had never felt before. I took it to the Tallier. He wrote it on the other leaf, the one we may add across and never down, and said the Mother's gift, and I was glad. Oskol was heavier after. I felt it on the stair.

9,106

[b]IV.[/b]

[i]In the Order's letters. The copyist notes the hand is steady and very small.[/i]

Mother.

The brother who reads me your letters reads out a name at the top of them. I asked him to read it as my number. He does not know it, so he reads nothing, which is better.

I sweep now, on the Sixth Stair, in the rooms past the long wall. There are rooms here the chronicle does not list. The stairs in them are knee-high, and I go up them on my hands. The dust keeps still. It is the one thing here that does.

I tell my cord at night. It has grown short for me. I have tied knots on. The Tallier says a frame walks toward the fewer, and he says it looking at my hands.

I have the collar still. The thread came out, and where it was there are holes. I cannot remember what they said. I count them. Four. Four wants five to close.

Bury deep this winter. The ground at Cold Adit is kind.

Bear what is given.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— 9,107[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Entry the Four Hundred and Fifth, Concerning the Gate
pages.by: This is from the leaf in the Order's Book, in the Warden's own hand, copied by me, and I have kept the lines a second hand added later where they fall, set off from his. The second hand is right, and the Warden knew it. I held the other lamp at the grate. The column of dead behind the man at the gate I counted as he came and again as he went, and the second figure is mine to keep.
pages.bb:
Set down by the Warden of the Ossuary of Nine Stairs, in the week of the Feast of the Laying, the walls standing at their count.

Concerning Four Thousand and Eleven. Root six. Open.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Four Thousand and Twelve. His number was corrected at his vows. Root seven. Open still.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The Rule writes no brother's name in this book, and I do not write his. He was entered at his vows under the Seventh Ossuary, and raised Ossuarch of that house in the year its Warden was carried to the Pogost. His count has not closed. Let the talliers carry it.

Let it be written that the gate of this ossuary is shut to him, and the gates of the nine, and of the hundred lesser, by order of the Wardens in agreement. The reasons are these.

I. That the Seventh Ossuary has sent no tally to the Ninth Stair these three Feasts, and its bell does not answer, and he is the one who came out of it.

II. That he came to our gate unsent, from the high road, with a column of the standing dead of no house we could name, and asked nothing, and waited.

III. That his frame, told at the grate on his own cord, stands above two hundred and six. The Rule blesses a frame that knits to less. The Rule makes no provision for the more.

IV. That he has read the weights on the Ninth Stair of his house. This is said, and unproven.

V. ~~That the dead~~

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]V. That he knew the lower lines under the Ninth Stair, the old letters, and said them aloud at the grate. Brother Tallier counted eleven lines. Brother Tallier has asked to be moved to the sweeping.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

He came to the gate on the third night after the Feast. He stood a night and a day. The dead at his back numbered thirty-six, root nine, and I set that down with thanks to the Mother.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Forty. The sweeper at the lamp counted forty. Forty is four.[/i]

[i]Before the Feast. He came on the ninth night before it. The Warden has the week wrong, and the Warden knows it.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The knots on his cord were told through the grate by two talliers, each alone. The first reached two hundred and nineteen, root three, and stopped, because the cord went on and his lamp had burned down. The second reached two hundred and twenty-six, root one, and said the cord was longer than when the first had held it. I have written both. Let the Wardens after me choose.

He said nothing to the reasons. At the reading he lifted both palms, as we brace at the Laying, and held them so while I read them twice. Then he turned and went down the high road with his column.

Let the gate stay shut. Let the lamp at the grate be kept lit.

Let the Rule be kept in this house, in all its clauses, and the fourth before the others.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[i]Below the rule-line, where the book is read by no one aloud.[/i]

His plate. I saw it through the grate by my own lamp. It is cut with names, as a warden's plate must be, the brothers who wore it before. I knew three of them. Stoyan, Mirko, Bratan: brothers of this house. Their bones stand in the niches of our Fourth Stair. I went down after, with the lamp, to be sure. They stand there. Their skulls turned to follow me, as is proper.

The names on his plate are cut deeper than any carver of ours cuts. On the left pauldron the plate has closed over Bratan's name, the way the skin closes over a thorn, and I could read only the first letters. I have worn Bratan's gauntlet since my vows. I took it off tonight. The fingers are as they were. I measured them against the lamp.

When he turned from the gate, the dead in the niches of the Gate Stair turned their skulls after him. They turn for a lamp. He carried none. Then every one of them lifted its hands, palms up, as a brother braces at the Laying, as if a weight had come down onto the ceiling of the stair. They hold them so. I have asked them to lower their hands nine times, and nine times nine. They face the stair still, and their hands are still raised.

The sweepers say the Gate Stair has one more step than it had. I have forbidden the saying. Tonight the tallier counts the Gate wall one higher than the Feast. I have left it out of the book.

It is in the book now.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— given under the Warden's hand at Nine Stairs, the walls standing at their count, the lamp at the grate lit[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Of the Unfallen
pages.by: His leaves lay under the stone in the roof-house for whoever came up after him, with his own figures down the margins. I lay under the cords beside him one winter. On the night of the man on the low ledge I was on the Pogost as well, further down, with a sweeper's pan. I lay flat too, and I did not count.
pages.bb:
Brother. You have come up to keep the roof after me. Let your eyes go dark first. Then look up.

Every cold point up there is a piece of the Mother. When she fell, most of her came down to the Hide, and the first brothers laid her where she lay. Some of her stayed up. It hangs in the dark still, uncounted, and every piece is a wound the Count must carry. We call them the Unfallen.

The roof is a frame of long bones with cords strung across it, nine by nine, eighty-one squares. You lie on the stone beneath and count one square a night, reduce it, and write the figure and its root on that square's leaf. Eighty-one clear nights to count the sky once. I have counted it thirty-three times, and it has never come out the same. Some squares are fewer. More are more. My master said the fault lay in the eye. I have made my eye very good.

When one falls you will know it: a white line drawn down the dark, gone before you have breathed. Do not cry out. Lay your hand on the cords where it crossed, read the angle off the frame, and go down the stair and wake the Seekers. Three brothers and three of the standing dead walk the line to where it ends. Twenty days, or a year.

What they carry home is always bone. White, colder than any bone of the niches, with no marrow in it, the ends broken clean. Once it was a thing nine of the dead carried between them, and no niche would hold it, and they cut a new one. We lay each on the Wall of the Come Down, with its number, and a name, which is the night it fell. The Wall stands at two thousand and sixty-eight. Root seven. It wants two.

The Wardens say the pieces come from every part of her, and so they do not fit one another. I have set two side by side under the lamp. Neither fits a bone of a man, or any bone the Seekers have brought. Each is shaped to fit something. And on the Ninth Stair they weigh more than they weighed on the road. The Seekers say so. The Wardens say the road is long.

One Seeker came back alone, and would not say where the line had ended. He said only that it was still coming down when they reached it.

I pray for them to fall. Nine times a night I ask the Mother to call her pieces home. When the last is down the roof will be dark, and the Count will close, and she will rest, and I may sleep. I have pictured that dark, with nothing in it. It is the most beautiful thing I know.

Some nights a point is gone that did not fall. You will look for the line, and there will be none. The Warden says those were never hers, and we do not write them. I keep them on a leaf of my own, under the stone. The dark where they stood is smoother than the dark round it.

On the lower stairs they say an Ossuarch can ask the Unfallen to come down early. The Rule says a bone comes down when it is ready. I did not believe it.

In my twenty-first year, counting the first square of the ninth row, I saw a man standing on the low ledge of the Pogost, where no brother goes by night. Very tall. No lamp. He raised both palms to the sky, as a man braces a ceiling, and they came down. Many lines at once, every one dead straight, all falling to him. They made a dry sound, like a floor of bones settling. The slope below him rang for as long as it takes to sing the Chant nine times. Then he turned his face up toward the roof. I lay flat on the stone until the grey came.

In the morning the Seekers went down with baskets. They brought up four hundred and nine pieces, and I wept, because four hundred and nine were down and would never hang again. That night I counted the square they had fallen from. It held the number it had held the night before. I counted it nine times. I have counted it every night since. It has never been fewer.

Keep your eye good. Count your square. Pray them down in their time. If you see a man on the low ledge with his palms raised, do not count. Go down the stair.

The leaf under the stone is yours now. When I began these pages there were seven on it. There are eight.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Five Thousand and Thirteen, of the roof, the thirty-fourth count of the sky begun[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What Rose in the Well at Old Upright
pages.by: A tallier took her words down at the gate on the back of a spoiled niche-tally, and left a gap wherever she said a thing he could not spell. The gate stayed shut. The Warden kept the leaf, and it is mine now. I was never at the gate with her; I have been to the altar at Old Upright, where the upper letters say what she says they say, and I have read the lower ones too.
pages.bb:
Three days past the thighbone citadel the ribs stand closer, and the ground is white as a washed plate. We counted our fingers at night, as the road tells you to. Ten, and ten. On the third night I had ten, and a knot in the smallest finger of my left hand, a hard warm seed under the skin, just at the joint. I told no one. The others kept to the ribs. I went where the ground sloped.

The altar is a slab laid across four knuckles, each as tall as I am. Letters on its face: OLD UPRIGHT. Under them, other letters, worn to a shine. Behind it, the well. No rope. No windlass. A lip of polished stone, knee-high to something taller than any man, and a stair cut down the inside wall, each step too deep for my legs. The air coming up was warm. It smelled of your lamps, brother, the sweet heavy tallow, and under that of a stair where a great many feet had gone down.

I set my bowl on the slab. My lantern I set beside it, and the flame leaned away from the well and stayed leaning. I said the Mother's names. I know three.

It came up slowly. Put it together yourself. I never could hold it all at once.

First the top of it. Long pale fingers, pressed tip to tip, rising out of the dark in a peak, the way hands are held for prayer, the way a crown is tall. Then more fingers under those, and more, joint after joint. I counted them, as a pilgrim counts. I had thirty. Then thirty again. Then I had lost my place, and the joints went on coming.

Below the fingers, where a face would sit, there was a bowl of bone, worn hollow, like the middle of an old step. Nothing looked out of the bowl. The bowl was turned toward me.

It stopped at the lip. Most of it stayed down. I know that, because the well kept breathing around it, warm, and slow, and a long way down.

The brothers call it the Marrow Pontiff. The salt-carriers call it the Herald of Bone, and walk wide of the knuckles. It was older than the altar. Older than the letters under the letters.

It spoke out of the bowl, and out of the stair, and out of my knees. Slow, the way your talliers read off a wall. The words were ours, set in an order nobody sets them.

It said, [i]Early.[/i]

It said, [i]Has she fallen. Is it after.[/i] I could not answer. It said, [i]After,[/i] as though I had.

Then it counted me. I felt each number come down on a bone like a thumb laid there, from the crown of my head to the soles of my feet. Two hundred and six. A whole woman, I thought.

It said, [i]Open.[/i]

Two and nought and six. Eight. I understand it now.

It said [[i]here she made a sound the tallier could not write; he gives it the width of three words[/i]]. It said, [i]Carried. You are carried in her. Carried thing, in her.[/i] Then, [i]Knelt, once. Inside. When she held.[/i] Then, [i]Kneel, as you knelt.[/i]

I asked what for. I had walked three days.

It said, [i]She has stood since before. She has never set it down. Someone kneels for her.[/i] And after a long time, lower: [i]One bone. She sets down one.[/i]

So I knelt. On the white ground, by the knuckle, with my face toward the bowl. It was warm under my knees. The well breathed.

It counted me again.

Two hundred and seven.

[i]Closed,[/i] it said. [i]Nine.[/i]

Then it went down. Joint by joint, the way it came, and the fingers last, still pressed together, and then there was only the warm air, and my lantern, still leaning.

I carried away my bowl and my lantern, and the knot in my finger. It is a bone now. I can move it under the skin. It is warm, the way your chrism is warm. My knees are warm too, and they bend slower in the mornings, and I have stopped minding.

That is why I came to your gate. Write me in the book, brother. Write me by my number. Two hundred and seven. A good root. I have a closed count. I am ready to be laid.

Hold out your own hand, if you doubt me. Count it.

[i][She would give no name. The Warden came down to the gate and asked her to hold out her left hand, and he counted it, and he sent the tallier inside. The tallier writes that the Warden stood at the gate a long time after, with his own hands behind his back.][/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [She asked to be written by her count. The tallier wrote two hundred and seven, in words, and ringed it, as they ring a closed count.][/color][/i][/right]

name: The Gilded Peak
sub: of the monks on the knee, and what they carried up the stair

pages.title: The Gilded Peak
pages.by: of the monks on the knee, and what they carried up the stair
pages.epi: An old monk on the landing, when I asked him whom they waited for: "Someone who is late, and will come."
pages.bb:
Hold one hand out in front of you, palm up. Open it wide, then close it, slowly, nine times. Let the hand learn it before the head does. The brothers of this chapter would have said the head never learns it at all.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Going up[/color][/font_size]
The Peak is the god's knee, broken up through the Hide when the body came down, and the monks cut their stair into the bone of it. I first climbed it in the summer of the one thousand and seventy-first year, while the Peak was whole and rang at noon. A brother met me at the landing where pilgrims who would go no higher left their bread. He did not ask my business. He only fell in behind me, a little lower on the stair than I was, and climbed the rest of the way there. I did not understand until I stumbled, near the top, and found him already braced to take my weight.

From the courtyard the miasma lay in the valleys like milk left standing in a pan, and the lowland towns under it showed only as lamps.

They called themselves the Kinrei-shū, the Gold Bell. A monk owned a bowl, a robe, and later a lantern, and nothing else. I sat one evening in their hall among them while they chanted. How the chant goes is not mine to give; a woman who sang it four winters tells you below, and so does the man who taught it. I will tell you that in the third of the long quiet places, the brother beside me pressed his shoulder hard against mine, and kept it there, the way you steady a man at the lip of a drop, and that I did not know until then that I had been leaning.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The bell at noon[/color][/font_size]
At noon they struck the big bell that hangs over the courtyard. I stood a few paces from it. The beam went in, and I felt the blow in my teeth and heard nothing, and every monk round me let out his breath at once, content. Two days later I was in a market in the valley when the noon stroke came down the mountain, and it rang so long the bread-sellers stopped calling to let it end.

A bell-caster tells you in this chapter what his wife heard. I stood in that market. She heard right.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What they waited for[/color][/font_size]
Going down at dusk I found an old monk sitting on a landing with an empty bowl across his knees, and I asked him to whom they prayed. He said the fifth name, the one I wrote once in the first chapter. He said it as a man speaks of a guest expected for supper, who is late, and will come. I have not heard it said so gently anywhere else.

Every other house on the Hide bars its door against the Unsaying. The Peak laid a place for it. I have stood nearer the Long Silence than those monks ever meant to stand, and I cannot call it what they called it. And still, every argument I have made against them since, I can hear the old man on the landing answering, in one breath, without raising his eyes from the bowl.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the gold, and the saints[/color][/font_size]
They gilded everything they meant to honour, and they meant to honour it by making it hard to see. The goldbeater in this chapter tells you how, and why, better than I can. I was never let into the sanctum. I will tell you only what I saw from its door on my first visit: a row of niches going away into the dark, and in each a shape so bright at the edges that the eye slid off it, and a novice with a dry cloth going from one to the next along the row, reaching up.

I have my own belief about the saints. I keep it in the bag with the gold. The goldbeater was nearer to them than I ever was. Read him slowly.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the bowls[/color][/font_size]
They came down to the valleys at dusk in fours, barefoot, with small bells at their belts, and asked for one thing. The lowlanders gave it, and forgot, and fed the monks bread for the forgetting. Where the gifts went, the Peak did not ask, or asked and got an open hand for answer. The bread-woman, the magistrate and the abbot each tell you a piece of what came of it. None of them has the whole. I have not either, and I have walked further along it than they did.

A monk of the Peak carried his teacher in his lantern, and the teacher burned his own name for fuel, slowly, down to nothing. I once walked a day behind a brother carrying his teacher down to the valley. He set his feet on each riser as though the stair were ice over a deep pool, and at the bottom he sat down on the last step and held the lantern in his lap until it was dark.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The tenth night[/color][/font_size]
The Pale Order learned that the Peak gilded its dead and gave them to the Quiet, and left the Count nothing. To the brothers of the Ossa there is no worse waste on the Hide. Their standing dead waited nine days under the mountain, and on the tenth night they climbed.

It was the spring of the one thousand and ninety-eighth year. The brothers will tell you that year comes down to nine, and they say it as though it closed the matter. I was in the valley, at a ford, with my back against a stone. I heard nothing all night. I have come to think that nothing was what there was to hear.

The monks did not fight. When the sun came, the flags of the courtyard had gone to glass and the sanctum stood open. What happened between, no two tellers give the same way, and I was not there to correct any of them.

I went up in the thaw. I did not go into the sanctum. I stood beside the door, never in front of it, with my shoulders to the stone, and looked down at my own palm until the sun was at the top of the sky. I could not have told you why I stood so until a letter came to me two winters later, folded inside a bowl. The Order's scribe gives the count of what he found. He has the stair right both ways.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the one who comes at dusk[/color][/font_size]
A barefoot man with a bowl walks the lowland roads and asks for a name, and a black flame follows him a little behind. What he strikes leaves glass, or dust, or nothing. Some say he was down in the valleys with his bowl on the tenth night. Some say he was first up the stair after, and opened the doors. Some say he walked out of the empty niche.

I know this much, and set it beside what they say. In a pilgrim-roll at the Ashwake scriptorium, in a hand three hundred and four years older than the fall, a scribe writes of a barefoot brother with a black lamp who asked him for a name and was given one. I saw the bowl go past Aumery's door, alone, while the Peak still sent its brothers down in fours. And once, at the Dry Ford, he held the bowl out to me. I have more names than most, and I gave him none. He waited, and went on down the road. I still cannot say whether he was asking for a name or offering to carry one.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Seven, from the valleys under the knee[/color][/font_size]
Seven works follow. Two were written on the Peak, one before the dead climbed and one after, and the other five by people who lived under the mountain and looked up at it every day. I have been up the stair. I trust the ones who looked up.

Now open your hand, and leave it open until you turn the page.

[center][font_size=26][color=#dcd3c2]UNDER THE GOLD
THEY WERE STILL LOOKING[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#6f685f]Scratched on the right-hand leaf of the sanctum door after the fall, shallow, as a nail scratches, with gold dust still in the strokes. No scribe of the Order could match the hand. I read it from beside the door with my back to the wall, and I have never read it from in front.[/color][/i][/center]


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]What I brought down from the knee. Keep them in the dark of the bag, and never set them out at noon.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Begging Bowl of the Peak[/font_size][/color]
A plain wooden bowl, its rim darkened by hands. It came to me from the lowland priest with the abbot's letter lying in it, and the priest was glad to see it go.

It is heavier than its wood. At an inn by the Dry Ford I set it on a table among carters. Their talk stopped, and started again on some other matter, and none of them could say what they had been discussing. One of them wept a little and laughed at himself for it.

Do not speak into it. Do not speak near it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Gilded Leaf[/font_size][/color]
One leaf from the last book the goldbeater beat, the one he never carried up. It stirs when you breathe near it, and now and then a moment before you do.

At its middle is a pinhole fine as a hair. I laid it over the back of my hand one noon, and the hand was gone, and light lay on my wrist in the shape of fingers. The pinhole stayed dark. Something small and warm crossed it, as breath crosses a mouth.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Black-Flame Lantern[/font_size][/color]
A lamp of the Peak, the gold on its case worn through at the handle. The flame is black, and still I can see the road by it. A brother of the Peak who had been in the valleys on the tenth night handed it to me at the foot of the old water-cut in the thaw, and asked me to hold it while he went up to open the doors. I held it. He did not come down.

He told me whose name it burns. I have never said that name within its hearing. Once at a fire I said another, a woman's, and the flame drew in toward me like a hungry man leaning toward a pot. It is very small now. I carry it carefully, as he did.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Tongueless Bell[/font_size][/color]
A bell the size of a cupped hand, gilded so thick it shows no face, only light. No clapper and nowhere to hang one, no seam and no mark of a mould. The bell-caster found it in the cold ash of his own furnace and swears he never cast it. I gave him more lamp oil than it was worth to him, and he let it go as a man sets down water he has carried a long way.

It stays cold. The Moor ash rides beside it in my bag, and the ash on that side has gone pale. Some nights I wake and the wrapping is warm. It has never rung where I could hear. Each time I find the wrapping warm I have lost something, and I have not yet found out what.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Saint Under Gold[/font_size][/color]
A small gilded figure the length of my forearm, seated, hands open on its knees. Nine such sat on the landings for pilgrims who would climb no higher. I took this one from its landing in the thaw after the fall, because the miasma was coming up the stair and I would not leave it anything.

I wipe its face each morning with a dry cloth. By night I have to wipe it again. Once, with a knife-point, I lifted the gold at the throat. There was more gold under it, and under that something warm. I laid the gold back and pressed it down with my thumbnail until no seam showed.

I have not lifted it again.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Courtyard Glass[/font_size][/color]
A palm-sized piece of dark glass, flat as still water, from the edge of the courtyard where the flags end. It is warm at every hour.

There is one shape in it, very faint, small and on its knees. Wherever on the Hide I take it out of the bag, the shape is facing the Peak. On bad roads I have steered by it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Burnisher of the Beating-House[/font_size][/color]
A finger-long tooth, fixed into a dark wooden haft. The goldbeater put it in my hand when I paid him for the leaf. He would take nothing more for it, and kept his eyes on his bench while I held it.

Nobody on the mountain would say whose teeth they were. I have never pressed gold with it, and the edge goes on wearing down.

pages.title: The Stair, Counted Downward
pages.by: I bought a lamp from her at dusk in a lowland market town and stayed while she put up her shutters, and she talked the whole time. She had been four winters a novice on the Peak. My change came back one copper short. She is right to keep someone beside her, and she still does, though it is not always the same someone when I pass.
pages.bb:
I sell lamps. Clay and brass, wicks of twisted linen, oil by the measure. Down here the miasma lies in the streets each evening, and people buy light like bread.

From the Peak you could see it below us, lying in the valleys like milk in a bowl. We chanted, and it kept to the low places, and the pilgrims thanked us.

Each syllable of the chant is sung on a single breath. You take the syllable as long as your chest allows, and then comes the silence, as long again. Novices counted the silences on their fingers so as to know when to breathe. We were taught the syllables were only fences, and the silences were the prayer. And we were taught never to listen to a silence alone. There was always a shoulder against yours in the hall, always someone breathing beside you. I thought it was kindness.

In my fourth winter I woke in the dormitory in the long silence of the night. Everyone around me lay holding their breath, asleep, all of them, the whole row. So I held mine. And I heard the room the way a room sounds when someone has just come into it and stands by the door. I heard how near. I will say nothing more of that night. I left before the thaw.

My work was the gilding. I beat the leaf between sheets of pressed bark until a breath would lift it, and laid it on bells and lamp-cases. Gold in full noon gives back so much light that the thing beneath it goes away. To be looked upon and unseen: that was holiness.

Only the masters gilded the saints. Novices were let into the inner sanctum at dawn to wipe their faces with a dry cloth, because the dark tracks ran from their eyes each night. By evening the tracks were back. We were told the saints wept for the living, for us, for the valleys. Once I held a loose flake to a saint's cheek for my master, and the flake rose from the gold toward me, a hair's breadth, and settled again. My master said the sanctum has drafts. The sanctum has no window.

They taught us the two hands on our own fingers. Open was the light that leaves nothing to look at; shut was the dark that leaves nothing to hold. Open, shut, a thousand times a day, until my hands did it without me. They still do. Some mornings I wake with my fingers closing.

Twice I went down with a bowl behind my teacher. We asked for names. A woman in this very town whispered her husband's name into it. The next season she sold us bread and asked whom we were praying for. I asked my teacher where the names went. He said, "To the open hand." Then he folded my fingers shut over my palm, and held them there until I stopped asking.

On the stair a teacher walks one step behind and below his novice, so that if the novice falls, she falls into him. His lantern burned black. His own teacher was in it, going out slowly. I climb the ladder to my loft and I still feel him there, one rung down. The night I ran, I went down the stair alone, and that was the first time in four years nobody walked behind me. I counted every step. There were more going down than I had climbed.

A pilgrim told me of the fall at my own counter. The standing dead of the Pale Order had gone up the stair for the bones, and by morning the courtyard was black glass and the sanctum doors stood open. I sold him a lamp and gave him the wrong change. That night I tried to say the names of everyone on the Peak, the whole row in the dormitory. I lost some partway. My teacher's name I had. Each year I have it a little less.

They say there are shapes in the glass, all turned toward the sanctum. I think of where my mat lay.

Now they speak of a barefoot beggar on the lowland roads, with a bowl and a black lantern, who comes at dusk and asks for a name. I close my shutters at dusk. I fear it is my teacher, come down the stair behind me at last. I fear more that it is one of the faces I wiped. And I fear he will stand where you stand now and hold the bowl out, and I will know which name he has come for.

Buy your lamp. Walk carefully. Between one lamp and the next I hold my breath for the length of one syllable, and I keep someone beside me.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [She signed with her fingers across the counter, open and then shut. I have written down what her hand did.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Second Cup
pages.by: I lodged one cold season in the loft over her ovens, and on my last night I wrote this on the back of one of her flour-tallies. That same night I heard her below me laying the table, and counted the cups as they went down, and there were three. I stayed up in the loft.
pages.bb:
They came down at dusk, when the miasma was settling into the lanes. You heard the bells before you saw them: small brass bells, and bare feet on the stones, and no voices. Three or four monks, thin as rakes, the gold on their lamp-cases catching whatever light was left. Children ran indoors. The old women went out with bread, because you fed the monks, whatever else you did.

They never asked for the bread. They held out the bowl, a plain one, black at the lip, and said the one thing they said. Put a name in it.

I had carried mine to the door for a month, the way you carry a stone in your apron. I remember that I was sure. I remember my hands were floury, and that I wiped them first, as if the bowl would mind.

You lean down and whisper into the wood. The name goes into the bowl the way breath goes into a cold morning: you see it, and then you see the morning. The monk laid his palm flat over the bowl, closing it, and bowed, and walked up the lane with the others. A small one walked behind him, a girl, one step down. I watched the bells go up the road until the miasma had them.

Then I went inside, and there were two cups on the table, and I could not think why I had set two.

That was the first night. I stood a long while with the second cup in my hand. It was warm. I drank from it, because it seemed a waste.

The forgetting has no edge. Where a thing is lost you can find the shape of the place it was. This has no shape. It is the gap where a tooth came out, and the tongue goes to it all day, and each time the tongue arrives it is surprised.

The house remembers more than I do.

There are boots by the hearth that come up past my knee. I cannot wear them. I oil them each spring.

There are notches cut in the doorpost with a knife. They climb to the height of my shoulder and then they stop. The lowest is at my knee. The knife is in the drawer. I have never cut a notch.

There is a hollow in the straw of the bed, on the side nearest the door. I sleep in the other side. I turn the straw and by the new moon the hollow is back.

At the table one stool is worn pale where a hand rested on it to rise. My hands rest elsewhere.

I think it was a man. Some mornings I think it was a child. The lamp-seller by the well says it was my husband, and says she knows because she was the girl who walked behind the monk. She told me this across her counter, and would not look at me, and gave me the wrong change. I have no husband. I have a ring I cannot get off over the knuckle.

Whoever it was, I wanted them gone. I remember wanting. The wanting is still here, whole, with nothing in it, like the bowl.

Every season since, I set two cups. I have stopped asking myself why. The second one is always warm.

This year, at the start of the cold, the beggar came. Barefoot, as they were. A shawl the colour of old blood. The bowl. Behind him, a little to one side, a lantern with a black flame, and the lane was lit by it all the same. The monks came in fours. He came alone, and there are no more monks. The Peak is glass.

He held out the bowl and said it. Put a name in the bowl.

I told him I had already given one. He waited. I told him I wanted it back. He waited the way the chant used to wait, the length of a syllable, the length of the silence after it.

I looked into the bowl. The wood was dark, dark past where the bottom should be. And from far down in it something breathed out, slow, the breath of a sleeper on the side of the bed nearest the door. I knew the breath. I knew it the way you know your own stair in the dark.

I shut my door on him. I sat with my back to it until the bells had gone.

I do not know if I was afraid he would take another name, or afraid he would give one back.

The notches are the same. The boots are oiled. Tonight I have set three cups, and I cannot think why.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Two small rings side by side, as on every one of her flour-tallies.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Thin as Breath
pages.by: He mends pots now in a river town in the lowlands, and he did not once set down the hammer while he talked to me. He was never a monk, only the lay man at the foot of the sanctum stair who kept their gold coming. At the end he asks that the barefoot man be given a message. I have not given it, and the barefoot man has not asked me for it.
pages.bb:
I was never a monk. I ate. The monks were light, and I was the weight that kept their gold coming: a lay man in the beating-house at the foot of the sanctum stair, with three hammers, an anvil of the god's own bone, and a stone for a pillow.

You take the gold as the pilgrims give it: rings, teeth, a coin with the face worn off. You melt it and pour it to a bar, roll the bar to a ribbon, and cut the ribbon into squares the size of a thumbnail. Each square goes between two leaves of pressed bark, two hundred squares to a book, and you beat it. Half a day with the heavy hammer. Cut each square in four, and beat again with the middle hammer. Then again with the light one, until the thumbnail is as wide as your palm and a breath will lift it.

Hold good leaf up to the sun and the sun comes through it green. My master said that was the one colour the gold had kept back. I was proud of my green. Mine was the thinnest on the Peak. Laid on a bell, it took the tone into itself and gave the bell no weight.

The rule was Radiance. A gilded thing must be erased by light. In full noon you should look straight at a saint and see a brightness in the shape of a man, and no man. Any seam, any lifted edge, any place where the size shows through, and the eye catches on it, and a face comes back. A face coming back was a fault in the work. I was beaten for one, as a boy. I have made none since.

We laid it on size boiled from sap and ash. Never from bone. Once a Pale Order brother climbed up to buy our size. My master burned the pot after.

Then the burnishing. Each gilder had a burnisher: a tooth set in a handle of black wood, long as a finger and worn smooth as water. Whose teeth they were, nobody said. They were warm in the hand in winter.

For the saints I beat the leaf, and the masters laid it. Every dawn a novice wiped the dark tracks from their faces, and every few seasons the tracks had worn the gold thin at the eyes, and it was laid again. I thought it was the damp.

When old Master Enshō went quiet, they called me up to the sanctum myself. He sat in his niche with his hands open on his knees, in the posture of the open hand. The monks said he had gone into the silence, and I was to lay him while the shape held.

He was warm. I put it down to the lamps.

I laid the brow, and the cheeks, and the lids. The lids were hard, because they were soft. At the mouth I held the leaf out on my card, and it lifted from the card toward his lips, and settled back, and lifted again. A draft, said the monk beside me. I looked at the lamps. Every flame stood straight up.

I laid the mouth. I pressed it with the tooth until the seam was gone. It was the best work I did in my life. At noon the next day I went up to look, and there was only light sitting in the niche, in the shape of a man, and no man.

He wept that night, the same as the others.

What I did after: I went on. I beat leaf for eleven more years. I was good at it.

Only, from that day, into every book I beat I let one leaf go with a flaw, a pinhole small as a hair, at the middle. The masters never found them. At noon the light fills a hole that small. I saw to it that mine went to the saints, and I cut them so the hole fell at the mouth.

I was down in the valley for more gold when the Order climbed the stair. I went back once, as far as the courtyard. From the edge of the glass I saw the sanctum doors standing open, and the niches, gold in the dusk, and one of them empty. I counted from the left three times, and lost the count each time.

Now I beat tin for lamp-cases. It takes a face well. You can see yourself in it.

Leave the pot. Come back tomorrow. And if a barefoot man comes to my door at dusk asking for a name, tell him I have gone to the river. Tell him I did the mouth as thin as I could.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [There is a pinhole in the middle of this leaf, small as a hair. I did not make it.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Bell with No Tongue
pages.by: He was mending pots at a camp beside a ring of stones when I found him, and he would talk for lamp oil and for nothing else. Every pot he picked up he tapped on the rim and listened to before going on. He tried to sell me the little bell, as he has tried with everyone who sits down near him. I paid what he asked.
pages.bb:
Thirty years I cast for the Gold Bell. The Kinrei-shū, if you want their word for it. I had the pit and the furnace at the foot of the stair, where the clay is good and grey, and every spring a monk came down with a wax model and a bowl of gold leaf and one syllable.

That was the order. One syllable to a bell. Ah, or Hu, or a sound with no letter for it that the monk would sing me once, low, and I would carry it in my chest for a month while the mould dried. You tune a bell by shaving the inside, a curl of bronze at a time, strike and shave, strike and shave, until it says the one thing and nothing after. My father cast for them before me. He said a Peak bell had to die quick. Other bells hum a long while after the stroke. The monks wanted the hum shaved out of it. One stroke, a clean word, and then quiet all the way to the edges of the valley.

They rang each bell once a day. Once. Then they sat and listened to the silence it left, and the silence was the thing they wanted. The bell was only there to make it longer. I asked a monk once why he did not simply sit in the quiet without the bell. He looked at me as a man looks at a child who asks why we eat. Then he said you need a door to know you are in a room.

Here is the thing I cannot set down. The one time they let me up the stair, it was to hang the great bell in the courtyard. Nine men and a rope. When she was hung the old master put the striking beam in my hands, as an honour, and I swung it with my whole back. I felt her take the blow. I felt her shiver up through the beam into my teeth. The courtyard gave back nothing. No stroke, no hum. The monks all breathed out at once, pleased, the way men breathe out when bread comes from the oven right. I stood there with the beam in my hands and my ears ringing with nothing. Down at my furnace, a long walk under, my wife heard her. She said it was the sweetest bell I ever made. She said it rang a long while.

The last bell they asked of me had no clapper. No tongue, no ring for a tongue to hang from. Tall and narrow, the mouth just so wide. The monk brought the size of the mouth on a cord, and I did not like the width of it. It was the width of shoulders. When the bronze was ready he came to the furnace with his bowl and held it over the crucible and tipped it. Nothing fell out that I saw. The pour weighed more than the metal. I weighed it twice. My father's scales, and they had never lied to me.

I did not tune that one. They told me not to. They said it already knew its syllable.

They carried it up gilded, and a year after, the dead went up the stair. You know that story. Glass in the courtyard. The doors open.

I let the furnace go cold after. Nobody wanted bells. Fourteen years it stood. Then one winter I raked the old ash to use for mould-clay, and there was a bell in it. Small as a cupped hand. Seamless. No sprue, no mark where any mould had closed. Gilded so thick I could not see my face in it, only light. And cold. In the ash, it was cold, and the ash round it was warm.

I did not cast it. I know every bell I cast. I know them the way you know your children's coughs.

It has no clapper. I have kept it wrapped in felt under my bench. Some nights, at the hour the Peak kept its long silence, I wake, and the whole camp is holding its breath in its sleep, and the felt is warm. I have never heard it ring. I only know when it has, because after, for a while, I cannot remember my wife's name, and then I can.

Tap the pot. Listen. That one's sound. That one is cracked; you hear it keep talking after. A good bell says its word and goes quiet.

I would sell you the little one. I have tried to sell it before. Nobody will take it, and I cannot say why I keep asking.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [His founder's mark, pressed into the leaf with a nail: the mouth of a bell, and inside it one syllable he would not sound for me.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Inquiry into the Bowls of the Gilded Peak
pages.by: His nephew sold me this draft out of the magistrate's effects, and could not read it himself for the white places. The gaps are the magistrate's own, and they have spread since I bought it; the space he left for his name at the foot is whiter than the paper round it and a little wider than on the night I first unfolded it. I have met the clerk he could not name. The clerk remembers him well.
pages.bb:
To the justices of the assize at ————, by their magistrate, in the matter of the bowls.

I was charged to inquire whether the monks of the Gilded Peak, begging under the mountain, do injury that may be brought before a court. I took depositions in four parishes over one winter.

[b]First. The parish books.[/b] Deposition of the clerk of Lower Stair, sworn. He keeps the book of births, marriages and burials. He showed me a burial entered whole: the date, the fee, the grave by the east wall. Where the name should stand there is a clean space. The paper there is whiter than the page around it, as paper is before a pen touches it. Asked whose grave lies by the east wall, he said a good one, well kept. Asked who keeps it, he said he does. Asked why, he wept, and could not say for what.

I counted the clean spaces in his book: thirty-one. On the second morning I counted thirty-three. The book is kept locked. I believe him.

[b]Second. The debts.[/b] Deposition of a moneylender of the river parish. She holds forty notes, witnessed, under her own seal. On each, the sum is whole, and the debtor's name is whole. The debtors swear they never borrowed. She does not remember lending. They pay all the same, each quarter day, leaving the coin on the sill of her back room. They sleep badly until it is done. The coin is gone by morning. The room is locked and she holds the one key. I sat a night in that room with a candle, awake. In the morning the sill was bare.

[b]Third. The killing.[/b] At the crossing in Harrow Lane, in autumn, a man was opened with a hay-knife before eleven witnesses at market. I took eleven depositions. All agree on the knife, the hour, the killer's brown coat, that he wiped the blade on his sleeve and walked home. All say he is known to them. None can give his name. Three pointed to the same door.

I went to that door. A man opened it, a plain man with a plain face. I asked his name. He gave it at once. I wrote it down. The page shows a clean space. I have asked him four times since, and have four clean spaces. He was civil each time. The court cannot try a man it cannot name, and I record that as the law stands.

The widow deposes that her husband put a name into the bowl in the spring. She does not know whose. She says he came home lighter, and sat by the door all summer, facing the lane.

[b]Fourth. The town.[/b] For the winter past, the town of ———— had no name. Letters addressed to it came back to the posting-house sealed. The bearers swore they had walked the road to its end and found a town there, with smoke and a bell, and could not match it to the letters in their hands. The people baked and buried. Asked where they lived, they said here. The priest rang the morning bell and said it rang short, one stroke under. At the first thaw the name came back, whole, and nobody could say from where.

A monk had come down at the start of that winter, with the bowl, and a small one walking behind him. The priest says a child of the town leaned over the bowl. The child laughs when asked what it said, and the laugh is dry.

[b]Of the magistrate.[/b] The law requires a witness who is also the inquirer to set down what bears on his own credit.

My clerk has kept these papers with me all winter. His board is entered in my book of expenses at a rate I agreed. His name is not entered.

In my own diary, in the ninth month, stands one line in my hand: [i]At dusk, at my door. Gave it.[/i] I have no ninth month. I have the diary.

I have sealed this report. My ring is cut with two letters. By lamp and by noon, I cannot read them.

[b]Finding.[/b] No injury can be brought before the court, for want of names. I find the lowlands quieter. I find that the clean spaces are whiter than the page, and that the whiteness is spreading at the edges, a hair each week, toward the words beside them. I recommend that nothing be done. I recommend that the monks be fed.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Your magistrate, ————[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Report of the Count Taken on the Gilded Peak
pages.by: The Order's scribe sent this up to his Warden in the season after the Peak fell, and it was bound among the niche-tallies. A sweeper copied it out without leave, and his copy is the one I had. The scribe asks at the end to be told his own name. I have looked in the Order's book where it is kept, and his number stands there, whole.
pages.bb:
To the Warden of the Ossuary of Nine Stairs, from the scribe of the fourth chapter, sent up the Gilded Peak to count.

[b]The stair.[/b] One thousand and ninety risers from the lowest gate to the courtyard, cut into the knee of the Mother. Gold leaf on every seventh riser, worn through by bare feet. I counted going up and I counted coming down, and the two numbers agree. I record this because it is the only count in this letter that does.

[b]The courtyard.[/b] Where the flagstones lay there is glass, black and smooth, flat as water in a bowl. It is warm under the hand, by noon and by night. I walked it heel to toe: forty-one paces across, forty-one deep.

In the glass are shapes, faint, as a face is faint in a dark window. They lie at every depth. All of them are turned toward the sanctum doors. Some stand. Some kneel. Our dead do not kneel, Warden, and I set that down without knowing what to do with it.

I counted the shapes twice. The first count was two hundred and six. The second was two hundred and nine. On the third morning I did not count them.

[b]The standing dead.[/b] The chapter sent up two hundred and six, anointed joint by joint, as written in your own hand. None came down. There is no bone on the stair, in the courtyard or in the dormitories. I found the shapes in the glass, if they are ours. The three I cannot account for I have left out of the book, as we leave out the Mother's gift. I do not know whose gift they are.

[b]The inner sanctum.[/b] The doors stand open, each leaf the height of three men. Words are scratched into the right-hand leaf. You have them from my first letter. I will not write them twice.

The saints stand in niches round the walls, as our dead stand, all facing the doors. They are gilded to the fingernail. No face can be seen under the gold at any hour. I tried them all. From the eyes of each run dark tracks down the leaf to the chin. I wiped one with my cloth. By morning the track was back, and wet. I have looked at that word a long while, and let it stand.

[b]The count of saints.[/b] The Peak's own tally, cut in gold across the lintel, gives one hundred and eight. I count one hundred and seven niches filled, and one empty. There is gold dust on the ledge of the empty niche, and no other dust. Warden, you know I have never found a niche without dust. From the empty niche to the doors there are marks in the gold on the floor. The chaplain says a thief. The marks are of bare feet, and they go one way.

I counted the saints twice more and had one hundred and seven each time, and on the last count I had the sense of someone counting with me, half a breath behind, as a teacher of the Peak walks one step behind on the stair. I stopped at a number I no longer have.

[b]The lamps.[/b] Beneath each niche hangs a lamp of the Peak on an iron hook. Every one is dark. The wicks are whole and the oil stands full. A lamp of ours goes out when its oil is spent. These went out full. The chaplain says such a lamp goes dark when the last of the name it burns is gone. I count one hundred and seven lamps. Beneath the empty niche, the hook is bare.

[b]What I heard.[/b] On the third night I sat alone in the sanctum with a lamp of our own. The miasma stands a third of the way up the stair now, flat as the glass.

Warden, I heard a breath drawn in. One long breath, from all round the walls, from every niche at once, drawn the way the Peak's novices drew it, they say, before the syllable. No syllable came. Then silence, as long again. Then the breath again.

I counted the silences as I was taught to count a wall. I cannot give you the number. Each time I set it down it is a different number, like the old lines under the Ninth Stair. And in each silence there was a small sound, dry, as of gold leaf lifting a hair's breadth from a face, toward me.

I have written that the chapter sent up two hundred and six. I ask you to check it against your book. I find I have it only from this letter.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Your scribe of the fourth chapter, whose name you have. I ask that you write it back to me.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Letter from the Last Abbot
pages.by: The youngest of them brought this down the old water-cut before the dead climbed, and gave it to a priest in the lowlands, who kept it folded in a wooden bowl worn black at the lip. Two winters after the fall I bought the bowl and the letter together for bread and salt. I think I know who the youngest was. She has one place in this book already, and I will not give her a second.
pages.bb:
To the brothers who are below with their bowls, and to whichever of you comes up the stair first when it is over.

The Order's dead have stood at the foot of the mountain for nine days. In the long silences we hear them counting, a sound like beads told on a cord. On the tenth day, I think, they will climb. I send this down with the youngest of us. She is light, and quick on the old water-cut. Feed her. Do not send her back up.

Hear it once more, as I said it to each of you when you came to us with your hair still on.

The Hush is the god's rest. For an age the god held a space open in it, and held us inside that space, and it grew tired. The Hush came in to let it lie down. Everything on the Hide is a wound that has not yet been allowed to close. We are wounds too. We have tried to be clean ones.

The Hush has two hands, and both are empty. Radiance, the open hand, erases by light: noon with no shadow, gold in full sun, a face looked upon until no one can say what it was. Absence, the closed hand, erases by dark: the palm that swallows, the gate shut over the sun. Neither hand keeps anything. So we keep nothing. A bowl, a robe, in time a lantern. You learned the hands on your own fingers. Do it now. Open. Shut.

The chant is one breath. The syllable is a fence, and the silence is the field it marks. The valleys believe the syllable holds the miasma off our slopes, and they feed us for it, and I have let them believe it for forty years. I told you the silences are the prayer. I will add one thing now, since there is no time left for it to harm you. This year the silences have grown longer, and I have shortened nothing. The whole hall waits together for a syllable that is slow to come. Wherever you are, keep a shoulder against a brother's when you chant. Keep it there.

The names. Every name you carried up in your bowls I gave to the open hand, at noon, over the lip of the east stone. I kept no tally; tallies belong to the Pale Order, and they may keep them. Yet I will set down this much. An empty bowl should weigh what its wood weighs. Ours have grown heavier. I asked the open hand whether it forgets the names or holds them. The hand stayed open, and empty, and that was the whole of its answer.

You will be asked why we did not fight. Say this. The Order believes we gave their Mother's bones to nothing, and they are right. They believe a bone out of its place is a wound in the world. We believe a bone kept in its place is a wound held open. Both houses have told the truth, and so there will be blood on the stair. My brothers are too light to strike, and I would forbid it if they were strong. A blow is a name shouted. We have spent our lives unlearning how to shout. When the dead come, we will be in the hall, one breath each, and when each breath ends we will let the silence go on. They will cut us down and raise us before we touch the flags. That is their mercy. Let them have it. I am giving my name away.

My teacher's lantern is nearly out. There is a little of him left in it, a syllable or two. I will carry it into the hall. If it goes dark before they reach the top step, I will take that as leave.

Now the last thing, and I ask you to do it without asking me why.

When the stair is quiet, the first of you up must go to the inner sanctum before you look for me. Open the sanctum doors. Both of them, wide, and set a stone against each. Do not wipe the faces that morning. Do not count them. Do not stand in the doorway; stand to one side, with your back to the wall, and your eyes on your own open palm. Wait there until noon. Then take your bowl and go down, and ask for names as you were taught.

If someone walks with you on the stair, one step behind, where a teacher walks, let him. You were always my best at the bowl.

Open. Shut.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the abbot, who is giving his name away; written at the hour of the long silence, with the gold for the sanctum still unmixed on the table[/color][/i][/right]

name: The Polished Heart
sub: of the lodge at the head of the cold lakes, and the winter its dead came home

pages.title: The Polished Heart
pages.by: of the lodge at the head of the cold lakes, and the winter its dead came home
pages.epi: Every soul is a thread. I only hold the end of it up to the light, so it can see where it goes.
pages.bb:
If there is a glass in the room with you, leave it as it is. Do not cover it for my sake, and do not uncover it. By the end of this chapter you will have an opinion about it, and an opinion is all that valley has left to give anyone.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The valley of cold lakes[/color][/font_size]
The spinning-woman under An-Vhar who gave me the Soul's name told me where to go for the rest of it. Down, she said, and west, to where the Old Spinner's threads come up through the skin like roots through a path. She wound the loose end of her yarn round my finger before she let me go, and I walked with it on for nine days because I did not like to take it off.

The valley is long and narrow, with a chain of lakes down its floor, each colder than the one above it. In winter, when the lakes skin over, you can see the threads a hand's depth down in the ice: pale, lying every way at once, like hairs caught in wax. I lay on my belly on the third lake one noon and tried to follow a single strand with my eye. I lost it under my own reflection. When I stood up there was a white mark on the ice where my breath had been, shaped like a mouth, and it did not fade until dusk.

The dye-women of the Lower Reach would not rinse cloth in that water. You could not tell afterwards, they said, which threads were your own.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]A guest in the ring[/color][/font_size]
The lodge stood at the head of the valley, where the strands in the ice lie thickest. It stands still, if walls are standing. Grey felt blows about the yard.

I sat in their circle once, years before the end, at the outer edge where they put guests. A keeper began the names and they went round from mouth to mouth. I will not give them to you in order; the circle-keeper does that, below, and he kept that office far longer than I kept my place. What it was to sit there, I can say. Somewhere after midnight I noticed my own mouth moving with the rest and could not remember having started. By the grey hour I could not have said where the ring ended and I began, and I did not mind, and that frightened me more afterwards than anything I heard in that valley.

A boy with grey hands brought round the water at dawn. He did not look at any of the glass in the yard. He looked at me, for longer than a boy should look at a guest, and then went on with the jug.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What the lodge sold[/color][/font_size]
Every house in the valley paid the lodge for felt and ash and one lesson, and I have watched the lesson kept in a dozen houses of the dead. The women moved from room to room with the grey cloths over their arms, fast, without talking, the way you close shutters before a storm. The lodge's people believed it. The valley believed it. I believed it for as long as I was in the valley, and I have covered glass myself, in a house where a man died with nobody else to do it.

The mirror-maker gives you the trade from the grinding side. He was honest. He says he believed the lesson the way he believed quicksilver runs downhill. I have never found a better way to say it, and I have tried.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The loose winter[/color][/font_size]
It came when the ice first held at the ford, in 1106 by the Ashwake reckoning, three nights past the new moon. I was on the hill above the lodge when the runners came up from the Reach. I had come to buy felt. I stayed forty nights.

What the Pir did in those nights you have twice over below: from the man who kept the ring round her, and from her own leaves. I leave them to each other. I will only say that on the last night I was near enough to hear the ring stop, all at once, as a mill stops when the race is shut, and that the quiet afterwards was the quiet of a room where somebody has just understood something.

The dead came home that night. I saw them come. There was no walking in it. The lane held frost and ash, and then it held them. They went to the doors. The valley sent them up to the lodge, and walked behind them. I did not walk behind. I stood on the hill, where I could see the whole yard, and so I saw the felt come off the coat, and heard the dead draw breath at the glass as a congregation draws breath before it sings.

One of them did not stop. The flax-beater tells of her, the blind one. She passed out of the yard where there was no gate and climbed toward me in the dark. She asked me the way. I answered her. I will not write what I said.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What he carries now[/color][/font_size]
The boy with grey hands kept every one of them. They go about him small and pale, trailing their threads. The valley calls him Needle-Brother. I call him the Polisher still, because that was his name when he brought me water.

He hung the coat back on its post and asked the dead into the iron, and it stood up off the post as a knight twice his height, with a lamp burning where the heart-glass had been. I watched that knight taken apart at the knees in the Hollow Wood by things that came out of the ground, and I watched the lamp in its breast draw down to a bead. By morning it stood at his shoulder again, whole. He told me he had not mended it. I believe him. The glass keeps its own count.

For the rest, he sells one thing, which is a little time. A widow of the upper valley tells you how he does it. I have watched him do it three times and I have nothing to add to her, except that each time, before he began, he looked at the covered glass in the room for a while, as though he were asking its leave.

I sat at a fire with him in the Barrens a winter ago. I asked him whether he was sorry. He watched the lights go round him for a long time and said, "The villages still bring me their dead. I keep them." I took it then for half an answer. I have since decided it was the whole of one.

I know something of where the long way went, the way the lodge sent every covered thread for a thousand years. I have walked a good distance down it. I stopped. I did not stop because I reached an end.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Leaves out of the valley[/color][/font_size]
Six works follow. Three reached me through the Pale Order, who sent copyists up the valley after the loose winter to count what the lodge had left, and found almost no bone to count. The other three I had from a tinker, a hiring fair and a fire in the Barrens. I have taken no side in that valley, which is why both halves of it still sell me felt.

When you have read them, look at the glass in your room, if there is one, and decide.


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]From the valley of cold lakes. Do not set any of them facing you while you sleep.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Covering Cloth[/font_size][/color]
A square of grey felt the size of a hand-glass, darkened with ash at the edges, with a dent in one corner where a stone sat on it. It came to me in the box from the fair, with the thread-reader's leaf folded inside it.

It has been laid over a glass once, on a night when nobody in the house had died. The Polisher keeps the felt he pulled from the coat folded small in his own coat, and has never used it. I keep this one folded the other way from his.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Mourner's Needle[/font_size][/color]
A steel needle as long as a forearm, threaded with something pale that is nearly light. The Polisher carries three. He gave me this one at the fire in the Barrens and would not say what for.

The thread has never run short, and nobody has wound more onto it. At night, if I lie close to the bag, I hear it hum, faintly, as a string hums in a wind that is not blowing.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Pir's Mirror[/font_size][/color]
One of the small hollowed rounds from the Pir's coat, rimmed in black iron, with a thumb-print pressed into the wax on its back. It fell from the coat's shoulder on the first night the iron stood up, and the Polisher let me keep it.

Look into it and you see your face, then a face behind yours, then another behind that. The last face in every round of that coat is turned away. When I count, I begin at the second.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Polishing Felt[/font_size][/color]
A pad of grey felt worn through in the middle, stiff with ash and a little blood. I picked it out of the yard where the felt blows about.

It is worn in the shape of a hand, and the hand is smaller than the Polisher's is now. The circle-keeper knew at once whose it was. I offered it to him. He would not touch it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Heel of a Loaf[/font_size][/color]
The heel of a small dark loaf, hard as a whetstone, with a thumb pressed deep into the crumb. It has been in my bag a long time.

In that valley a woman presses her thumb into bread she hands to someone she fears for. I have not eaten it. Some mornings it is warm on the thumbed side. The apprentice's leaf tells as much as I will about how it came to me.

pages.title: The Names Said Over
pages.by: A copyist of the Pale Order, sent up to count whatever bone the lodge had left, sat with the old keeper in the empty yard and wrote this; the whole while, he says, the keeper polished a little round mirror and never once looked into it. The copyist's abbot would not shelve a leaf with no count in it, so it came to me at the gate of the Ossa for a candle. I was in that yard again last thaw. The felt lay folded by the glass, and the glass was brighter than before.
pages.bb:
Sit, if you are staying. Sit in the ring. The stones are worn where the knees went. Forty-one of us, and the Pir in the middle, and the names going round.

I kept the circle. That was my office. I laid the felt, I lit the one candle, I began the first name and I ended the last. Veiled Crone. Spindle. Weaver. Tangle. Knot. You say them down the ring, mouth to mouth, until they come back to you from the far side and you cannot tell whose mouth they left. We sat so from dusk to the grey hour. By then no one is sitting. There is only the saying. That was the teaching: say her long enough, and remembering and the self become one thread.

She has four faces. The Spinner draws you out. The Weaver sets you in the cloth. The Unraveller takes you out again when your length is done. And the Hollow. The Hollow is the eye of the loom, the empty place in the middle of the weave, where the pattern shows through. Every Tithed life goes back through that eye at the end, and is woven again. I have said it at more beds than I have years.

Our work was the glass. A dying thread gets lost; it wants to see where it goes. So we polished. Felt and ash, one of her names to every stroke, until the glass gave back the pattern and the thread could read its way. Then, at the death, cover every mirror. Grey felt, a stone on the corner. A soul that meets its own face stops to look. Covered, it goes on by, through the eye, into the cloth.

The Pir's Coat hung on its post by the door. Iron and small round mirrors, every Pir before her sewing on more, until it weighed what two men weigh. The foundling polished it. Twenty years, that boy. Quiet. Good hands. I gave him his first felt.

Then the winter. A whole valley came loose at once. We felt it in the circle before the runners came: the names went round and came back short, as though someone in the ring had stopped saying them. Nobody had.

The Pir put on the coat. She sat in the middle and looked into the Hollow, and we said the names around her for forty nights. I kept the count. I kept it right. On the fortieth she spoke. I will give it to you as she gave it, and I will not help you with it.

[i]"There is no loom. It goes on and on, and it never finishes."[/i]

Then her hands opened, and whatever she was holding ran out of them, and she was lighter than the coat.

I turn those words over every night. A loom has an end. A cloth comes off it and is folded. If the cloth never comes off, then all those beds, all that felt over all that glass, so they would pass. Pass into where. There. You see. That is the thing I cannot say in the ring, so I say it in the yard, to a stranger, with the candle out.

The dead came home that winter. They stood in the doorways asking which way. And the boy took the cloth off the coat. Every mirror at once. Each of them met its own face, and stopped.

He broke the first rule of the house. He kept them. He keeps them still, going round and round him the way we went round the Pir, each with its thread hanging loose behind. The villages pay him for it. They call him Needle-Brother, and their mirrors are turned about when he goes by.

I say he is a thief of the dead. I say it every morning, with the first name. He took them off her road and hung them on himself like beads.

And I say, at night, with the last name: he was the only one of us who heard her and did not cover it.

Perhaps the Pir saw wrong. Forty nights is long. The lodge counted forty-one faces in her mirror. She counted more.

This is one of them. I polish it. One of her names to every stroke. Some nights I count forty-one, one for each of us who sat in the ring. Some nights I lose the count, and there is one more at the back, very small, and it has my face, and it is waiting to see whether I will cover it.

I keep the felt beside it. I have not decided.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [He gave the copyist his office in place of a name and asked to have it written large: KEEPER OF THE CIRCLE.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Grinder's Slates
pages.by: A tinker bought a crate of broken glass for the tin in it, and these slates were at the bottom; he let me have them because they were no use to him. The grinder writes of a man in a grey hood who came at dusk and asked for a large glass. It was a small glass that man asked for. I would know.
pages.bb:
Every mirror on the Pir's Coat came off my wheel, or my father's wheel, or his father's. Set that down first, so whoever reads this knows whose hands these were.

[b]The glass.[/b] Green glass from the furnace-town, the one pane in six without a seed in it. Cut the round with the wheel and the tooth. Grind on the stone with water and grit, coarse, then fine, then finer, until the thumb finds nothing. Then pitch and rouge, and the long hours. The lodge wanted every glass hollowed a little, a dish as shallow as a cupped palm. My father said a flat glass hands you back and a hollowed one draws you in. I have ground four hundred and some. I believe him.

[b]The silver.[/b] Tin beaten thin as a fingernail paring, laid on the slab. Quicksilver poured on and worked in with a rag until the leaf goes bright and soft. Slide the glass over, weight it, tilt it, and leave it nine days to weep off what it does not want. The lodge had me seal every back with ash-wax, and the Pir pressed her thumb into the wax before it set.

[b]The orders.[/b] A slate came down each spring: so many rounds, of such a width, and one of the Crone's names to be said at each turn of the wheel. I said them. A customer who pays for a word over the work gets the word. Pitch, rouge, Spinner. Pitch, rouge, Weaver. You lose count of the names long before you lose count of the turns.

Each spring the slate asked for more rounds than the spring before. I thought the lodge was growing. The lodge stayed the size it was. The Coat grew.

[b]The rule.[/b] They taught every house in the valley: a soul going out halts before its own face. Cover the glass, and the dead pass on, down through the eye of the loom, to be woven again. I believed it as I believe quicksilver runs downhill. The lodge folk were the ones who had looked.

I keep one question on this slate, so it stays out of my mouth. What does a dead man see, passing, in a hollowed glass, sewn on the breast of a woman who is staring into the Hollow?

[b]The last order.[/b] Autumn, the year the valley came loose. Seven small rounds, and one great round for the heart, a hand across. The slate said: deeper than any before. I ground it eleven weeks. The Pir came down for it herself. She held it to her breast, over the coat, and said it would do. Then she said, [i]Grind no more for us[/i], and paid me for three years.

They say a lamp burns now where my heart-glass was sewn. Nobody has brought the glass back. I would know it by its weight in the hand.

[b]What they ask for now.[/b] Since the Needle-Brother walks the lanes, the valley turns its glass to the wall. So I make backs. Boards on hinges. Felt lids sewn to fit. A carter paid for a glass that shows nothing; I frosted him one with sand, and he went home glad. The widow from the upper valley wanted one hollowed the lodge way, to stand on her sill facing the lane. I made it true and charged her half.

A man in a grey hood came at dusk and asked for a large glass. I hold up the test-glass for every buyer, and I held it up for him. It gave me the shelves, the door, the lamp on the hook. He thanked me and asked the price. I told him it was spoken for. I sweep the grit off the floor each night, and that night there was nothing in it to sweep.

[b]The faces.[/b] A glass ground true gives one face. I know my trade. Still, when the lamp is low and the silver has only just set, I see my own face, then one behind it, then one behind that. My father counted three in his, and called it the depth of the glass doubling back. I counted nine in the spring. In the last round I finished, the one the lodge never sent for, I counted till the lamp went out.

They wait behind me, turned the way I turn, all waiting to be asked which way.

I have hung a cloth over it. Tonight I heard the cloth move, the small sound felt makes against glass when something on the far side draws near to read it.

I left it covered. Tomorrow I will lift it and count again.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [His shop-mark, scratched in the corner of every slate: a little circle, hollowed, as the lodge liked them.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Stitch at the Throat
pages.by: The second of the Order's copyists came to her door for her husband's bones, and went home with this instead. I have stood in her lane since, on a day the Polisher came through. The small light that keeps low at his shoulder still ducks its head at every doorway, though there is room enough.
pages.bb:
When Oswy died I covered the mirrors. Everyone does. My mother did it for my father: grey felt over the glass, a stone on the corner so the cloth won't slip.
