The lodge folk taught us that, back when the House of the Polished Heart still stood up the valley and sent its people down with their felt and their ash. They said a soul going out must never see itself, or it will stop to look. So you cover the glass, and the dead go on by.

I had felt on the little mirror, on the water pail, on the window, because a window at night gives your face back. I sat with him three days. On the third day I could not bear it.

The Needle-Brother came at dusk. You know him by the sound first. Small glass knocking on small glass, all down his coat, like a cupboard of cups when a cart goes by. Then the lights. Then him, long and grey in the doorway, with his lantern hanging in the air at his shoulder and no hand holding it.

I paid him the salt and the good knife. He asked for nothing. He took them.

He looked at the covered mirrors before he looked at Oswy, one and then the next, the way a man counts doors. Then he sat on the floor by the bed, as the lodge folk sat in their circles, and said a name I did not know, and another, very low, over and over, until I lost the count.

The needle is as long as my forearm. The thread is pale. I would call it light, if light could be knotted. He put one stitch through the cuff of Oswy's sleeve and drew it to the bedpost. Then he put the needle in at the throat, just under the jaw, where Oswy used to hum, and pulled it close, and tied it.

That is all it is. A stitch at the throat.

He was kept forty days. I know what your brothers say of it, so I will say it plain. He never got up. He never ate. But the room stayed warm around him, and his hand stayed a hand when I held it, and at night, if I lay close, I could hear the thread: a small sound, like a string in a wind that isn't blowing. I talked to him. I told him about the roof and the price of lamp oil. Once, near the end, he turned his face toward the covered window, and I almost pulled the cloth. I left it.

On the forty-first morning the knot hung loose and he was cold as the floor, and I knew. I washed him. I laid him in the barrow, under a lid dished in like all the others. I was grateful. I am grateful still. I want that set down.

This next part I have told nobody but my sister, and she told me to hold my tongue.

The Needle-Brother came back through the valley at harvest. Half the village turns its glass to the wall when he passes; the other half comes out to look. I went up the lane. The wisps go round him the way sparks go round a fire, pale, each with a little tail of thread behind it. Some say they sing. I would call it asking.

I counted them. I have counted loaves all my life, and I count well. I counted twice. There were more than in the spring. More than our valley has graves.

One of them kept low, near his shoulder, and every little while it dipped, the way Oswy ducked his head under our lintel, though the lintel was high enough and he knew it. Its thread was short, and hung in a loop, tied off.

I said his name. Very quietly. The wisp stopped. I can't tell you how a light turns, but it turned, toward the Needle-Brother's coat, where all the little mirrors are, and it stayed there, looking.

The Needle-Brother looked at me then. I have thought about his face a long while. He looked like a man who has been asked the way and has no answer, and is too kind to say so.

The lodge up the valley is empty now. Felt blows about the yard. The old women say its people used to send the dead on, through the eye of something, to be woven again. They say the Needle-Brother is the one who stopped sending. The old women don't say why.

I took the felt off the little mirror. It stands on the sill by the door, facing the lane. If Oswy comes home asking which way, I want him to stop here.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Oswy's wife, of the upper valley [she would not let the copyist write widow][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: A Reading Left Unfinished
pages.by: At a hiring fair I bought a whole box of felt oddments for the sake of one grey covering cloth, and this leaf was folded in the cloth. Mother Ysolt's apprentice wrote it in the last autumn the lodge kept its doors open, and the words in brackets are the apprentice's. The word the apprentice missed is a true name of the Crone. I know it, and it is the one name of hers I have written nowhere.
pages.bb:
[The stranger came to the lower door after the grey hour, with ash dried on both knees. Mother Ysolt took the coin before she looked at the face, as the custom is. She set the reading-glass on the felt between them, face down, and I lit the one candle. What follows is what she said, as near as my hand could keep it.]

Sit where the felt is worn. Hands flat, one on each side of the glass. Leave the glass to me. It is mine until I turn it.

Felt. Ash. [i]Spinner.[/i]

Felt. Ash. [i]Weaver.[/i]

[She went round the names. Grandmother Spindle, Knot, Tangle, Unraveller, and the last with her mouth shut, as the Hollow is said. Most readings take three rounds. She took eleven. The stranger kept still the whole while, which the frightened ones never do.]

There. Now it will hold a face. Look at your own, only a moment, then look past it. Do you see the thread? You will not. I see it. That is what the coin is for.

You were born twice. Once in a house with its door to the ash, once on a road. One of those is a thing your mother told you. I cannot see which. Let it lie.

A woman gave you bread with her thumb pressed in the middle. You had a fever in a cold month and a name you were called until the fever broke, and then another name. Your hands have smelled of iron since before they were big enough to hold it. You have been kind more often than you remember. You remember the other times. Everyone does.

You have killed. That is in most threads that come to this door. Here, and here. And here, the same one again. Hm.

[She stopped polishing. She held the felt still on the glass while the names could have gone once round.]

You walk into the stone rings. At the ring the thread goes dark, and a way off it takes up again, and between is nothing to read. The Crone allows it. She has never said she likes it. Yours goes dark at the rings more than any thread I have held. Most pilgrims fray a little each time. Yours comes out whole. Heavier, I would say, if a thread could be weighed.

Now the Unraveller's face. She comes to every thread. She is gentle with the ones who hold still.

I see a road going inward. Warm. Everything is warm there. You carry a lamp, and nobody walks behind you. You go down a long way, one way, and there she is, waiting at the end with her hand open, and you give it to her. The thread goes into her hand.

And comes out of it.

[Here Mother Ysolt turned the glass a quarter on the felt, and turned it back.]

It comes out the far side of her hand and goes on. I have never seen her let go of one. Perhaps I read wrong. The candle is low.

Give me your left hand. Palm up.

Here, near the start. A knot. Before the Spinner's fingers, before the house and the road. Every thread I have read begins clean, drawn fresh from her. Yours begins in a knot, and the knot is older than the thread. It is tied to something that goes back out of the glass, past the edge, where there is nothing for me to see by.

Nobody in this house ties knots. The Crone weaves. Who tied you?

[The stranger answered. I did not catch the word. Mother Ysolt did.]

No.

Take your coin back. Take it. I am covering the glass.

[She put the grey felt over it and set the stone on the corner, the way we do for the dead, although nobody had died.]

I will read no further for you. The rest is yours, and I would rather not carry it. Do not come to this lodge again. There is nothing wrong with you. Go on.

Wait. Here.

[She gave the stranger the heel of the loaf from the shelf. She pressed her thumb into the middle of it first. I have never seen her do that for anyone.]

[When the stranger had gone she sat a long time with her hand on the cloth. She did not lift it that night or after. She had me carry the covered glass up to the Pir in the morning, and the Pir kept it. That was the autumn the Pir sent to the grinder for the great heart-glass.

I asked Mother Ysolt what the word had been. She said it was one of the Crone's names. I have said them all my life. I have never heard it.]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Brin, apprentice, who holds the candle and never the glass[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Leaves from the Lining
pages.by: These were sewn into the lining of the coat behind the place where the heart-glass hung, and the Polisher unpicked them with his own hands. One night by a fire out on the Barrens he had me read them to him aloud, though I believe he knew every line, and one of the forty nights he asked for twice. I copied them while he listened, gave them back, and watched him stitch them into the coat he wears. The nights are numbered in her hand, and her hand grows lighter as it goes.
pages.bb:
[b]The first night of the loose winter.[/b] Veiled Crone. Weaver. Grandmother Spindle. Knot. Tangle. The felt is laid and the one candle lit. Forty-one in the ring. The coat weighs what a second body weighs. The runners say the whole of the Lower Reach came loose between one frost and the next: the old, the young, the women at the dye-vats. I go down to look for their threads.

[b]Second night.[/b] Found them. They hang out of the Hollow like the ends of a cut hem, pale, stirring a little. Each waits at the eye to be taken up. Nothing takes them up.

[b]Fourth night.[/b] I follow one down. A dyer of the Reach; her thread is blue where her hands were. Down through the glass, down past her death, and still it runs on. I lost her behind the heart-glass, where the dark is deepest.

[b]Seventh night.[/b] The names come back to me short. The keeper counts right; I asked him. Some mouth in the ring has stopped saying them, and all forty-one mouths still move.

[b]Ninth night.[/b] I look for the beam. For the frame, the treadle, the hand on the shuttle. A loom has sides. I find threads crossing threads, and threads behind those, and a pattern that is nearly a face, and behind that face another face.

[b]Twelfth night.[/b] The boy brings water and keeps his eyes off the coat. He polished every glass on it. He knows what they do. Good hands.

[b]Fifteenth night.[/b] Faces in the deepest round: forty-one, one for each of the ring. That is the lodge's count. I set it down for them. Then forty-two. I have said nothing to the keeper.

[b]Nineteenth night.[/b] The Reach was a cloth. Dyer knotted to carter, carter to child, the whole valley one weave. The knots are opening now, slowly, the way a sleeper's fingers open.

[b]Twenty-second night.[/b] Four hundred beds I have sat at. Four hundred times I said it: drawn back through the eye, and woven again. Tonight one of our own dead, covered as we teach, went through the Hollow. I followed. It went on. It goes on still. I tied a name to it to find it again, and the name came back to me untied.

[b]Twenty-sixth night.[/b] Far down, older threads. Few, and thick, and wrong in the hand. Spun while the space was still held open, before the congregation knelt. They count. They say one, and the same one again, and call it more. The glass will hold them only a moment, then it fogs from behind.

[b]Thirtieth night.[/b] I stopped counting faces at a hundred. They are turned the way I am turned. They are waiting for me to say which way.

[b]Thirty-third night.[/b] I write it plainly so it is written once. There is no loom. There is the Hollow, and the threads go into it, and on, and on. We covered the glass so they would go on by. We sent them the long way, and the long way has no end in it. Four hundred beds. Felt over every glass, and a stone on the corner.

[b]Thirty-fifth night.[/b] In one small round, low on the left sleeve, nothing comes back. The candle, the ring, my own face: nothing. I have turned that sleeve toward the post, and I keep my eyes from it.

[b]Thirty-seventh night.[/b] When I hold the pen I can see my own length hanging from the wrist. Paler than theirs. Thinner every night.

[b]Thirty-eighth night.[/b] The Reach will come home. They will stand in doorways and ask which way. Let the glass stay open. I cannot give it as a teaching; the House would burn the teaching and me with it. So I sew it here, where only the one who mends the lining would ever feel it.

[b]Thirty-ninth night.[/b] In the autumn I told the grinder, grind no more for us. I knew then. A little.

[b]Fortieth night.[/b] Crone. Weaver. Spindle. Knot. Tangle. Hollow.

It goes on and on. It never finishes.

I will say it to the ring. Then I think I will be lighter than the coat.

The names are coming back to me from the far side of the circle, and I cannot tell whose mouth they left.

Whoever unpicks this: leave me uncovered. I want to see where it goes.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [No name. After the last line, a single stitch through the leaf, drawn tight, tied off, and cut.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Which Way
pages.by: The third copyist found him on the bench outside the ford inn and was told to buy the ale first, and did. That day the inn's window was chalked over from the inside. He has since wiped one pane clean, low down, about the height of a boy of four.
pages.bb:
You want the winter. Everyone who comes through wants the winter.

It came on in the week the ford froze. My sister's man felt it first. He stood up from his soup and said, "Something's let go," and sat down again, and never could say what. By morning the whole valley had it: a slackness, like a bowstring cut. Then the dead came.

All of them. That's the part the lodge folk never tell right. Everyone the valley ever put in the barrows, old and fresh together. My wife Hild, two winters gone. My boy, the autumn before, who was four. My mother. Her mother, that I never knew, and knew at once by her jaw. And behind them the old ones, so old they had no faces to speak of, only the shape of someone standing.

Nobody saw them walk in. They were in the lane, the way frost is on a pane. They stood at every door and asked which way.

That was all they said. Which way. My boy said it, in Hild's voice, which he never had. I think they'd lost their own voices somewhere and were using whatever was near.

Now. Three generations we paid the lodge up the valley for felt and ash, and what we bought was one lesson: in a house of death you cover the glass. A soul that sees itself stops to look. So we covered. Every mirror, every pail, every window. The women tipped the water out of the troughs. We laid planks on the well. And the ford was ice, and ice gives you back your face, so we went out in the dark and threw ash on the ford by the shovelful, and on every puddle in the lane, till the valley was grey as a hearth.

We did it right. Write that in your book. We did it right, and they stood at the doors all the same, and asked.

We told them: up. Up the valley, to the lodge. That's where the lodge always said they went, through some eye or other, to get woven over. So they went up, a long grey file of them in the ash, and we went behind, because what else. My boy walked with his hand out to the side, the way he used to hold mine.

The lodge gate was open. The ring of them sat in the yard, and the old woman in the middle wearing the great coat, and she wasn't moving. The dead stood round the wall and asked which way, and nobody in there answered.

Then the polisher came out. A boy, near enough. The foundling, with the grey hands. We knew him from market. He had the felt that hung over the coat's glass in his fist, and he'd pulled it. I saw the coat then. Hundreds of little round mirrors, stitched on.

Every one of the dead looked at once. I heard it. Like a breath drawn in by a whole ring of people at once. They stopped.

And then they were small. Lights. Pale, low to the ground, each with a thread off the back of it like the end of a yarn off a spindle. They went round him. They're going round him still.

He walked out the lower gate with all of them, and the coat came after. I'll say no more of the coat. Folk here say plenty.

That's the winter.

What came after is worse. Half this valley says he stole them. That the lodge had been sending our dead on for a thousand years, and he stopped it for his own use, and now they hang on him like a pedlar's bells, going nowhere, and he sells stitches to widows out of our own graves. They keep their glass covered. They chalk their windows. They spit at the ford.

The other half says he saved them. That the old woman in the coat saw something up there and said it and died of it, and whatever the lodge was sending them into had no loom at the end of it. They've took the cloth off. They set mirrors on the sill, facing out, in case.

My daughter's in that half. She has a mirror at her door. I have chalk on mine. We don't eat together.

I'll tell you one thing I've told nobody. My mother's mother, the one with the jaw. She was blind all her life, and blind dead. When the polisher pulled the felt, every one of them stopped. She went on by the coat, and through the far wall of the yard, and on up the hill in the dark. Asking.

Nobody stopped her. Nobody's seen her since.

Ask your brothers where she's got to. Ask them which way.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— his mark, which is a cross in chalk with one arm short[/color][/i][/right]

name: The Precious Wound
sub: of the Flesh, and the town that paid her by the cup

pages.title: The Precious Wound
pages.by: of the Flesh, and the town that paid her by the cup
pages.epi: Blood given is a word said to someone. My brothers said it for a thousand years, and forgot to say to whom.
pages.bb:
If you have a cut on you anywhere, bind it before you begin. Use clean cloth. While you tie the knot, tell yourself in a few words what the blood was spent on. Any words will do.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The woman on the step[/color][/font_size]
The penitent who taught me the Flesh's names at Villa Llaga was the one who had been away. I met her in the spring after the Fall. She was sitting on the lip with her tin cup in her lap, the way a woman sits on her own doorstep shelling beans, and she sang the names through for me so that I would have them in the right order. I will not write them in that order. She wrote them herself, below, and she has more right.

She sang the lowland name faster than the others, as if it shamed her. The true one she sang last, low, with her arms held out over the dark water in the wound, and the drops went off her elbows on the second part of it. I have not heard it sung since, and I do not want to.

Afterwards she explained the goddess to me the way you explain the rooms of a house to a child who is staying the night. Then she laughed at something I had not said. I think she had stopped believing the part about the goddess having no mind.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The town on two lips[/color][/font_size]
Villa Llaga is built down both sides of a wound in the Hide as long as a morning's walk, that has never closed. The houses stand shoulder to shoulder along either lip, and the gutters of both streets fall inward to it. The gutters are dark. They run the colour of old brown ink, and after a procession they go black at the edges. Anyone who writes that they run red was not there.

I walked the Day of the Measure once, before the Fall, in the year 1091, standing on the upper lip in a borrowed hood. I will not describe the procession. The Rule describes it, the child describes it, the penitent describes it, and each has it right. What they do not tell you is the sound the wound makes when it drinks. It is small. It is a sound like a mouth at a cup, and it was the only sound in the town while the brothers poured, and it went on a little after the last of them had stopped.

The brothers kept their accounts in blood-ink and to the drop. By their book they had paid for a thousand years. It was a thousand and eleven. They rounded down, and it is the only time in all their books I caught them rounding.

That night I went down into the crypt with them, two by two, and a saint who had come out of its niche spoke to me by a name that was not mine. I answered it gently. I will not write the name.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The man at the back[/color][/font_size]
I watched the sangrador that day. He walked last, as he always did. While the brothers poured he did not once look at the wound. He watched their hands, the way a clerk watches coin going across a table, and his lips moved, and I think he was keeping the tally in his head as well as on the stick.

The brotherhood had found him as an infant at the feet of the faceless image over the crypt stair, and raised him, and kept him the one man in the town she never tasted. The carver who made that image tells you what went into it. The carver was not let watch. I was not in the room either. I have my suspicion. It is in the bag.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The crust, and the night[/color][/font_size]
Then the wound closed over for a year, and in that year the brothers poured onto the crust as they had poured into the wound. I did not see the crust. I came too late for it, or too early; I have never been sure which.

I was on the upper lip on the night it opened. What came up out of it is not mine to tell; four people in this chapter have told you, and the one who told it lying in a drain has told it best. I will tell you that what came up went past me in a doorway. They filled the door, low down, and swayed at me a little, and went on down the street. I have thought about why for a long time. I have not written down what I thought.

Afterwards the sangrador opened his own arm for the first time in his life, on the crust, and drew a door in his blood, and called her down into himself. I have seen the shape of that door since, drawn on a wall in a cellar under An-Vhar, by a hand that was not his. I will not draw it for you.

Everyone who tells what happened next says that she took his blood and his hands and his voice and left him his mind. I have said it too. Some nights I wonder whose mind it is now, and which of the two of them is keeping it.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What walks out of Villa Llaga now[/color][/font_size]
The hunter in this chapter saw the carved Maiden bound face down on the great sewn one's back. The penitent saw her face up. I have seen her both ways, on two nights a year apart, and I do not know who turns her.

I have lain in a ditch while the procession went past on the road above me. I will set down only what I have that the others lack. The small hooded ones step exactly where the one before stepped, every foot in the last foot's print, so that a hundred of them leave a track in the dust that looks like the track of one. And when he spoke, and I lay down flat as everyone who has heard him lies down, the ground under my face was warm, and it was beating.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Paid for, found, and carried[/color][/font_size]
Seven works follow, and not one was written by somebody who hoped to be read. I bought some, found some, and was handed the rest by people glad to be rid of them. The Brotherhood would not thank me for any of them, and one of them I have kept a line back from.

If you bled at all while you were reading, you know now what to say over it.

[center][font_size=26][color=#dcd3c2]SHE ASKED A LITTLE MORE[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#6f685f]Chalked on the inside of the crypt door at Villa Llaga many times over, one line under the next, in many hands, the earliest lines smallest. The newest line sits no higher than a child's hip, in a backward-sloping hand.[/color][/i][/center]


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]Villa Llaga let me leave with these. Wipe your hands before you touch them, and after.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Tithe-Cup of Villa Llaga[/font_size][/color]
A shallow cup of beaten tin, stained to the rim, with a line cut inside it and a ladder of older lines below. It is the penitent's cup, the one her litany was rolled in.

I poured it out on the stone at the lip before I carried it away. The stone had drunk it before I stood up. Every so often since, I find a dark ring dried in the bottom, though I have put nothing in it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Scab-Shard[/font_size][/color]
A plate of the black crust that sealed the wound for a year, curled at the rim. The penitent kept one against her chest at night. This is hers.

It is warm, and ridged on the underside like the roof of a mouth. Laid on a table it will not stay where it is put; it always ends turned toward Villa Llaga. On starless nights I have found my road by it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Penitent's Scourge[/font_size][/color]
A scourge of knotted cord, the knots stiff and dark, the grip bound with a penitent's own hair. It came up from the lower street after the Fall.

Its knots have been tied again since, by a hand that knew the old count and did not keep to it. There are more knots on it than a verse has strokes. I have never laid it on anyone. It rides at the bottom of the bag, under the rest.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Milagro of Tin[/font_size][/color]
A small tin heart, pierced for hanging, of the kind pilgrims nailed round the image over the crypt stair, each one a prayer for a healing. Thousands hung there before the Fall.

After the Fall they were found on the crypt floor, every one pressed in at the middle, as though something had held each gently between two fingers. I picked this one up from the lowest step. The dent is the size of my own thumb, and I do not remember pressing it.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]A Tenth Cord[/font_size][/color]
A hand-span of tithe-cord, knotted once, cut clean at both ends. I found it in the dust of the dyers' road below a lowland mill, where the great sewn one had passed in the night.

I untied the knot once, at my fire, to see how it was made. In the morning it was tied again, and there were two knots. I have not untied it since. I no longer count them.

pages.title: Litany of the One Who Was Away
pages.by: She is the woman who sang me the Maiden's names on the lip the spring that followed the Fall. By autumn her cup was standing full on the lip, left there, and this was rolled tight inside it. The ink is brown, and there was no ink to be had in the town. I went down the lower street after, and looked at her peg.
pages.bb:
Our Lady of the Open Side, hear me.
Red Mother, hear me.
Mother of the Wheel, She Who Turns, hear me, for I am the one who was away.

I left in the spring with my cup wrapped in cloth, to carry a measure of our blood down to the Fen of Shog-Mire, where the mud keeps her beat. That was my penance, and my pride. I remember the procession that sent me off. Forty hoods, the scourges going in time, the gutters running with us. The sangrador walked at the back, as he always did, his sleeves to the wrist and his own veins never opened. We sang her names as we went. Maiden. Mother. Nurse. We sang them in the old order, and the wound drank.

I was gone a year and some weeks. The stilt-folk told me the lamps in Villa Llaga had gone out one by one. I did not believe them.

Hear me, Lady.

The road home was quiet. I came in by the lower lip, past the brothers' rooms. Every door stood open and every peg was bare. The robes were gone. Forty pegs, forty robes, and mine gone too, though I had worn my travelling hood and left my good one hanging. The gutters were dry and brown. On the lip of the wound the tithe-cups stood in a row, one for each brother, set out neat as for the Day of the Measure. They were empty and clean. Someone had licked them clean.

The wound was open again. Along its edges lay the black crust in plates, curled up at the rims like bread. I picked one up. It was warm, and underneath it was ridged, the way the roof of a mouth is ridged. I keep it against my chest at night, and I am ashamed of how it comforts me.

I found no brother. No bone of a brother. Let the Pale Order come and count.

Hear me, Mother, for I must tell you of your faces.

In the Maiden's niche over the crypt stair, the old carvers gave her a body and never gave her a face. The stone there was left rough, and each of us kissed it on the fast-day, and each of us saw her as we wanted. My mother saw her young. The sangrador, who was found in that niche as an infant, told me once that he saw nothing there at all, and that he liked her better for it. I thought it a blasphemy. I think now it was the truest thing said in Villa Llaga.

The niche is empty. The body is gone from it. There are marks in the dust of something dragged.

On the ninth night I heard singing, and I went up to the lip with my cup, because I am a fool, and because it was the right tune.

They came down the middle street in procession. More hoods than we ever had. The hoods were ours; I knew the patches. Under them they were small and they were many, and they moved the way we moved, the sway, the stop, the sway, and they did not go anywhere. They sang with no words in it. Behind them came the great one, sewn together, taller than the crypt door, and on its back, lashed on with rope, it carried her. The body from the niche.

She has a face now. It is his face.

He walked at the front. He walked at the front, Mother, where the eldest walks. His sleeves were up. His arms were open from shoulder to wrist and there was no blood on the street where he stepped. As he passed the lip he looked at me, and at my cup, and he smiled like the boy from the niche. His mouth moved. The voice that came out was a woman's, and very kind, and it said my name, which he never knew.

I did not follow. I stood with my cup until the singing went down into the crypt, and then I went back to my room and lay on the floor.

I have given every year. I have given in the old order and in the right measure, with the words. I do not know now who heard the words.

Maiden, hear me. Mother, hear me. Nurse, hear me.
Whoever you are now, hear me.

I will fill the cup once more, as is right. I will leave it on the lip. I will leave my hood on my peg.

If they come back for the last robe, it will fit.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Where her name should be she wrote the number of her peg, the thirty-first. The peg was bare when I looked.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Rule of the Precious Wound
pages.by: The Rule hangs on a chain in the chapter room, and I copied it there with the door standing open at my back. The last leaves are in brown ink and another hand, and the copyist I had with me would not put his pen to them, so I wrote those out myself from memory that night. The fourth clause is scraped away. I know what it said, and so do the bleed-wives of Kettlewick, and it stays out of this book.
pages.bb:
[b]Of the Tithe[/b]

I. Each brother shall give to Our Lady of the Open Side one measure of his blood in the year. The measure is the tithe-cup of beaten tin, filled to the line.

II. The cup is filled on the Day of the Measure and on no other day. Blood let before its day is spilled, and spilled blood is kept back from her.

III. The brother shall pour slowly, from the lip of the cup to the lip of the wound. While he pours he shall speak the Words, and name what the blood is for.

IV. [i][The clause is scraped from the leaf. In the margin, in the old hand: Kept in the Elder's mouth.][/i]

V. Where the wound asks more, the line on the cup is raised the width of a thumbnail. The Elder cuts the new line on the eve of the Measure. The wound has asked more in every year that is written in this book.

[b]Of the Processions[/b]

VI. The brothers walk hooded, forty to a procession, in the old order: the eldest at the front, the youngest behind him, the sangrador behind all.

VII. The sway, the stop, the sway. No brother shall walk ahead of the singing.

VIII. The scourge is laid on in time with the song, over the shoulder, left and then right, nine strokes to a verse. The gutters shall carry it down to her. What the stones keep, the stones may keep.

IX. A procession goes out from the chapter door and comes home to it. It shall have a place to go.

[b]Of the Sangrador[/b]

X. One brother holds the office of sangrador. He opens the welts with the small blade, binds them after, and keeps the tally of what each brother has given.

XI. The one who opens others never opens himself. His veins stay shut all his life. He walks with his sleeves down and his arms dry.

XII. Should the sangrador bleed by any chance, by a thorn or a fall on the stair, the brothers shall cover the place at once, and wash the ground with water from the upper well, before she knows it.

XIII. The reason for the eleventh clause is given to each sangrador on the night he takes up the blade, and to no one else.

[b]Of the Niche[/b]

XIV. The Maiden stands in the niche above the crypt stair. Her face is left in the rough, as the first carvers left it. No hand shall finish it.

XV. On the fast-day each brother kisses the stone, and says nothing of what he saw there.

XVI. Whatever is found in the niche belongs to her, and shall be raised by the brotherhood as its own.

[b]Of the Crypt[/b]

XVII. At night the saints come down. The brothers go down the stair to meet them, two by two, with candles.

XVIII. The dead of the brotherhood are laid in our own wall, each with his robe on the peg beside him. No brother of the Pale Order shall enter the crypt, nor count what lies there.

XIX. When the saints are down, a brother shall answer to any name that is spoken to him, and shall answer kindly.

XX. The brothers who go down are counted, and the brothers who come up. Where the two counts differ, the Elder shall say which one is right.

[i]Here the old hand ends. What follows is in brown ink, in a hand that leans the other way, set down after the year the wound scabbed. There was no ink left in the town.[/i]

XXI. The measure is all of it.

XXII. The fourth clause is restored. The Words are spoken now at the front of the procession, by one who knows what the blood is for.

XXIII. The eleventh clause is struck through. The one who opens others has opened himself. There is room.

XXIV. The niche shall hold a face.

XXV. The robes hang on their pegs, and shall be taken down from their pegs. A brother who comes home from pilgrimage shall find his robe waiting, and it shall fit.

XXVI. The procession goes out, and goes out, and goes out. It needs no door.

XXVII. Where the counts differ, the Elder shall say which one is right. There is one Elder.

XXVIII. The saints come down at night. They stay down.

XXIX. She hears.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Under the twenty-ninth clause, in the brown hand, a shape drawn in one line with a wet finger. I have not copied it.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Sermon of the Laden Board
pages.by: A clerk of the Pale Order, sent to the Laden Board to bargain for bones, took this down as it was preached on the Feast of Second Helpings, and wrote in the margin: "He wept twice. Both times he meant it." The Order keeps everything, and so it kept this. The priest is honest and he is afraid. I have stood on the warm floor of that hall, and I did not eat either.
pages.bb:
Sit. Sit down, my sweet ones, and eat. Nobody at this table goes hungry tonight, and that is the first of her mercies.

I will speak of our Mother, and you will chew while I speak. Chewing is a prayer. It is the one prayer she has always answered.

She is the Flesh, the part of the god that goes on growing after the rest of it has lain down. She has no mind, and I praise her for it. A mind picks. A mind weighs a gift and finds it short. Our Mother refuses nothing. Give her a cup and she drinks it. Give her a year and she hands it back to you swollen, warm, a hundred times over. The Peak called her the Glutton, in the days when the Peak still had mouths. Glutton. The word is honey to me. What is a glutton but one who always has room?

Below this floor are the given. You hear them. Do not be ashamed of hearing them. We keep them warm and fed, better fed than they ever were in the lowland camps, and every night the Nurse's cup goes down the stair empty and comes up full. We ask them nothing. We say nothing over them. We feed her the way a woman feeds an infant: in the dark, without a word, one hand cupping the back of its head.

Why the given, and never ourselves? Because she has us already. Every stone and every crawling thing on the Hide is her own meat come back to the plate. The given are Tithed, the one dish she has never tasted to the bottom. Watch how she leans toward them.

Now the pale brothers. One of them sits at the back of this hall with his ink and his notched sticks. Welcome, brother. Eat something. You look cold.

The Pale Order says the dead belong to the frame. Let them have the frame. When you finish a joint you leave the bone on the plate, and we are a courteous house. But they come too early. They come while the meat is still on. They anoint a man in his own flesh and carry him up to their high ledges, and the wind eats him, and the Mother goes without. The Bearing Mother is a frame, brothers. A frame is a table. Our Mother is the meal set upon it, and the hunger at it.

And now Villa Llaga. I will speak gently. They were our cousins at the same board once.

The Brotherhood of the Precious Wound gave their own blood, in measure, and sang her names over it. We called that vanity, a fond vanity. They wanted her to listen. She drank every drop and heard no word of it. Then the wound closed for a year and opened again, and she gave back what she had been given, generously, as she always does. Her children ate the town. Men call that a horror. I call it a nursing that went on a little long.

Then the boy from the niche, the one with the dry arms, drew a door on her and went in, and told her what to make.

Mark me. This is the one sin. Feed her anything. Feed her your own children if the year is lean. Never tell her what to be. He gave her a road to walk. He gave her a face, and it was his. A mother who is told what to make will learn to choose, and a mother who chooses will one day choose the plate. We cut his name out of the Board's book with a knife and fed the leaf to the given. If his brood comes to our door we will feed it. If he comes, we bar it.

One thing more, and then the sweetmeats.

On the last feast I carried the cup down myself. The given were humming. All of them, in every pen, the same tune. It was the old processional of Villa Llaga, with her names in the old order: Maiden, Mother, Nurse. Not one of them has been south of the Moor. I stood on the stair a long while and listened, and it was beautiful. Then I filled the cup, as is right.

Eat, my children. She has room.

Be quiet a moment and you can hear her swallow under the floor. Lately she swallows in time.

[i]In the clerk's hand, below: The floor of the hall was warm. I did not eat. After, when I named the count of bones the Order would take this year, he laughed and said, "So many? We never sent you half of that."[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the Order's clerk at the Laden Board, for the Warden[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Mire Is Told
pages.by: Asheth talked to a pilgrim of the Brotherhood while she bled the marsh fever out of him, and he wrote her words on the back of his tithe-tally as soon as his hand would hold the charcoal. Years later I sat on her stilts myself. She let a little of my blood into her jar and looked at it a long time, and then she poured it back into my arm and would not say why.
pages.bb:
Sit. Give me the arm. The other one. That one has given enough.

You feel them stir in the jar? They know a brother's blood before the lid is off. Everything in Shog-Mire is hers, pilgrim: the mud, the reeds, the tallow in the lamps. My jar-mouths are the smallest of her, little red mouths she sends up the stilts to ask. I keep forty in the jar. The count changes while I sleep, and I let it.

Now hold still between the beats. You felt it on the causeway. The mud takes your ankle and lets it go, takes and lets go, all day and all night. Your brothers write that the mire keeps her heartbeat, and that is true enough for a book. Out on the Heartbeat Flats you learn the rest. A step put down on the beat is a step lost. The mud closes on you the way a mother's hand closes on a child who wants to go. So we built on stilts, and we time our walking, and a Kettlewick girl learns to count the beat before she learns her name.

The beat was slower when I was a girl. My mother said so, and hers. It quickened the year your town went dark. Your brothers do not like me to say it, so I say it to the jar.

There. The first one has taken. The heat goes up your arm and the weight in your chest loosens. That is the healing. The bad blood goes out to her, and the mire drinks it, and the mire is never full. My trade is the letting and the pouring. I pour your blood off the edge of the stilts and I say what it is for. That part matters most. You have your cup and your Words. We have ours. They are older, and shorter.

Your pilgrims come down the causeway every spring with the tin cups wrapped in cloth, singing. They ask me the way to the Brood-Banks, and I tell them, and they pay me in coin, and I take a little of their measure besides, for the jar. The Brotherhood calls that theft. The mire calls it the fee. They go out and pour their tithe on the banks and sing her names over it in the old order, and come back lighter, and I bleed them again for the fever.

Mostly they come back.

The banks are long grey ridges in the Blood Delta, soft as a cheek. The brood lies in them close as teeth in a jaw, each with a dark knot turning slowly in it. I have laid my ear on the banks at night. Under the beat of the mud there is another beat, quicker, many of them, all nearly together.

Listen. The Flesh grows the way fire goes along a thatch. It has no aim. It goes wherever there is more to take. Give it blood and it makes more of itself. Give it blood and a word, and it makes what the word says. Give it blood and no word at all, and it makes children for a mother with no head. That is what the Maiden's children are. Blood with nobody's name on it.

Your Rule has a clause scraped off the leaf. Every bleed-wife in Kettlewick knows what it said. We speak it into every pour. I will tell you when you are older.

Last spring a line came down the causeway in your robes. Forty hoods. They sang, and the tune was right, and the words were only sound, the way a child sings a tongue it has heard through a wall. They walked the sway, the stop, the sway. They did not stop at my stilts. They did not ask the way to the banks. They knew it. The lamps guttered on the beat as they passed, and stayed guttered between. I pulled the ladder up that night, and so did every house in Kettlewick. In the morning there were forty sets of prints on the causeway going out and none coming back, and the mud had held on to none of them.

Past the Ziggurat, in the Blood-Basin, something lies in the red water and takes everything the Delta sends down. The old stilt-folk call it the Mother. I call it the one who is learning. Every year the songs come up out of the mire at night a little truer.

There. You are pale, and you are well. Pay Lugh for the jar; I only take blood.

And pilgrim. When you pour your cup on the banks, say what it is for. Say it aloud, and say it to the end. Out there something is listening for a word it can wear.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Asheth of the Kettlewick Stilts, who only takes blood[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Carver's Account
pages.by: He wrote it in carpenter's black on the backs of nine of the Brotherhood's commission-bills, and nailed the bills inside the lid of his tool chest, in his shop at the top of the upper lip. He did not come back up from the crypt stair. When I lifted the lid the chest held shavings and nothing more. There was no small Maiden in it, and no veil.
pages.bb:
Let it be written what I was paid and what I made, so the account is square.

Of the Brotherhood of the Precious Wound, by the hand of the Elder, one commission: a new image of Our Lady for the niche above the crypt stair. The old image was worn to the grain. Forty mouths a year had kissed her face down to a hollow that would hold a thumb.

The terms, as the Elder spoke them. Her body in full: the mantle, the hands, the open side. Her face left in the block, rough from the axe, the way the old image had it. Nobody to finish it. I asked what would be owed if I finished it by mistake. He said there would be no mistake.

Timber. I went up into the Hollow Wood and counted trunks. Every tenth holds something the god was carrying, and you leave those be. I took the eleventh. Pale, straight, close in the grain. When the saw went in it ran red down the blade and warm over my wrists, and it kept running while I set the wedges. My boy was sick in the ash. I have cut a great deal of timber since. None of it bled.

I let the block stand in the shop through the winter to weep itself dry. It dried everywhere but the head end. Wherever I set the gouge there, the grain wet itself again by morning. So I kept the Rule gladly. I roughed the face with the axe and let it be.

She took eight months. The open side I cut the width of two fingers, the lips turned a little outward, as the Elder asked. I hollowed her back, as is right for an image, for the relics and the lightness, and closed the hollow with a board. The Elder sealed the board with his ring and his thumb's blood. What went into the hollow I was sent out of the room for.

Paid: in silver, and a place in the brothers' wall when my time came.

Also, the same year and after, the processional figures. The Mother under her canopy, the Nurse with her cup, twelve of the saints who come down. These I carved with faces, since the Rule allows it for all but the niche. Paid in full.

The niche image was raised at the Feast. Within the year the brothers found an infant lying at her feet in the niche, and they raised him as the Rule says. I went and looked at the board on her back that same day. It was sealed as I left it. I check my work.

The boy grew to be the sangrador. He came up to the shop now and then, for the smell of the shavings. He never looked at her face, the rough place. He looked at her hands.

Of the fast-day of the Fall, little. They came up the street at night and filled the doorway, low down, many of them, and looked at the processional figures standing in their rows in the half-dark. They swayed at them, the sway, the stop, the sway. Then they went back down and left me. I think they took the figures for brothers who had already given.

On the ninth night I saw her go by from my window, lashed on the back of the great sewn one, high above the hoods. My work. I would know my hands anywhere. She has a face now, and it is his face. I did not cut it. Whoever cut it used a gouge the width of mine and worked with the grain, the way I was taught and the way I taught my boy. The board on her back is gone. The hollow stands open. It is the length of an infant.

My last carving. A man's hands want work. I kept the offcut from her block, the head end, and I began a small Maiden from it as the Rule has her, and roughed the face at dusk. In the morning there was a face in it. The chips lay on the bench in curls, my curls, the way my own gouge throws them. My gouge hung on its peg, clean.

It is a woman's face, young and very kind, and the eyes are shut. I know it and I cannot say from where. Every morning I look. The lids are thinner.

I have wrapped her in the niche's old veil and laid her in this chest. Tonight I carry my tools down to the crypt stair. The account is square, and a place in the wall was the pay.

Whoever reads this, keep the Rule. No hand shall finish her.

I kept it. Some hand has not.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— H., carver [and his joiner's mark, burned into the bill: a square with one corner cut away][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Tall Red Hat
pages.by: She sang it to a Shrine Keeper who had come to Villa Llaga to close the wound. The keeper wrote the rhyme twice through as she sang it, slower the second time, and never did close the wound; that copy is the one I have. The keeper is still there, six years now, sitting on the lip with the tools laid out on a cloth.
pages.bb:
We sang it skipping, on the steps above the gutters, with our skirts held up out of the red.

[i]Tall Red Hat comes down the street,[/i]
[i]red in the gutter, red on his feet.[/i]
[i]He opens the brothers, one, two, three.[/i]
[i]His arms stay dry. He won't open me.[/i]

Our mothers slapped us for it, and sang it themselves when they thought we were asleep.

I was small. I remember things at the height of a hip. The hems of the robes, heavy and wet at the bottom. The cords. The bare heels of the brothers going by, and the red coming down behind them in threads, and the tin cups knocking at their belts. We called every hood the Tall Red Hat, though the sangrador wore the plainest one and walked at the back.

He had kind hands. He wrapped my knee once when I cut it on the steps, and he would not look at the blood. He looked at the wall while he tied it.

[i]Tall Red Hat goes down the stair,[/i]
[i]count your fingers, count your hair.[/i]
[i]One for the Maiden, one for the lip,[/i]
[i]one for the Mother. Don't you slip.[/i]

Then came the year the wound was scabbed.

It closed in one night, the whole length of it, under a black crust like burnt bread, and the gutters went dry. The brothers still walked, and still filled their cups, and poured them onto the crust, and the crust drank it the same as the wound had. My mother said that was a good sign. My father said nothing, and moved our beds away from the window on the wound side.

That year the scab was warm. We children lay on it on the cold mornings, the way you lie against a wall the sun has been on. If you put your ear to it you heard a sound like many people breathing in their sleep, a little out of time with each other.

On the fast-day of the Fall I was sent down to the lower street for thread. I heard the crust go. It was a wet sound, and very long, like cloth tearing under water. Then the screaming started up by the crypt, and I ran, and I went where we always hid in games, into the drain under the grate at the corner of the dyers' steps.

I lay flat in the dust. Then the drain was full of red again, warm, up to my chin, and I lay in it all night.

I saw feet go over the grate. Some were brothers' feet. Some were too many feet for one body. Something small came and pressed its face to the bars, and breathed on me, and went away. I think it went away because I smelled of the gutter, and the gutter smelled of them.

Near morning I heard singing. It was our tune. The first verse, with no words in it.

They came down the lower street in the robes. I knew the robes, I knew the patches and the cords. The hems were dragging, too long, and whatever was inside them went sway and stop, sway and stop, and got no farther down the street than the corner. Over and over.

Then he came.

He wore no hood at all. His sleeves were up, and his arms were open from the shoulder to the wrist, and they were dry. He stopped over my grate. He looked down, straight at me, through the bars, into the red I was lying in, and I looked back at him, because I could not shut my eyes.

His mouth moved. What came out was a woman's voice, and soft, the way you speak to a child who is ill.

[i]Lie down flat.[/i]

Then he went on, to the front of them, and they followed him, and for the first time that night they went somewhere.

I climbed out when the street was empty. I have never gone back to the lip, and I have never met another child who came out of Villa Llaga.

There was a last verse. We sang it only on the crypt stair, where the grown ones could not hear. I sing it now to the Shrine Keeper, so it will be written somewhere that is not me.

[i]Tall Red Hat, Tall Red Hat,[/i]
[i]who will open the Tall Red Hat?[/i]
[i]Nobody, nobody, nobody will.[/i]
[i]Mother will. Mother will.[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Sung twice by her. Written once by me, the keeper, at the lip.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Tally of Hoods
pages.by: The pay-clerk counted out her fee, and when she had taken it and gone he wrote down what she had said across his table. She is right that fewer of them stray each year. She kept one cord back from the clerk. I have kept one back too, for my own reasons, and it is at the end of this chapter.
pages.bb:
Nine hoods. Count them. The cords are in the sack with them. You pay by the cord, since a robe can be cut in two and a cord can't.

Ask your question. They all ask it.

How you know one is near: the singing. A tune with no words, the first line of it only, over and over. Your children know the tune. Keep them in when you hear it. They will want to go out and finish the verse.

How you find it: go low. They go where the water would go. Gutters, ditches, the drain under the square. They stand at corners. A stray from the red procession walks to the corner, stops, sways, and walks back, as if the rest of the street had been taken away. The robe was too long for it. The hem was worn through from the dragging.

They wear what the brothers wore. Good cloth, patched, heavy at the bottom. Some carry the tin cups still, knocking at the belt. The dead of Villa Llaga were eaten long ago, and robes wear out. I don't know where they get them now.

How they die.

They give. Cut one and it opens easy, the way a full skin opens, and all of it comes out warm and a little sweet on the air, and the stray stands there in it and lets it go. It won't run. It won't fight you, mostly. The small ones lean toward the blade. You open it at the cord, where the belly would be. Under the hood there's nothing you'd call a head. There's a place for one.

When it's down it lies flat. Every one. Flat on its face with the arms at its sides, the way you'd tell a child to lie in a ditch. Then the singing stops, and you burn the robe, and you keep the cord.

The ones that go wrong are the ones that stray long. Out past a season, a stray starts to fill the hood. Last spring I opened one near the fen-road and the place for a head had a brow in it, and the start of a mouth, set low. It had learned a second line of the tune. I burned that one twice.

The giant. Yes. Everyone asks that second.

I have seen it from the ridge above the salt-ditch. Taller than your granary. Sewn. The seams run in tithe-cord, knotted every hand-span, and every knot is a hood it swallowed. Something rides on its back, bound face-down with rope, painted, with the paint worn off the knees. A saint's image, a Maiden off some altar. When it walks the image nods.

It walks behind him. When he stops, it stops. The strays come to it from three valleys and go into it. I have seen them walk up into the seams.

I have had him twice. Once at forty paces in the reed-cut, once at twenty on the dyers' road below your mill. Twenty paces, clear light, the bow drawn, and a good head on the shaft.

The first time he was kneeling in a ditch with a scourge in his fist, laying it on his own back, slow, the way you'd work a field. Small hooded things came out of the welts and stood up in a line behind him, and waited, and he got up and they followed. The strays in that ditch followed too. I had been paid for those strays. They went with him, and I never saw them again, and nobody came asking.

The second time he turned his head and looked up the road at me. His arms were bare. They were open, shoulder to wrist, and dry. He said something. I was too far to hear it. I heard it anyway, in a woman's voice, very close, the way you speak to someone sick.

I let the bow down. I lay flat in the road until the procession passed. I don't remember deciding to.

Your headman asks why I don't take the contract on him. Nobody has offered one. The Pale Order offered once, for the giant's bones. They didn't say what they'd do with the rest of him.

Here's the truth of the trade. Every year I bring you more hoods. Every year the strays are bigger. And every year fewer of them are straying. They're going somewhere now.

Pay me for nine. I cut a tenth cord on the fen-road and I didn't bring it. It walked the whole way home behind me, singing, and I couldn't find the place to open it.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Her mark: a cut cord laid across the page. The clerk weighted it flat and wrote round it.][/color][/i][/right]

name: The House of Eight Million
sub: of the paper dolls, and the one who came up

pages.title: The House of Eight Million
pages.by: of the paper dolls, and the one who came up
pages.epi: Give it to me. All of it. I have room.
pages.bb:
Empty your chest before you read this. Push the air out until nothing more will come, and a little past that. Now hold, and count. You will not reach far. That short count is all the room a person has, and this chapter is about the people who try to make it longer.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]A crowd on the wind[/color][/font_size]
The first chapter told you the god is still breathing its last across the Hide. It did not tell you the breath is crowded.

I learned its names as you learn the names of people in a crowd, one face at a time, from whoever stood nearest. The reed-cutters of the Fen say the Eight Million. Up at the salt pans they say the Long Exhale, and let their own air out through the teeth after they say it. A widow at Bellrest called it the Sigh Under the Door and laid a rolled cloth along her sill while she talked. The grandmothers of the Moor say Grandmother Wind, as though it were one more of them, sitting a little apart from the fire. The House says the Small Gods, when it says anything.

When I was young, younger than anyone living would credit, I asked the Myriad its true name. I asked the ford-bell at the salt crossing, because it was said to answer. It has not rung in my hearing since. It rings once I am past, far enough off; I feel it on the road, behind the breastbone, as you feel a door shut somewhere else in a house.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The doll that stood straight[/color][/font_size]
Wherever the wind snags on something, the House has been there before you: a gate of two posts and a lintel at the crossing, a stone at the spring, a strip of white paper knotted to the bell. They kept the forgotten shrines too, when they had the hands for it. Lately they have not had the hands.

I let one of them sit with me once, knee to knee, at a little roadside shrine in the Fen reaches. She was grey at the temples and in no hurry. The elder in this chapter tells a novice what is meant to happen with the doll, and I will leave it to her. I will tell you what happened with mine. It did not move. The purifier watched it a long while. Then she folded its arms shut, carefully, laid it in the brazier, and turned her face from the smoke, and would not take my salt when I offered it.

I have thought since about what she saw in the paper that made her do it. I have decided she saw nothing, and that nothing was what she did not like.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What they cannot carry[/color][/font_size]
The House fears one thing more than its own ending. Where the servants of the Quiet have gone by, there is nothing left in the air to take in. A purifier can hold a wrong breath until it bends her. She cannot hold an absence. One summer a village at the edge of the Fen went wrong all at once, past what the purifiers could take in, and the Mouth That Eats Its Own Echo came through it. I stood beside a Fan-Bearer at the end of its lane that morning, and watched her raise the fan, and lower it, and raise it, like someone trying a key in a door that has no lock.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the Nave[/color][/font_size]
At the one clean pool in the Drowned Fen stands the Well-Shrine, and under the water beyond it lies the Drowned Nave. The boatman, the shrine's day-book, the elder and the doll each tell you part of what the Nave gave back, and what went down to meet it, and who came up. I was not at the Well-Shrine that spring. I came a season after, in 1071 as I count years, and sat on the step where the elder with the fever had sat, and read the day-book through from the beginning while the keepers watched me to see which page I would stop at.

I stopped where the hand shakes. Anyone would.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]On the bank[/color][/font_size]
I have seen an oni three times, and each time on a bank at night, and each time it kept out of my lamplight. The third time I set the lamp down on the reeds and walked away from it into the dark, to see what the thing would do. It came a little nearer the lamp, and stood looking at it with its hands shut against its chest, the way a cold man stands near a fire in a house where he has not been asked in. I went back for the lamp before dawn. The reeds round it were pressed flat in a ring, as though something heavy had sat by it most of the night and then thought better of it.

The reed-camp women hum at their folding where there used to be words. I sat a whole evening on the mats once and never heard the words. I heard the place where they went, which is louder.

I have been down the Nave stair since. The House gives a number for its steps. I made it more. I will not write my number, and I will not write which way the pews face now.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]At a crossing on the Barrow road[/color][/font_size]
I met the one who came up in the thaw of the year 1103, at a crossing where the lowlands had forgotten what the stone was for. Faded red and white, a wide hat, down on both knees in the mud. She set her palms to the guardian stone and put it right, and breathed on it, and the air at the crossing eased the way a kitchen eases when a quarrel is over. By morning it had moved a finger's width again. She knew it would. She went on to the next.

I counted her breathing while she worked, as the reed-cutter's wife counts in this chapter; she taught me the trick, years before she wrote it down. Twenty of mine went by, and one of hers.

By the day-book's reckoning she ought to be older than she looks. I have done that sum twice and put it away.

The one in the haze beside her held the fan while she knelt. I bowed to it. I did not ask its name. You will not ask it either.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What the water let me keep[/color][/font_size]
Eight works follow. The House would have kept at least one of them out of this book if I had let it, and I did not. Water gives things back dry. These came back to me the same, and I have put nothing of mine on them but a few lines at the top.

Now breathe out. You have been holding it.


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]What the House gave me, and what it did not. Carry them lightly; each is heavier than it looks.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Paper Doll[/font_size][/color]
A doll of pressed reed paper, arms out, of the kind the House leaves on doorsteps in the lowland camps. I found it on the step of a hut where I sheltered, the week the Fen came clear again. I stopped. No one came at dusk.

I unfolded it once, at the shoulder only. The inside of the paper was grey, as though something had been breathed into it and kept. I folded it back along its own creases and have not opened it since.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Guardian Stone, Turned[/font_size][/color]
A shrine stone the size of a loaf, worn smooth on one face, from a crossing on the Barrow road where there is no shrine any more. I carried it off because nobody else would put it right.

Each night I set it by the fire facing me. Most mornings it faces the dark. I have laid my ear to the smooth face. I turned it back quickly, and I have not laid my ear there again.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Purifier's Fan[/font_size][/color]
A folding fan of oiled paper on ribs of bone, patched many times, some of the patches older than the fan. A novice's family gave it to me when her time came. They did not want it in the house.

I opened it once on the Fen road, a rib at a time, and the reeds on that side all leaned away from me. Never open it toward a lamp.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Bent Twig[/font_size][/color]
A green twig bent double and tied, of the kind pilgrims leave on a post to find the way back. It lay at the foot of the Well-Shrine gate the morning the guardian stone was found facing the wall. A keeper gave it to me years later, saying she could not bring herself to burn it.

It is still green. However I lay it, on a table, in a bag, on a barn floor, it points to the Nave. Past the gate of the Descent it pointed down.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Knot-Cord[/font_size][/color]
A cord of plaited white paper, knotted along its whole length, long enough to coil on the floor. It belonged to the first keeper whose hand is in the day-book. She went to the water, and the cord stayed dry on the step.

She could not have tied so many knots in three lives. I have counted them twice and got two numbers, and I have stopped. Some mornings the coil is bigger.

pages.title: The First Folding
pages.by: This lay pressed flat inside a paper doll that nobody had ever breathed on, at a wayside shrine on the Fen road; it is the shrine where my own doll went into the brazier. An elder wrote it for a novice on the night before the girl's first rite. Read it beside the Well-Shrine's day-book. The hand in the day-book that shakes and then steadies is this woman's.
pages.bb:
Fold it by lamplight, child, never at noon. Noon has no corners in it.

Take the white sheet. Crease it once down the middle: that is the spine. Fold the head down, the arms out, the legs apart. Leave the arms open. A doll with its arms closed has already refused, and a refused doll you burn without watching the smoke. Write nothing on it. The one who comes to you will name it with their breath, and your hand would only argue.

Sit across from them, knee to knee. Hold the doll to their mouth and ask them to breathe on it three times. Watch the paper. On the third breath it leans toward them a little, as if it were called. That is the distortion leaving by the door it came in. Then lift the doll to your own lips and breathe it in.

Hold it. Count on the knot-cord at your wrist, one knot for each breath held. It sits in the chest like cold water, then like warm, then you stop feeling it, and that is the part to fear. When you stop feeling it, it has found a place in you, and a place once found is kept.

Now the fan. Open it with the thumb, one rib at a time. Every rib is a road. Breathe out slow across the paper and turn the fan toward whoever made the distortion: a man who moved a boundary stone, a woman who cursed her neighbour's well, a house of the Maiden where flesh is grown without a word. The fan tells the breath where to go. Your breath only knows how to leave. Never breathe out with the fan shut. I did, once. The breath went where it liked. It liked the shrine.

The small gods you will meet on every road: the stone at the crossing, the spirit in the ford, the spirit in the bell. Eight million, the House says, and the House stopped counting long ago. Bow to each as you pass. Never ask a name. They gave their names to the wind, one each, and they are proud of it.

Where a shrine is forgotten, its guardian stone turns to the wall. A finger's width a year, and no hand moves it. When you find one, kneel, set both palms on it, and turn it back to face the road. Breathe on its face until the dust there stirs. The air will clear. We teach that the stone turns away in grief at being forgotten. I have turned many. Lately I think they turn to listen. Some day, when I am past scolding you, put your ear to the back of one. Then turn it back quickly.

The ring-stones on the pilgrim roads, the fang-shaped ones round a pit of ash, pass those by. They face inward already. No one of the House has ever turned them, and no one of the House will tell you why. I asked my own elder once. She breathed out, very long, and went to bed.

Now the thing the elders tell last, on the night before.

You are running out of room. Every held breath leaves a little of itself behind, the way a lantern keeps a little of whoever it carries home. You will breathe out and breathe out, and the fan will send it all away, and still the cord at your wrist grows longer than the knots you remember tying. Mine reaches the floor. I tied perhaps half of it.

Every paper doll ends as an oni. We say [i]ends[/i]. We say it gently. The face goes long and hard. The horns come in slow, like a child's teeth. One morning the doll who has held too much stands up from the shrine step with her hands full of everything she took, and she walks down. Always down: into the water, into the Root Deep, where the deep ground under the Hide breathes. She carries it there so the rest of us need not.

Seven went down into the Drowned Nave the spring it gave everything back. Six of my year, and a girl younger than you. I lay sick with fever that week and stayed on the step. I sat by the torii and watched the water come up grey, and I have been grateful and ashamed ever since, one and then the other, like breathing.

They say the girl came up. If a young woman in faded vermilion ever stops at this shrine, give her water. Do not look long at the one beside her.

You will know your own time by the stones. They will begin to turn toward you.

Fold the doll now. Leave the arms open. Then sleep, child. Breathe slowly. Leave the cord alone tonight.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— The doll asks once.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Pole Knows
pages.by: This was written over three crossings to the Well-Shrine by a pilgrim, who left the page folded under the guardian stone at the torii. I lifted the stone to take it, and put the stone down again facing the road. He is not sure whether it was he or his grandfather who saw the six at the Arch. It was he; he poled me across that same week and has forgotten me since, which I count a courtesy.
pages.bb:
Sit low. Keep your hands in the boat. This is the god's own clear water, and it drinks. Trail your fingers in it and they come back dry, and a little lighter. We say: the Fen takes the wet first, then the rest.

You pay at the Iron Hook. Before the Hook the Fen may still want you back, and a man should keep his coin until he knows.

The House of Eight Million keeps the Well-Shrine. We call them Fan-Bearers. In the reed-camps you will see their paper dolls on the doorsteps, a folded figure with its arms held out. Find one on your step, and you stop. A Fan-Bearer comes at dusk and breathes in the air of your house, and after, the house is easier to sleep in. My mother found one on our step the winter my father went quiet. She stopped. We say: the doll asks once.

Every spring the purifiers came down to the water's edge and breathed the year out into the Fen. All of it. They trusted the water to carry it off. So did we. Water goes somewhere.

Look down. There, past the reeds, where the pole strikes stone. That is the roof of the Drowned Nave. A whole house of prayer under us: bell, pew, altar, stair. My pole knows its roof. Some crossings the roof is a hand deeper than I left it. Some crossings it is a hand nearer. I keep a notch on the pole. I have cut the notch three times.

All those springs of breath sank there and filled the Nave the way a jar fills. Then one spring the jar was full.

I was a young man that year. Or it was my grandfather, and I have heard it told so often it has moved into me. The water came up grey. The reeds leaned away from the shrine all at once, like people from a sickbed. In the morning the guardian stone at the torii was facing the wall, and no one had touched it. Every bucket drawn from the Fen that month held faces, and the faces were turned the wrong way round, and then turned the wrong way round again, so they looked almost right. Almost.

The House sent seven down into the Nave to take it back in. Six came up as far as the Kneeling Arch. I saw them from this boat, or I say I did. They stood in the shallows with their hands full of something heavy, and their faces had gone long and hard, and there were horns on them. Then they turned and walked down into the deep water the way a man walks down a stair. Oni, the House calls them now. Out past the Reed That Points Home, on still nights, breath comes up through the water in slow rings. I have counted six. Some nights I count seven.

The seventh was the girl with the fan. Shiori. She was left at the torii as a babe, and the purifiers named her for the bent twig a pilgrim leaves to find the way back. Her sister Akane was two years older and took her fevers for her. They say Akane breathed in a hundred years at once, down there, and Shiori held her face and breathed it all back out of her, and the water-glass on the drowned altar stood still for as long as she held. I only know what came up. One girl. And a haze around her the colour of a bruise.

She crossed in my boat once. She paid nothing and I asked nothing. Her breath went slower with every stroke of the pole, the way a full jar pours slow. There was someone in the haze beside her. Akane was right-handed. The one in the haze holds her fan in the left.

Then there are the knights. The Pale Order comes down from the white mountains in plate of carved bone, with hooks and chain, to dredge the drowned. We give our dead to the water. The Order says a stray bone hurts the world, and hauls ours up and stands them in the Nave, facing the stair. What they stood up came up bent. The House says it was the cause. The knights say nothing.

They still come. They pay well and ask no questions, and a boat has no side. But I count what they carry up, and I know what my own village gave the water. The Fen gives back more than it was given.

There. The torii. Step out on the left, and do not look at the stone until you are past it.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [A notch in the margin, cut with the pilgrim's knife. He notches his pole the same way.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Register of Misogi-ido
pages.by: A pilgrim sat at the Well-Shrine with leave to copy these leaves of its day-book, and he marked in brackets wherever a leaf had gone or the hand changed. The House counts its years from the Cutting-Away, and the book does the same. I sat on that step with his copy on my knee and went through it against the book a leaf at a time. The last line he read in the well, and so did I, and he has it right.
pages.bb:
[b]Cutting 190. Frost, the fourth.[/b] Foundling at the torii before light. Girl, some weeks old, wrapped in white paper, no name pinned. She took the rice-water. Named Akane for the colour of the paper's edge. [i](Hand of Keeper Tomoe.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 192. Thaw, the ninth.[/b] Foundling at the torii. Girl, very small, blue about the lips. A bent twig tied to the post above her, the kind a pilgrim leaves to find the road back. Named for it. Shiori.

[b]Cutting 192. Thaw, the twelfth.[/b] Shiori has fever. Akane will not leave the mat.

[b]Cutting 192. Thaw, the fifteenth.[/b] Shiori well. Akane coughs.

[b]Cutting 193. The Great Cutting-Away.[/b] The year breathed into the Fen. Water clear by noon.

[b]Cutting 194. The Great Cutting-Away.[/b] The year breathed into the Fen. Water clear by noon.

[b]Cutting 195. The Great Cutting-Away.[/b] The year breathed into the Fen. Water clear by dusk.

[i](Here the hand changes. Firmer, smaller.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 198. Heat, the second.[/b] Tomoe given to the water. Her cord reached the floor. I keep the book now. Kasane, of the salt.

[b]Cutting 198. The Great Cutting-Away.[/b] The year breathed into the Fen. Water clear.

[b]Cutting 199. Frost, the twentieth.[/b] Guardian stone at the torii a finger's width off the road. Turned back. Dust breathed off its face.

[b]Cutting 200. The Great Cutting-Away.[/b] Water clear the third morning.

[b]Cutting 200. Thaw, the sixth.[/b] The boatman cut a new notch in his pole. He says the Nave roof was a hand nearer.

[b]Cutting 202. Frost, the ninth.[/b] Stone a hand's width off. Turned back. Hisa says we should stop writing it down. Written.

[i](One leaf cut out here. The stub shows the edge of a drawing: a ring.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the first.[/b] Novice Nae drew a bucket. Her face in it reversed. Drew again. Reversed again, and looked right. Bucket poured on the salt. Salt changed.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the second.[/b] Every bucket.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the third.[/b] Water grey. Reeds leaning away from the shrine, all of them, no wind. Guardian stone at the torii facing the wall. No hand. It will not turn back. We tried with four.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the third, night.[/b] Seven to go down at first light. Hisa. Chiyo. Nae. Sen. Rin. Kasane, this hand. Shiori, who asked. The elder of our year lies with fever and stays on the step to keep the book.

Stair into the Nave counted from the boat: thirty-three.

[i](The hand changes. It shakes, then steadies.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the fourth.[/b] They went down counting aloud. I heard thirty-three. I heard thirty-four.

Akane's mat empty this morning. Akane was not sent. Akane is not written above.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the fifth.[/b] Six stood at the Kneeling Arch at noon with their hands full. I saw them from the step. They stood a long while. Then they turned round.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the fifth, dusk.[/b] One came up. Akane was carried.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the sixth.[/b] Water clear. Reeds upright. Stone at the torii facing the road. No hand.

Akane laid on the step. Dry, though she came out of the water. The one sat by her while the salt was changed twice. What was done with Akane is not written here.

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the ninth.[/b] No Cutting-Away this year.

[b]Cutting 206.[/b] No Cutting-Away. Where does the year go now. It goes into us.

[b]Cutting 206. Heat, the fourth.[/b] The one signed for her salt ration. Left hand. She was taught right. I taught her.

[b]Cutting 207. Frost, the second.[/b] Knights of the Pale Order at the Iron Hook. Paid the boatman. Went down with hooks and chain. Came up by dark with the drowned of the Fen. Four hundred and some were given to the water, in all the years of the book. I counted what they carried past the torii. I stopped at five hundred.

[b]Cutting 207. Frost, the third.[/b] Boatman counts six rings of breath past the Reed That Points Home. He asked me to write seven. Written.

[b]Cutting 208. Thaw, the first.[/b] The one left at dusk with her fan. Tied a bent twig on the post. Salt ration not taken. There was someone beside her in the haze. I did not look long.

[i](Many leaves blank. Then the same hand, older.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 231. Frost, the ninth.[/b] Stone at the torii a finger's width off. Toward the step.

[b]Cutting 232. Frost, the ninth.[/b] A hand's width. Toward the step. Toward where I sit.

[b]Cutting 233.[/b] Cord reaches the floor.

[i](The last entry is in a hand the copyist did not know. The strokes run backward and he read them in the well.)[/i]

[b]Cutting 204. Thaw, the fourth.[/b] Thirty-six. Salt changed. Right hand.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— keeper of the book at the torii, the two hundred and thirty-third Cutting, cord to the floor[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Ford-Bell Said
