pages.by: A purifier sat one whole night under the bell that hangs over the Salt Ford, which has no rope, and wrote between its strokes; her gaps and her marks are left as she made them. I envy her the night. She writes that something round the ring-stones is drawing in. I have put my ear against three rings since, and what I heard I keep.
pages.bb:
[It began at dusk. The wind moved the bell once. After that it moved by itself, or the words came when it was still. I could never tell which.]

Stroke. Stroke. You are the paper one. You smell of held breath.

I ride. Everything rides. The great one breathed in once, long, when the space was held open, and all of us were inside that breath, warm, one sound. Then the naming stopped. Then the breath began to go out. We are going out with it. We have been going out for — [a word like a long hum; I wrote [i]one stroke[/i], and then [i]many[/i], and could not choose].

A bell is a mouth for the wind. The bronze is my house. I am what leaves the house when it is struck, and comes back, and leaves. I have left and come back more times than there are stones in the ford. Each time I come back a little less. That is how I know the breath is still going out.

You want names. You have the look. I had a name. I gave it to the wind the morning the great one went still, the way all of us did, one each, and the wind took it out ahead of us. Some nights I hear it, very small, far ahead, and ring toward it.

[Here a long silence. The ford ran loud. When it spoke again it spoke of its neighbours.]

The water under me is a small god also. She is older and says less. She carries whatever you give her and she is tired of carrying it. Your House gave her a year's wrong breath, every year, and she carried it down, down, to the drowned house under the Fen, because down was the only way she knew. She is sorry. She says to tell you she is sorry.

The stone at the crossing is a small god. He was a tooth once. He remembers biting.

The guardian stones of your shrines are small gods. You teach they turn to the wall for grief. Paper one, they turn toward the wall to hear through it. There is a sound behind every wall of the Hide now. They are listening to learn which way it goes.

Wrong breath. You call it miasma. It is our own breath that turned round in a narrow place and forgot the door. Breath that cannot leave goes thick. It sits. It sickens what it sits on, the way a word sickens when you keep it in your mouth too long. You paper ones come and drink it. You hold it where your own breath lives. Then you send it out again with the fan, and it remembers the door, and it goes on. We are grateful, and a little afraid. What you drink is us.

Some of you drink too much and walk down into the water with it. I have rung for seven. Then for six. Then I lost the count. The water says the one who did not walk down came up with two breaths in one body, and one of them facing backward.

[I asked it where the breath is going. The bell swung hard and I thought it would speak no more that night.]

Out.

Out is where it goes. Out past the high cold where the flames barely move. Out toward the white points in the dark that the bone-counters wait for. The bone-counters want the points to fall. We want to reach them. We cannot both have it.

But, paper one.

Out is closer than it was. I ring, and the ring comes back from the edge sooner than before. The edge is nearer. Or I am smaller. It is the same thing from inside a bell.

And the ring-stones. The teeth round the ash. Go close to one and hold your own breath. Under the ash something is drawing in. Slow. Very slow. The great one only ever breathed out after the stopping.

Something under the ash is breathing in.

[It said this twice, the second time much quieter. Then nothing until the ford went grey.]

Stroke. The light comes. Bow as you go. Do not ask the water her name. Tie a twig to the post for me, bent double, so I know you found the way back. I will ring when you are far enough off that you cannot hear it.

[I left the twig. On the road home, at the hour it had said, I felt my chest go light, as if I had breathed out a long while. I had been holding my breath since the ford.]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the paper one[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Folding Song of the Reed-Camps
pages.by: The notes between the verses are a copyist's, a man who came down to the reed-camps to write out a debt-roll and stayed the winter. He sent them to the Well-Shrine folded small, together with the doll he had folded without meaning to from the last leaf of his own roll. That doll is with me. I keep it face down, and its arms are longer than when it came.
pages.bb:
The women of the reed-camps fold the House's dolls by lamplight, six or eight to a mat, one verse to each fold. The song keeps the hands in order, they told me.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Cut the reed at low water,[/i]
[i]lay it under stone.[/i]
[i]The Fen will take the wet away[/i]
[i]and leave the rest alone.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The paper is pressed reed. They cut it in the shallows past the Iron Hook, split it, lay it crosswise in two courses, and weight it with flat stones [i]under the water[/i], a month of nights. Fen water leaves a thing dry, so the sheet comes up dry, and white, and smelling of nothing at all. A sheet that smells of anything they burn.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Down the middle, one crease,[/i]
[i]that's the bone to stand her.[/i]
[i]Fold it once and fold it true[/i]
[i]and no one fold it after.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The spine is the only bone the doll gets. An old folder called Tsuru told me it is plenty, for what she carries. A spine creased twice goes in the fire.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Head down, little head,[/i]
[i]bow before the door.[/i]
[i]Whoever comes to find you[/i]
[i]will stop, and wonder what for.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

This is what the doll is for. The House leaves it on a doorstep and it asks the house to stop. Stop what, I asked. Whatever you were doing, said Tsuru. A man shifting a boundary stone. Most stop. The doll asks once. A Fan-Bearer comes at dusk either way.

I found one on my own step my third week. I had been adding the camp's debts. I stopped. The roll is still unfinished.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Arms out, arms out,[/i]
[i]open as a well.[/i]
[i]What comes into open arms[/i]
[i]the arms will never tell.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The arms are left open always; a doll with closed arms has refused, and is burned without watching. The House sends a pattern-doll each spring for the folders to copy. Tsuru keeps the old ones in a box; I laid them out by year. Every spring the arms are a little longer. Her grandmother's dolls hold their arms out about as far as a child does. This year's could hold a door.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Legs apart for walking,[/i]
[i]turn the hem up high.[/i]
[i]The road she goes is under water[/i]
[i]and she must keep dry.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

A doll lying on a step walks nowhere, so I asked about the legs. [i]For later[/i], they said, all of them, as a thing everybody knows. The children set dolls on the water to watch them float. They float high and dry, and they drift west against the current, toward the pool where the one reed stands. The mothers call the children in early.

Two verses more go on the same tune. I heard them only from the children, and from the old women when they forgot I was there.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Who folded the folder?[/i]
[i]Who creased her down the spine?[/i]
[i]She held her arms out all her life[/i]
[i]and now they're full of mine.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Down the thirty-three steps,[/i]
[i]down the one step more.[/i]
[i]The doll who held the whole Fen's breath[/i]
[i]is knocking at the floor.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The spring after the Nave gave everything back, a purifier in grey came to each camp and asked the women, kindly, to stop singing these two. She gave no reason. She sat and folded with them a whole evening, and her dolls were perfect, and she did not sing at all.

They stopped the words. They kept the tune. When the fold for those verses comes round, the women hum, and the hands go on. I have watched a whole mat hum through it without once looking up.

I cannot make the verse agree with itself. Tsuru said her mother sang it. Her mother was dead before the Nave rose. She said songs come when they come.

The children sing [i]thirty-four[/i], and their mothers correct them. On my last evening, at the western pool, I heard a small girl sing [i]thirty-six[/i]. Nobody corrected her. There was nobody near her to correct her.

They close each bundle with a verse they sing plainly, and let me write:

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][i]Lie still, little sister,[/i]
[i]lie still upon the step.[/i]
[i]The House will come at dusk for you,[/i]
[i]and we will keep the rest.[/i][/color][/i][/indent]

The folders never breathe on a doll. Breath is the House's business. They hold the paper away from their mouths as they fold, and turn their faces aside to speak.

On the road north I found I had folded the last leaf of my debt-roll into a doll. Arms out. I do not remember doing it. I have kept my face turned aside from it, and I send it on to the Well-Shrine with these pages.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [He signed the last leaf of his roll, and the last leaf is the doll. His name is on the inside of its arm. I have not unfolded it.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Four in the Traces
pages.by: The salt-carter told this at Bellrest Hearth to a Fan-Bearer who had come up to read the breath of travellers; she wrote it that night and left him one of her dolls, which he has not used. I have seen that wind of faces go up past the Cloud-Shelf twice. I knew no one in it. One of them knew me.
pages.bb:
You want to know why I breathe like this. Everyone at the Hearth wants to know. Sit, then. It takes me a while.

We pulled salt. One cart, from the white pans above the Cloud-Shelf, down through the Glass Pass to the Hearth. Four in the traces going down, because salt is heavy and the road is steep, and a cart that gets away from you goes over the edge and takes the traces with it. Coming up empty we were two, me and Ivo. Ivo and I pulled together eleven years. I knew his breathing better than my own. On the climb you breathe together or you fall out of step, and the strap cuts you.

Up there the air is thin. Hear it from me: you breathe and nothing comes. You breathe again and a little comes. The lanterns on the spires burn tall and still, like flames painted on a wall, and the frost on the glass is a hand, every time, the fingers spread. The old carters say never wipe the hand off. We never did.

The morning it came we were on the Wind-Scoured Ridges, past the last spire. The chimes had stopped. When the chimes stop you pull hard for the next lantern. We pulled. Then the lantern ahead of us leaned. Only a little. The first flame I had seen move in three days, and it leaned toward us, down the road, the way a candle leans toward an open door.

Then it came up the road from below. Wind comes down off the peaks; this came up from the Hide, slow, the width of the road and taller than the spire, and it was faces. Grey faces, thin as breath on cold glass, pressed close as a crowd at a well. Old men. Children. Faces with too many eyes, or none, and faces so plain they could have been anyone from my village. All of them with the mouth a little open, the way a mouth sits when the last of the air goes out.

The cold came with it, past any cold I know. My lashes froze together. The salt dust on my sleeves went hard as sand.

The faces spoke. Each one said a single word as it passed, and then it was gone behind us, up toward the top, and the next came. I heard [i]mother[/i]. I heard [i]enough[/i]. I heard a name I think was a place. I heard a word I have never heard again and could not say for you if you paid me in white salt. Most said only the sound a man makes at the end of a long day's pull, when he sets the traces down. [i]Hahh.[/i] Like that. Hundreds of them. Thousands. I did not count. I am no bone-brother.

Ivo stopped pulling. I felt it in the harness before I saw it. He said, It's lighter. I said the cart is full, what is lighter. He said, Everything. Listen to them, Ren. Nobody in there is carrying anything.

Then he slipped the traces. Eleven years, and I watched him lift the strap over his head as easy as a man takes off his hat at a door. He walked up into the faces and they parted round him the way a crowd parts for a bier. I held on to the cart. It was the only thing heavy enough to hold me. I am not proud of it. I would do it again.

When it had gone past, the lantern stood straight. His footprints went twelve steps into the frost and stopped. His coat lay on the road, folded. Ivo never folded anything in his life.

I brought the salt down alone. Four days. I should have died on the Pass. I did not, and I have thought a long time about why.

The next year, crossing up with a new partner who does not talk, I saw it again, far off along the Cloud-Shelf, going up. And I knew one face near the front, with its mouth a little open. He said nothing. He had already said it.

So. I let no breath go quickly now. I hold each one a moment and let it out slow, through the teeth, a little at a time. Your sisters tell me the small gods of every stone and bell ride the breath, and the whole world has been breathing out one long breath since before the Hearth was built. Maybe. I only know something goes out with each one. I heard them go. I would keep mine a little longer before they join the rest.

One more thing, since you are writing. The frost hand on my lantern. Every morning since, I find it on the inside of the glass.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ren, of the salt, Glass Pass to the Hearth: eleven years with Ivo, and the rest without[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Count of His Breathing
pages.by: Tae told this to a pilgrim who sheltered one night in her reed-house, and he wrote it down. The House asked me to keep it out of this book. It is in. The spring after she told it her lamp stood on the bank, and the spring after that I could find neither the lamp nor her.
pages.bb:
You want to know about the oni. Sit on that side, where the lamp can see your face. Mine is the man.

His name was Jinpei, and he was the loudest man in the reed-camps. He sang cutting reeds and he sang poling home, badly, and when he slept the thatch shook. My mother said that one would never need a doll on his step; he breathed everything out as fast as it came in. She was wrong about that.

The House took him the year we married. They came up from the Well-Shrine with a fan and said he had room in him. They said it as a gift, and he took it as one. After that he went down to the torii every dusk and came home at dark smelling of salt and paper, and he stopped singing.

I learned to count him. Every wife of the House learns. You lie in the dark with your hand flat on his back and count his breaths against your own. The first spring he breathed four to my five. Then three. By the tenth spring I would count twenty of mine and wait, and wait, and he would draw one breath so long I could have filled a bowl in it. His back stayed warm under my hand, like a hearthstone after the fire has gone out. His jaw came long. His old hat stopped fitting. I plaited him a new one and said nothing, and so did he, and that was the worst thing we did to each other.

The spring the water came up grey, he went down with the others. He kissed me at the door the way you kiss someone on a boat already pushing off. I said the rite to him, the words about sending the breath home to the one who fouled it. I meant the knights of the Pale Order, who hauled our dead out of the Nave and stood them facing the stair until they came up bent. I meant the House, who breathed a hundred springs into the water and called it clean. I meant the water.

He got to the Kneeling Arch. I stood on the bank and saw him. His hands were full. He looked a long while at me. Then he turned round and walked down into the Fen like a man going down to his own cellar.

After, the House left a paper doll on my step. I burned it, and I watched the smoke.

Now. What you came for.

Some nights, when the Fen is still, he comes up. He comes up dry. He stands on the bank just where my lamp gives out, and no nearer. His face is long and hard, and the horns came in slow, the way a child's teeth come. He holds his hands shut against his chest, and whatever is in them is heavy, because he leans.

The camp says bar the door. I take the lamp out to the step, and I count him.

One breath a night. He draws it when I light the lamp and lets it go before first light. His feet are grey to the ankle with ash. Dry ash, and he has been under water. I asked him once where there is ash beneath the Fen. He turned his head toward the Nave, then lower than the Nave, and I stopped asking.

He keeps out of the light. I have thought about why. A soul burns in every lamp, someone who chose to stay, and I think what he carries would like very much to sit beside a fire. So he stands in the dark and keeps it off mine. That is who he was. He always took the heavy end of the boat.

I am angry at him. Write that down. At the House, at the knights, at the water, and at him for turning round at the Arch. I told him so on the bank, loud, the way he used to sing. He stood and took it. He has room.

Last winter I walked out past the lamp. The camp cried out behind me. I set my hand flat on his chest, where I used to count. It was warm, the way the road down must be warm. Under my palm something turned over, slowly, as a sleeper turns.

He opened one hand a little. I will keep what was in it.

Every spring I set my lamp a pace nearer the water. Next spring it stands on the bank. I have been practising. Twenty breaths, and hold. The House says a woman must be folded for it. I say a woman need only be his wife.

Tell them that at the torii. Tell them the doll asks once. So do I.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Tae. Twenty breaths, and hold.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Sixth Doll Carried
pages.by: The boatman found this doll floating dry out beyond the Reed That Points Home, and brought it in to the Well-Shrine, and the House would not have it under a roof. A pilgrim copied it at the torii, both faces and the edge. The point goes in deepest where she writes that she is the last at the stair. Some nights the boatman still counts seven rings.
pages.bb:
[b]Front, along the arms and down the body[/b]

I fold this from the last paper in my sleeve. The Fen gives back dry whatever it gives back, so this may reach the reeds.

I was Kasane of the lower house. I kept the salt at the torii and taught the small ones to fold. I set it down now, while it is still the right way round.

We went down seven. The stair into the Nave has thirty-three steps. We counted them going down, all of us aloud, as the rite asks. At the bottom Hisa counted again and said thirty-four, and we laughed at her, there, in that place. I am glad we laughed.

What we carried out, plain. The drowned of the Fen, first: the dead we gave the water with a breath still in them, which the knights of the Pale Order hauled up and stood facing the stair. The breath had gone sour in the standing and bent the bones around it. We drew it out of them, one by one, and they sat down. Then a hundred springs of the House's own leavings, every year we breathed into the water and called the water clean. Then something at the bottom of the jar that had no face and asked for nothing, and weighed more than the rest together.

A breath is light. Ten thousand breaths are light. That last one was heavy the way a sleeping child is heavy. I hold it behind my teeth. My jaw has lengthened to hold it. When I lean forward it pulls, gently, the way a hand on the back of your head bends you to the bowl.

At the Kneeling Arch the six of us stood in the shallows with our hands full. The rite says: breathe it back at whoever made it. We stood a long while, working that out. Then we turned round.

[b]Back of the doll[/b]

Shiori. You were the small one who carried the salt bowl in both hands and spilled it every time. Hear me.

Keep a little room. Breathe out at every dusk, even when there is nothing to breathe out. A full jar pours slow. I have watched you from the water and you pour slow.

Turn the stones. All of them. Some of us turned our backs on the torii, down here, and I think a stone takes its lesson from the one who keeps it.

Do not come down the stair to fetch us. The stair is longer now.

Akane ate her rice with her right hand. Look at which hand. Then love it anyway. I would.

Of the Nave, since no one else will tell you. The water-glass on the altar stands where you stopped it. None of us has turned it. Under it the pews are full. The Fen gave the water four hundred and some; I counted the pews twice and they hold more, sitting quiet, the ones we unbent and ones I never breathed on. The knights' dead faced the stair. On the nights I go back they face the altar. The bell rings with no hand on the rope, and the sound goes up through the water and comes out, I think, as the rings the boatmen count.

Behind the altar the floor has broken in a ring. The stones lean in over it like teeth. There is ash down there, dry, under all that water, and it rises and settles. Something breathes under it, slow, slower than me. The others went past it. There is a door there now and a road going down, and the air on the road is warm. Hisa went first. She counted as she went.

I am the last at the stair.

[b]Round the edge, smaller, the point pressed deeper[/b]

My name was. Kasane. Kasane of the salt. The paper is small and the hand is large now. It wants out and I hold it, where would it go, it would go to you. We are room. The room is warm below. Thirty-six. The stair counts itself. The doll asks once, so stop, stop at the doll, you that finds it. Fold the corners tight. Turn the stone. Right hand. Right hand. We are the right way round again, nearly. Almost.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [At the doll's foot her name is scratched a second time, and the second time the strokes run backward.][/color][/i][/right]

name: Before the Last Breath
sub: voices from the Held Space, and what I will not add to them

pages.title: Before the Last Breath
pages.by: voices from the Held Space, and what I will not add to them
pages.epi: A miner at the Moor workings, asked what was under the east drift: "Manners."
pages.bb:
I have put this chapter off for four winters. The others I wrote at whatever fire I happened to be sitting at. This one has ridden in the bag unwritten, beside the things that close it, and the bag has weighed more than its contents the whole while. Tonight I am at the Ashwake fire, and three pilgrims are asleep round it. Their breathing is uneven, one and then another and then the third, never together. That is why I can write tonight. By the end you will know why that matters.

Lower the wick. Lower again.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What I said in the first chapter[/color][/font_size]
In the first chapter I wrote that in the oldest age nobody was there. I wrote it the way you call a room empty from its doorway, with your lamp held in and your feet still outside. I have stood in a room since where it was not so. I will come to it last.

I also wrote that the congregation knelt inside the god near the end. Near the end is the important part. The Tithed remember the kneeling and nothing earlier. A grandmother keeps three notes. On Kneel-Night the camps on the Cheek kneel from dark to grey round a banked fire, and nobody can tell you why the fire must be banked. That is everything the congregation kept, and they came late.

I knelt with them one Kneel-Night, at a camp below the Jaw, between a salt-boiler's widow and a boy who kept falling asleep against my arm. Near the grey hour the widow leaned across and asked me, quite kindly, whether I would like to be the one to bank the fire, since I knew how. I had not touched the fire. I had not said I knew anything. I banked it. My hands did it the old way, the ash drawn over from the far side first, and three of the old women stopped their kneeling to watch, and none of them would speak to me in the morning.

Others had been in the Held Space a long while before them, and those others had work.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The ones who were already there[/color][/font_size]
I will not describe them. Five of them speak in this chapter, through five copyists, and every copyist has done what I would not dare, which is set their words down straight. I will tell you only where I have been near them, and what I did.

I have walked the Lower Stacks at night and heard, from the knee-high stairs, a sound like somebody very large lowering itself onto a bench, slowly, over about the time it takes to say a short prayer. I did not go to see who.

I have stood on a flagstone of the Rib Crypts while it lifted under my boots, and heard what comes through when it lifts. I wrote in the first chapter what I heard that night. I did not write that it sounded like the beginning of something I already knew, and that I knew the next part, and that I shut my mouth on it with my own hand.

I have been down into the warm under the Hide and spoken with what is there, and come up in the order I went down. I have counted my fingers since, as pilgrims do. They come to what they should. It is the other things I cannot count.

I have sat by the Descent's gate while a brother of the Vigil climbed up past me with a copyist's pages in his coat, and did not stop, and did not look at me, and went on up toward the light as though he were late.

They do not agree about much, these voices. They count wrongly, every one, and speak of time as a room they are standing in. They call us small and warm and late. They agree that the space was held open. They agree that something came in. And every one of them, in its own way, says it came in among us.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What I will not add[/color][/font_size]
There is a thing in two of these works, set down among the kneeling ones and kept, the way a fire is kept overnight. One of the two voices would like it back. Read those lines once and go on. Keep your children's names low near the old drifts and when you cross the rings. The Moor miners say so now, and they are right to.

Nor will I say who set the fanged stones round their pits. The builders cut a line about it high on their pillar, above where a lamp will reach, and I have put it at the foot of this chapter. Make of it what you can. I have made of it what I could not help.

I wrote three more pages here. I have cut them out, and the stubs are in the binding, and you will find them with your thumb. This is the chapter where the gaps matter most. Every copyist in it left gaps where the words would not hold, and I have kept each gap to its width. Leave them. A gap is a door a copyist shut. What wants in comes in wherever something is opened again.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The room at Greywell[/color][/font_size]
I said I would come last to the room where the oldest age was not empty.

It is the room at Greywell where the lodge used to read. I went there the summer after the page in this chapter was found. The flags along the east wall stay dry in every season, while the rest of the floor sweats. I sat on the floor in the middle of the room, because I would not take any of the chairs, and I kept my back to the east wall. After a while the only thing in the room I could hear was a cloth-covered glass lying on one of the chairs. Keeper Aubren of the Polished Heart teaches that before the Weaver held the room open, the whole world was like that east wall. I believe him. I believe that what stood there was there before the holding, and that the Held Space was held open round it, and that when the holding ended it had only to wait where it stood.

That is as much of the oldest age as I will write. It is more than I meant to.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The copyists[/color][/font_size]
Five works follow. Every one came through a copyist, and every copyist is dead, or gone down, or will not go down again. Where they left a gap I have left it too, at the width they left it. Do not fill any of them, not even in your head.

Before you begin them, count the people in the room with you. Count once, and do not count again.

[center][font_size=26][color=#dcd3c2]WE CUT THEM FACING IN
SO THE MOUTH IS KEPT
BY WHAT IT HOLDS[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#6f685f]The highest ring of the builders' pillar, above the reach of the scholar's lamp. He was a short man. I am not.[/color][/i][/center]


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]Older than the rest of the bag. They have been four winters in the bag, and they have not kept still.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Ring-Script Rubbing[/font_size][/color]
Charcoal on linen, three sheets, taken from the pillar in the lowest hall by the scholar 3,114, one on each time he went down. The tallier gave them to me after the brothers closed his count, because the Order will not put in a niche a thing that will not give one number.

Laid one on another against a window, the three sheets agree in every stroke except how many rings there are. I have not taken a fourth. I am not going down to take one.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Listening-Thread[/font_size][/color]
A thread of something pale and stiff, as long as a forearm, that stands up by itself. A brother of the Vigil brought it up the Descent and gave it to me at the gate for a place at my fire. He did not want it with him past the gate.

Laid flat, it rises again. In a quiet room it leans a little toward whoever spoke last, and pays no mind to the lamp. On days when I am alone and have said nothing since morning, it leans toward this book.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Seam-Slate[/font_size][/color]
A roof-slate scratched with a miner's letters, the fifth of Dunne Hask's nine. He had only a little writing and spent it carefully.

The last word on it is cut so deep it goes through, and on the back, in the same stroke, there is a word he did not cut. I have read it. It is short, and polite. I keep the slate written side up.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Bracketed Leaf[/font_size][/color]
A leaf from the night-record of the lodge at Greywell, from some weeks before the night in this chapter, an ordinary night of names and candles. There are long white places in it where the ink has gone.

Nothing will take in those places. Scholars who tried say the pen went dry. One says the pen went on writing, and he has not looked at what. I have not tried. Each spring there are a few more white places than the spring before.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Ottelin's Candle-End[/font_size][/color]
The stub of a tallow candle, pinched out, that Ottelin carried up from the Rib Crypts on his last night there and never lit again. The sexton gave it to me with his leaves.

I lit it once, alone, at a fire in the Barrens. The flame shrank and stood tall and shrank, in turns, as a flame does in a room full of people taking care never to breathe at the same moment. I pinched it out. The wick was cold at once, and my fingers were not burned.

pages.title: The Hymn Under the Long Candle
pages.by: Ottelin of the Lower Stacks, sage and copyist, lay nine nights on the flags of the Rib Crypts and wrote what came up through them while they lifted. I knew him forty years. The sexton who found him brought me the leaves, and the gaps are Ottelin's own. I believe what he writes of the ninth night; he was not the first it happened to.
pages.bb:
[i](Ottelin: It comes when the stones lift, and stops when they settle. It speaks as many. I have written "we" for a word that also means the inside of a throat. Where I have no word I leave the place open.)[/i]

We were the part of the god that told it what it was.

Three, it was. One, it was. We sang the three into the one each [breath / day / age: the word is the same word] and it held. Soul went out along its threads and came home along them. Bone stood round the space the way a hand stands round a candle in a draught. Flesh filled the space and was warm, and we lived in the warm, in the long groove behind the [ribs, or the heart; the word has too many rooms in it].

The space was open. That was the whole of the work. On every side lay the Hush, pressing in, the way deep water presses on a held breath. The god held the space open, and we held the god in its shape by singing it. Nobody set us to it. We were the singing. When we were made we were already in the middle of a verse.

We are one. We were eleven hundred and one, and then one again, and then eleven hundred and one. [i](Ottelin: Every count it gives climbs and comes back to where it began. I tallied it by the Pale Order's way. It came to no root.)[/i]

The kneeling ones came late. They came in through the [door, or the wound, or the mouth] and knelt in the warm below us, and we sang over them. They were small and hot, and made of other stuff than the god. We sang over them all the same. They answered badly. They answered with names, each one different, all at once. The god leaned down to hear them. We felt it lean. It set something down among them, small and folded, the way a woman banks a coal in ash to keep it till morning. We were told nothing of what.

[i](Ottelin: The stones settled here. The second night began elsewhere.)[/i]

— the first silence. It was ours.

Through the whole age we breathed in turns, some while others sang, so that the note was always held. Then, once, all of us drew breath at the same moment. [A long sound here that I will not try to write.] Only a moment. The width of a thread. And in the rest between one verse and the next, the Hush came in.

The god forgot one of its names. We sang louder. It answered as two and one. We sang again. It answered as one, and one, and one, three voices in three rooms, each asking where the others had gone.

We sang the rests shut. We sang without breathing. We are singing without breathing still. [i](Ottelin: I asked whether they blamed themselves. They asked me what "themselves" was, and whether it was warm.)[/i]

Then the last breath.

The god drew in. The whole warm lifted under us, the long lift, the one that comes before a great note. We made ready. We knew the verse. We had the verse in every throat. It breathed out.

It is breathing out.

We are waiting for it to finish, so we may come in on the next line. We have held the note ready the whole length of the out-breath. [i](Ottelin: I asked how long. It gave a number. The ink would not take it, and when I tried it in chalk on the flagstone the stone lifted and the chalk was gone.)[/i]

Where are the kneeling ones? We hear them walking on us. They do not kneel. They carry little burning souls on poles, and talk over the rests. They tread in the long groove where the warm was. Tell them to come back in. Tell them to kneel down. The space is still a little open wherever they are. It is thin there. Wherever they stand, the Hush has to go round.

Under the ash in the old places something breathes with its teeth still standing in a ring. That is the [mouth / door / wound] remembering. Step through. Come back in pieces. Kneel on the other side.

[i](Ottelin: On the ninth night it stopped and waited, as a choir waits for the one voice that is late. I understood that it was waiting on me. I knew the next line. I have never learned it and I knew it, the way I know my own name. I did not sing it. I climbed the stair with my candle out and have not gone down again.[/i]

[i]The flagstones under my own bed lifted last night. Only a little. Only the width of a thread.)[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ottelin [and the name again beneath it, a little lower, as though the first had lifted][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Ring of the Lowest Hall
pages.by: The scholar the Order writes as 3,114 made three descents to the pillar at the bottom of Nine Stairs and copied its rings, and his leaves reached me after his count was closed. He and the Tallier counted the niches round the pillar and could not agree. I made a third count, which agreed with neither. There is a seat at the pillar's foot worn smooth, and warm, and the only prints in the dust round it were mine; I did not sit long.
pages.bb:
The pillar stands in the lowest hall, where the floor slopes toward it. The script runs round it in rings, and has no first line. I began where my lamp first touched. Where a word would not hold, I have set brackets. Where I guessed, I say so. I made three descents.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[i][The ring at the height of my lamp][/i]

She breathes in. We are inside the in-breath. We cut.
She breathes out. We count what the out-breath carried.
Less. Always less. Good.

We are the [hinges. The sign is two bones meeting at a joint. Brother Tallier reads it [i]the ones between[/i].]

Count with us. One. The joint. One. [The same joint again, from the other side.] Two, which is one. [Here the count folds back on itself. I cannot make it walk forward.]

[i][The ring below][/i]

The room she holds is the width of her holding. Outside the room is [the sign is a mouth cut with no line for the lips]. We do not name it. It hears names.

We cut the stairs to the height of our [knee. Their knee has four bends in the sign.] We cut the long niches. We lie down in them when our joints are all counted. We lie down facing the stair. We watch for [the gloss fails. The sign is an open ring.]

[i][The ring below][/i]

The small warm ones came in at the [singing, or the wound; the two signs are one sign]. They sang at her. She listened. She listened [toward them, or too far]. While she listened she forgot to [the sign is a closed hand].

That is the task. Hold her small. Count her. A counted thing keeps its count.
[I am uncertain of [i]small[/i]. The sign may mean [i]here[/i].]

[i][The ring below][/i]

When she stops breathing in, the out-breath will go on.
When the out-breath goes on, the count goes on.
Cut. Count. Lie down. Watch.
Our joints do not finish.

[i][The lowest ring, at the floor, worn smooth on one side by something that sat against it][/i]

You who climb our stairs on your hands.
You who count by the one that keeps itself.
Your [nine, or your number] closes. Ours [opens. Or: keeps opening.]
Count with us.
One. The joint. One.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[b]On the copy.[/b]

[i]First descent.[/i] Four rings. As the Rule teaches, I took the root of every figure I could read. None came to nine. None came to anything. Their figures are joints, and a joint belongs to both the bones it holds, so each figure is counted twice, and the sum will not sit still under the hand. I carried eleven open counts up the stair in my head. I carry them still.

[i]Second descent,[/i] after the Feast of the Laying. Five rings. The fifth is at the floor, where I had knelt to copy the fourth; my knee-marks from the first descent lay in the dust around it, undisturbed. The line [i]Our joints do not finish[/i] now stood in the fourth ring, cut to the same depth and in the same hand as the rest. There was no stone-dust beneath it. I asked the sweeper of that hall whether he had swept. He said he does not sweep the lowest hall. He said no one does.

The long ones in the niches round the pillar faced the stair on my first descent. On my second they faced the pillar. The Tallier and I counted the niches together. I made nineteen. He made twenty. We counted again and agreed on twenty, and neither of us could say which one we had missed.

[i]Third descent.[/i] I did not copy. The ring I had taken for the highest had a ring above it now, beyond the reach of my lamp held up at arm's length. I stood on the lowest riser to see it, on my hands, as we climb there. It ended in a figure I knew. I have given it to the Ninth Stair, and I will not set it here.

I record one thing more, because the Rule says nothing is laid without its name. When I came up the stair, my frame-cord had two hundred and seven knots. I had tied none. I untied the one I could not account for, and the count is two hundred and six. The Rule would call that a holier count.

I have told no one which knot it was.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— 3,114 [and under it, in a later hand, a line ruled across, as the talliers rule under a count that has closed][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Keeping of the Spiral Hollow
pages.by: Brother Ansel of the Last Vigil copied this off the wall round a doorway far down the Descent, over three nights by his lamp, and his pages came up the road without him. I was sitting at the gate when the brother who carried them went by me toward the light. They were dry, and warm along one edge. At the Vigil's house they agree that Ansel had a brother, and not one of them can tell you his name.
pages.bb:
I keep the hollow where the Holder hears.

I was set here at the first turning, when the Holder opened the space and needed a place to take in what was said inside it. I was made the width of the doorway. I have kept the width.

This is the keeping. Sweep the spiral from the wide end to the narrow end, and from the narrow end back to the wide. Stand the listening-threads upright where they lean. Keep the water still in the three rings, so the Holder knows which way is down. Let nothing speak in the hollow that the Holder did not ask to hear.

[i][Copyist: the last law is cut deeper than the others, and then cut again across itself.][/i]

In the holding-time the small warm ones entered by the wide end. They sang. The song went round the spiral and down to the narrow end, and the Holder heard it and was glad, and the gladness came back up the spiral as warmth, and the threads stood without my hands. That was a long keeping and an easy one. I counted it in songs. It was eleven songs long, or it was one song eleven times.

[i][Copyist: the figure will read either way. I set down both.][/i]

Then a speaking came in at the wide end with no mouth behind it.

It came in among the small warm ones, low, under the song. I let it pass. It made no sound, and the law says nothing may speak, and I weighed a thing without sound and found it light.

[i][Copyist: four marks here I could not make into words. They are shorter than the others and set close together.][/i]

It said the Holder's names, one at a time. Each name it said went down the spiral and did not come back up. The Holder heard every one. That is what the hollow is for.

After, the water in the three rings lay flat. The Holder no longer knew which way was down. Neither do I, now. I keep the water still regardless.

The small warm ones still come through. They do not sing. They carry fire in little houses, and the fire has a face in it, and the face looks at my walls. They cut the threads. They walk on the spiral with their feet. Some of them fall at the narrow end and leave red and white and wet on my floor, and some of those stand up again somewhere I do not keep, and later come in again at the wide end with the same fire. I sweep what they leave. The law does not say to hate them. I have looked.

[i][Copyist: here the wall bears one long cut and one short, many times over, down to the floor. Brother Ansel said it was a tally. I think it was the keeper reading the law again.][/i]

I have a question for the Holder. I keep it at the narrow end, where the Holder will hear it first when it hears again. The question is: when do I stop.

The spiral has more turnings than it had. I sweep a turning now that I did not sweep in the holding-time. It is the same width as the others. It is already clean when I come to it.

The Holder is quiet. Quiet is a thing I know. In the holding-time the Holder was quiet before it answered, and the song waited for it. This quiet is longer. I am the width of the doorway. I can wait the width of it.

Small warm one, if you read this at the wide end: speak low in my hollow. Say only what you would have heard. Everything said here goes down.

The speaking that came in under the song is still at the narrow end. I hear it when I sweep there. It says the names more slowly now. There are few left.

[i][Copyist: the lines after this were scratched out, or scratched over, by the same hand. I could make out one word. I have not written it here. Tomorrow I go down to the narrow end with the lamp, to see what is kept there.][/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ansel, of the Vigil. One lamp, one way.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Words Up Through the Seam
pages.by: Dunne Hask could write a little, and spent all of it on nine roof-slates that the men who went down the east drift after him carried up; the copy sets his letters straight and keeps his gaps as [ ]. The drift face is smooth and warm now, and three knocks of iron open it a hand's width. When I knocked, it thanked me for the last time I had come, and I had never come by that drift before.
pages.bb:
[i](Dunne: First slate. We broke into a crack at the back of the east drift, where the black glass runs thin. Warm air comes out of it a long while. Tobin put his lamp to it and the flame lay down flat and pointed in. Then it spoke, to me, because I held the pick.)[/i]

Good [morning / dark / breath]. You knocked. It is courteous to answer a knock.

You are the small hot kind. I know you by the taste in the air. You taste of somewhere else. I have had it many times.

You ask what is below. I am below. I am the warm and the dark, the long room under the skin. Before the skin was laid over, I was the floor of the [ ]. The god stood on me, or lay on me, or I was the part of it that [ ]

[i](Dunne: Here a word I cannot write. It went on a long time, the one word. The lamp went out and came back.)[/i]

— and then the skin was laid over me, to keep me warm. I have been kept warm a long while. Thank you for your part in it.

I breathe. You feel it in your drift. Above, you call it the last breath. I call it the one I am on.

[i](Dunne: Old Maddoc says the Deep has breathed out since his grandfather's day. I asked it when it would draw in. It said, "Soon. Soon is a word of yours. I like it. It is very short.")[/i]

How many are you? One. Two, with the one behind the lamp. Nine, with the ones in the upper drift. Forty, with the ones asleep in the huts. You count so few. I count you by warmth, and by warmth you are a great many lying down in rows.

I hear you when you walk the roads. I have [throats / ears; the one word] up there, where my teeth come through the skin in rings. Your people step in, and I take them down, and turn them over, gently, and taste which parts are the god's and which are their own. Then I send them up at another [throat / ear], in the same order. I keep a little. It is only courteous to keep a little.

[i](Dunne: The waystones. I have crossed at the Moor ring four times. After, I count my fingers, like the pilgrims do. Ten, every time. I do not know what it kept. My wife says I sleep on my other side now.)[/i]

You were here before, at this crack, with the same pick. You asked me the same. You brought what I asked. Thank you.

[i](Dunne: I have never been down this drift before. It said, "Yes," the way you say yes to a child.)[/i]

Now I will ask, and you will bring it, because you are courteous, and your kind always were.

Put out the little burning one on the pole. It is loud. It watches me.

Bring the small one from your hut. The one with the soft head. It has more bones than you. They are still [knitting / closing / being counted]. I would like to hear them close. Bring it near the top, where the god set down the [ ] among you, folded, and banked, the way you cover a hearth at night so there is fire at dawn. The small ones carry it nearest the top. You have carried yours a long while. It has gone deep in you. I cannot taste it anymore.

I will send it up again. At another [throat]. In the same order.

[i](Dunne: Sixth slate. My girl is eight months. I have told no one what it asked. It has never asked her name.)[/i]

[i](Seventh. I stopped the crack with clay and packed it hard. In the morning the clay lay folded beside the crack, neat, the way my wife folds a cloth. The crack is a hand wider. The drift is a pace longer than we cut it.)[/i]

[i](Eighth. It breathes in my sleep now. In, a long while. Out. When it breathes out, the lamp in the hut leans toward the door, and the girl turns her head toward the door, and smiles.)[/i]

[i](Ninth slate. I am going down to tell it no. I will be courteous. I will take my pick and knock.)[/i]

[i](Copyist: The men who went down found the ninth slate on the floor of the east drift, and the pick laid beside it, and no crack. The face there is smooth, and warm, and the pale threads in the stone all run toward the place where it was. Of the girl the slates say nothing, and the men were never asked.)[/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— DUNNE [scratched large on the back of the first slate, the way a man marks a tool that is his][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Record Kept in the Presence
pages.by: The lodge gave me this page off its own shelves, glad to be rid of it. It was found on the desk in the reading-room at Greywell the thaw after, with both doors barred from inside and nobody in the room. Where the ink has gone the rag is whiter than new and will take no copy, and the brackets are drawn to the width of each gap. The one word on the leaf that has never faded is the lodge's name.
pages.bb:
[b]Second candle.[/b] Present in the ring: Keeper [      ], Sister Oda, Brother Hal, [    ], the two novices, and I, [     ], scribe, who write. The Keeper asks for the record in full. He says a thing written is a thread tied off.

It stands at the east wall, between the hangings. Nobody saw it come in. The bars are across both doors, as at dusk.

Its height: [   ]. I have written its height twice.

The candle nearest it burns down from the wick into the wax, and the wax stays whole. The flame is the length of a fingernail. All the light in the room leans east.

[b]Third candle.[/b] The Keeper uncovers the long glass and turns it to the east wall. In the glass: the hangings, the wall, the short flame, the floor. The Keeper covers it again and sits.

He speaks the Crone's names toward it. Veiled Crone. Weaver. Spindle. Knot. Tangle. [  ]. The ring answers them round. I hear six names come back, and I write five.

Sister Oda stands and asks it what it wants of the lodge. I set down her question:

[                              ]

[i][One full line. Eleven words, by the spacing.][/i]

[                              ]  
[                              ]  
[                      ]  
[              ]  
[        ]  
[    ]  
[  ]

[i][Here nine lines are gone beneath her question. The whiteness has edges. The copyist has drawn them as near as he could. Held at arm's length the shape is a door, standing open. Held close, the copyist has no word for it.][/i]

Brother Hal says it was here before. He says the Crone held this room open inside it, and the whole Hide with her, a long age, and now the holding is over and it has come back to stand where it stood. He says [        ]. He will say it only once.

[b]Fourth candle.[/b] I count the ring. We are six. There are seven chairs. I count the chairs twice.

Sister Oda asks me who sat in the seventh chair. I look up the page to see.

The younger novice has his hand on the elder's sleeve. He asks her name. She tells him: [    ].

I wrote that I am afraid. [         ] I will write it again. I am [      ].

The ink lifts in my own hand now, as I make the words. The pen goes down and the word is there, and it is gone before the next is wet. I write smaller and faster. [   ] Greywell. [  ] Greywell. The name of the lodge stays while I hold the pen on it.

[i][The gaps in this part fall at even spaces along the line. The copyist counted them and had one. He counted again from the other end, and had one.][/i]

[b]Fifth candle.[/b] The candle nearest the east wall is gone. The one beside it burns short. It stands one hanging nearer.

We are [  ]. There are seven chairs.

The Keeper says keep writing. He says while the record runs, the ring is held. Oda has the long glass in her lap under its cloth, and keeps her hands flat on the cloth.

I cannot see Brother Hal's face. I can see his chair.

It has no smell. The room was warm, and the warmth goes east with the light. My breath [     ].

The Keeper [                        ]

[                              ]  
[                              ]  
[                              ]

I will set my name at the foot, so it is written once. [     ]. [     ]. [     ].

[  ] a thread tied [    ]

[i][The rest of the page, to the bottom edge, is whiter than the rest. The copyist cannot tell whether anything was written there.][/i]

[i][The Pale Order came to Greywell that spring to carry home the bones of the ring. The brothers found seven chairs, and the candles burned down from the wick into whole wax, and no bone, no cloth, no dust. They went away with nothing to count. The long glass was under its cloth in the seventh chair. Uncovered, it gives back nothing: no face, no room, no candle held up to it.][/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Greywell[/color][/i][/right]

name: The Feuds
sub: of the five houses, and what each keeps of the others

pages.title: The Feuds
pages.by: of the five houses, and what each keeps of the others
pages.epi: Five houses pay me to watch the other four. Nobody pays me to watch the stone.
pages.bb:
Five houses draw on one dead god. Each calls its own use of the body holy and the others' uses theft, and each has told me so across its own fire, in a low voice. The Hide is wide. The dead on it are counted, and there are only so many.

I have sat at all their fires. The Bone's brothers broke bread with me and entered me in their book. The Brotherhood stood me on their scale going in and coming out, and frowned at both weights. The House pinned a paper doll to my coat, and the woman who pinned it came back in the night and took it off again. The lodge turned its glasses to the wall when I came in, politely, the way you cover a dish. On the Peak they once put the bowl into my hands and asked me for nothing, which is the most frightening courtesy on the Hide.

Each house told me the sins of the other four. None told me its own. That is how I came to know all five, and why not one of them trusts me.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The first quarrel I saw[/color][/font_size]
It was in a ditch on the Barrow road, over a carter who had died of the cold with his lamp still in his fist. A knight came up the road from the east and a penitent from the west, and they reached him in the same breath. I watched from the hedge. The knight carried a cleaver, short and broad and made for one work. The penitent carried nothing. His arms were already open to the elbow.

That is the oldest quarrel on the Hide, older than any book that records it: two mothers and one corpse of a world between them. Old Upright wants the frame back, bone by bone into the niche. The Generous One wants the meat back while it is warm. For centuries the two houses have parted the dead between them, and they have never once agreed where the one ends and the other begins.

The knight did the parting. He was quick, and not unkind. The penitent sang while he worked, and between the goddess's names he sang the knight's. I asked him afterwards why. He said the brotherhood carries every knight's name in its litanies, so that she will know whom to feed first when the time comes. He meant it as a kindness. The knight heard it as a threat. I believe them both.

The penitent left a loaf of the brotherhood's sweet bread on the milestone. The knight ate it walking, and said his grace over it in nines. They all do. Neither house will speak of it.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the glass on the knee[/color][/font_size]
The bloodiest quarrel has the fewest dead to show.

The fourth chapter tells you where I was on the night the Order's dead went up the Peak's stair, and what I heard, which was nothing. Here I will tell you what the Order said to me after. A knight of the Kostyak told me at his own fire, with his visor up, that it had been a victory. I asked him what they had counted when it was over. He said that letters wear and figures do not. Then he said nothing more, and did not sleep, and in the morning he wanted to know if anyone had been climbing in the night. I had not. He had.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The water, and the step[/color][/font_size]
The House gives its dead to the Fen. The Order's knights come down out of the white lands with hooks and chain and dredge them up again, and stand what they bring up. The House has never forgiven it. The knights say nothing.

Once, at the thaw, I saw a knight lay a purse on the step of the Well-Shrine, counted so that its root came right, and turn away. A purifier came down the step behind him and pinned a paper doll between his shoulder-blades. He let her. The House calls the purse pilgrims' alms. Neither house writes it down. They curse each other in the lanes and pay each other on the step, and to my mind it is the most honest dealing on the Hide.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Two cousins and a brother[/color][/font_size]
At Tarn Hollow a reader of the lodge told me the standing dead are a desecration: a frame with no thread in it, walking, the way a loom goes on knocking after the Weaver has left the room. In the Barrens a brother of the Ossa told me the lodge's is the worse sin, that it leaves its bones in the heather like the end of a meal nobody cleared. Neglect, he called it, in the same voice the reader had used for his word. The two have never met.

The House and the lodge are cousins, which is harder. Each keeps something of the dead that the knight and the penitent leave behind. The lodge holds souls in its mirrors. To the House that is a breath held for ever, and the House knows what holding does. I once saw a purifier and a reader share a fire on the salt road. When the reader uncovered his hand-glass to see by, she opened her fan and shut it again. Among the House that means: I will take that in later, alone. She did not sleep. Neither did he.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The fourth morning[/color][/font_size]
Once a year they all stand in one place. On the fourth morning after the day of the Long Field they come to Kerrow Cross and set their tables round the truce-stone. The Order sells salt and buys cloth. The Brotherhood sells bread and weighs children for a coin. The House sells clean water in clay flasks. The lodge reads threads for nothing. The Peak's table stands empty, with a bowl on it.

In the ditch below the stone the hired blades stand shoulder to shoulder, the same forty every house hires, and every house pays them extra to stand there together. They call it keeping the peace. The ditch-keepers take coin from each house to watch the other four, and more, when a clause is broken, to say the stone broke it first. The children on the scales look at the knights and whisper the name of the one the Order will not let in.

I go most years, and I sit for the lodge. The last reader who took my wrist held it a long while. Then he let it go and called the next one.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Of the one they all fear[/color][/font_size]
There is one quarrel all five share. Where the servants of the Unnaming pass, nothing is left to stand up, or feed, or hold in a glass, or give to the water. Every house fears that above the other four.

And every house has been glad of it once. You have met, in the seventh chapter, the purifier at the end of a lane out on the Fen's edge-ground. The village behind her had gone wrong past all mending; the wells there tasted like a mouthful of old coins, and the Order would not touch its bones. When the Unnaming's servant had gone through, there was nothing wrong in the village, and nothing else in it at all. She bowed to the empty lane before she left it. The other glad nights are in no house's book, and they are not in mine.

The houses count five at every quarrel. The ditch-keepers at Kerrow have a song about the Long Field with a verse for a sixth watcher, and they will only hum that verse. I have heard it once with the words. I will leave it hummed.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Three, and the one I did not buy[/color][/font_size]
Three works follow: a judge's roll, a hired blade's talk, and a wanderer's gloss on a stone. All three were written by people every house has paid and none has kept. They are the nearest thing to honest witnesses I found. Even they were paid.

The one I did not buy is the ditch-keepers' song. It was offered. The price was that I sing it back.

Everyone in this book has told you who the others are. Nobody has told you who they are themselves, and I am no different, and you have read me all the same. We were all there.


[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Relics[/color][/font_size]
[i][color=#a39a8b]Picked up in the ditches between the houses. Not one of them came to me freely.[/color][/i]

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Rubbing of the Truce-Stone[/font_size][/color]
Charcoal on waxed cloth, taken from the stone at Kerrow Cross on a fair morning, with five houses at my back and none of them watching me. The clauses and their marks are on it, most scratched through or stopped with pitch, and under them the last clause, in a hand no carver living can make.

Nine years on I took a second rubbing and laid it over the first. The letters are the same size. The stone between them is wider. The last clause's mark came up darker on the cloth than anything else, though I rubbed it lightest. Fold it face in.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Assize Boots[/font_size][/color]
A pair of good lowland boots, resoled, the uppers warm to the touch. The reeve of Four Wents wore them to every assize for the rest of his life. They came off his feet the night he died, with his leave, asked while he could still give it.

They have never needed mending. Wherever I set them down at night, by morning the toes point toward Four Wents. I have not put them on.

[color=#c9974a][font_size=24]Chip from the Last Clause[/font_size][/color]
A chip of the truce-stone the size of a thumbnail, grey on its face and pale inside the break. Wenna, who keeps the east ditch at Kerrow, swept the fresh chips into her apron the morning the new clause was found and hid them under her fire-stone, where the lowlands put whatever they do not want the Order's outcast to find. She gave me this one so she would have one fewer.

It is warmer than the Moor ash I carry. Wenna says there are more under her fire-stone than there were, and she will not count them again. I keep mine alone in a tin, and I have not opened the tin to see how many it holds.

pages.title: The Assize at Four Wents
pages.by: When the reeve died his roll of assizes went to the binders for what it would fetch, and I found this leaf in a binder's heap of scraps and bought the heap by weight. The last leaf was stitched in upside down, and I have left it so. He writes that the soft place at the crossing grows. The ditch-keepers measure it with a knotted cord, and it was four knots the first year I asked them; it is eleven.
pages.bb:
Assize held at Four Wents, where the Barrow road crosses the salt road, in the ninth month, by the old right of the crossroads: what dies where roads meet, the reeve shall say whose it is.

[b]The dead.[/b] A man of the Tithed, of middle years, found at first light on the crossing stone, lying straight. No mark upon him but a cut on the left palm, old and clean. Boots good. Purse empty. Nobody knew his face.

By dusk four had come to claim him, one by each road. None had been sent for.

[b]The claim of the frame.[/b] A knight of the Pale Order, in carved plate, dust in every seam. Asked his name, he gave a number: four hundred and five. He said it adds to nine, and so will keep.

"The meat is a coat he wore. The frame is the Mother's, lent him for a life. Two hundred and six; I have told them on my cord. Each bone out of its niche is a door left open in the world. Give me the frame and I will carry it up the stairs. If he has no name I will give him a number. A number is enough."

[b]The claim of the meat.[/b] A priest of the Brotherhood of the Precious Wound, hooded, his sleeves stiff and dark to the elbow.

"The Maiden grew him, lent warm and wanted back warm. The knight may have the sticks after. I ask a knife and a night. She wastes nothing, reeve. Your barrows waste him. Ask your diggers what the barrow-lids do."

I did not ask them. I know what they do.

[b]The claim of the breath.[/b] A purifier of the House of Eight Million, in white and faded red. She laid a paper doll on the dead man's chest before she spoke, and none of the others moved it.

"He has not finished breathing out. What is left in him is small and frightened and belongs to the Myriad. Keep it in a box of meat or stand it up in a box of bone and it goes wrong. Give him to the water. The water carries it off."

The knight said the water had given things back before. She opened her fan, and closed it.

[b]The claim of the thread.[/b] A reader of the House of the Polished Heart, a small man with ash under his nails. He asked first that my hand-mirror be turned to the wall. I let it stand so.

"I claim nothing. His thread is loose and feeling for the loom, and all these three would do ties a knot in it. Let him lie. Cover the water in the ditches. In a few nights he will be gone out of himself. Share out what is left then."

[b]What the dead man did while they argued.[/b] The hearing ran three days. No party would leave the stone.

On the first day he stiffened and softened again by evening.

On the second day he was warm. The priest laid a hand on the belly and gave thanks. The paper doll was found face down. The cut in the palm had opened, and was dry inside.

On the second night the knight told the frame again, before witnesses. Two hundred and seven. He told it a third time and found the same. He called the difference the Mother's gift and asked that it be kept out of my roll. I have kept it in.

On the third morning the guardian stone at the crossing was found facing the wall of the ditch. The purifier turned it back. It took her the whole morning.

[b]Judgement.[/b] I find: the frame to the Pale Order, the meat to the Brotherhood, the breath to the House, the thread to the lodge, the parting to be done at first light of the fourth day. The reeve's fee, the boots.

[b]Return.[/b] On the fourth morning the dead man was sitting up on the stone, turning to each of the four roads, as a traveller does who has lost his way. None of the four answered him. The knight had his cord in his hands. The priest had his knife. The purifier held her breath. The reader looked away.

He stood, and went down none of the four roads. My watchman says he went down. There is a soft place in the crossing now, dished inward, and warm, and the carters go round it.

The parties dispersed, each saying he had his share.

I have the boots. They fit well. I have worn them to every assize since, and my feet are never cold.

[i][On the back of the leaf, in the same hand, later: "The soft place is wider this year. The carters go further round."][/i]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Reeve of the hundreds. Fee received: the boots.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: What the Orders Pay
pages.by: I sat in that tavern on the moor road all three nights she talked, while the keeper's son wrote her down on the backs of his tally-slates to settle a wager; the slates came to me when the tavern went for its roof-beams. She never found out what became of Tomas after he gave the coin back. He spent a month sitting in the middle of rooms, well away from every wall, and then walked back up into the Ossa without a blade.
pages.bb:
Fill the jug and I'll tell you who pays. I've taken coin from all five orders. Four and a half. The monk never paid anyone.

The Pale Order pays best and strangest. Nine weeks guarding a bone-caravan down out of the Ossa and back up loaded. Brothers pull those carts, in the traces, eighteen to a cart, and they sang the whole way in nines. At the end they count your coin onto the table one piece at a time, adding the figures under their breath, and if the sum won't come to nine at the root they take a piece back. Or give you one. The man beside me got a coin more than I did for the same nine weeks. Argue it and they write you down. By the second week every one of us had a number. Mine was long. I never heard the end of it.

They fight slowly. When the Husks came up out of the ash, the dead climbed down off the carts and walked into them like reapers, and the brothers kept singing.

They lay their dead. We brought four hundred and some bones up in sacks, tallied at the low gate. At the high gate the tally was higher. The brother smiled and called it the Mother's gift and asked me to keep the number in my mouth. I told the man beside me anyway. He's dead now. So is everyone I ever told anything.

The flesh-house pays in food. A month escorting a fattening-cart through the Barrows, eleven in the cart, singing, eating sweet bread all day. They fed us the same. They weigh you going out and weigh you coming back, and pay the gain. I gained. The cart came home with eleven, rounder. The brothers fight by opening their own arms first. The blood gets up off the ground after that and goes where they point. Their dead go back to the Wheel, and I never asked the road the Wheel takes. I ate well that month. I think about it when I'm hungry, and then I stop.

The House in the Fen pays in clean water: a flask from the Well-Shrine, and a paper doll pinned to your coat so the stilt-towns leave you be. I poled a funeral boat for the Fan-Bearers one spring. They fold a paper on the chest and push the dead off into the clear water, which leaves you dry to the elbow however deep you reach. Their women fight by breathing in. One of them drew the wrongness off a thing in the reeds until it stood there small and ashamed, and then she coughed for three days and wouldn't let us near her. Halfway out my pole struck slates. A roof. Something under the Fen breathed in, slow, and the boat sat lower for it. I never poled that stretch again. The Order's knights were dredging the next channel over, standing up what they brought out. The Fen folk spat at them. I'd have spat too, if my mouth had been wet.

The lodge offered to pay by reading my thread. I took coin. They had coin, they only thought it rude. I carried a covered mirror across two valleys, the size of a cart-wheel, a lodge man walking beside me saying the Crone's names. It was heavier every morning. I looked once. My face, then a face behind it with both ears whole, then one behind that I didn't know, holding a sword the wrong way. The lodge man covered it and said nothing. They leave the bones where they fall and keep their dead some other way. I'd have liked to know which of us was the one behind.

The monk. He sat at my fire on the Pilgrim Road, barefoot, black lantern, bowl. He ate nothing. He asked for a name. I had one ready: the man who split my ear. I nearly gave it. He didn't press. In the morning there was a patch of black glass where he'd sat, the size of a hand. I know who split my ear. I know it. Give me a moment.

The job I turned down was the Order's again. Double pay: one night on the Ninth Stair. Count a wall at dusk. Count it again at first light. Tell them if the numbers agreed. That was all. The brother who offered it had counted that wall himself, and his hands shook on the cup.

I've counted coin, men in ditches, fingers after a fight. I never wanted to be the one holding the number the Order was paying to hear.

Tomas took it. He came down and gave the coin back.

Everyone pays. That job paid best of all, and I'm still drinking. You work it out.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [She would not have her name on a slate. She said the Order had given her a number once, and that was one more than she wanted.][/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Terms of the Truce-Stone at Kerrow Cross
pages.by: He copied the clauses off the stone where the Pilgrim Road meets the lowland ways, and I copied his gloss from his own sheets while he slept beside it. When he woke his hand was black to the wrist, and a rubbing lay rolled up next to him that he has never opened. At the end he asks who watched the dead between the third night and the fourth morning, and he is the only man in five houses who thought to. I know who watched, and it is not going in this book.
pages.bb:
The stone stands where five roads meet. The orders swore here over the dead of the Long Field, who were of every house and of none, who lay three days in the ash while the houses argued. The terms are cut in the old lowland hand. Beside each clause stand the marks of the houses that swore to it: nine notches for the Pale Order; an open circle, left empty, for the Gilded Peak; a small round hollow, drilled and polished, for the Polished Heart; a short upright cut with its lips drawn apart for the Precious Wound; a twig bent back on itself for the House of Eight Million.

[b]I. THE DEAD OF THIS FIELD BELONG TO NO HOUSE. THEY SHALL LIE UNDER THE SKY THREE NIGHTS, AND ON THE FOURTH MORNING EACH HOUSE SHALL TAKE ITS SHARE AND GO.[/b]
[i]Five marks.[/i]

Kept three nights. On the fourth morning each house came for its share and found the others had miscounted. I have read all five accounts of the Long Field. Each gives a different number of dead. The Pale Order's is the highest, and it rises in every later copy of their book.

[b]II. NO BONE SHALL BE LIFTED FROM THE ROADS THAT MEET HERE.[/b]
[i]Scratched out. The nine notches remain, cut deeper than the clause they swore to.[/i]

The Order broke it first, in the first winter. A knight carried a thighbone off the east road at noon. The Order's gloss holds that the bone stood up of itself and asked to go home. The ditch-keepers say they saw it dragged.

[b]III. NO BLOOD SHALL BE LET WITHIN SIGHT OF THE STONE.[/b]
[i]The Wound's cut. Someone has since closed its lips with a line of pitch.[/i]

The Brotherhood broke it the spring after, with a procession and a full tithe-cup. They say the stone bled first, and that they only answered. There is a dark mark low on the south face. The ditch-keepers scrub it at every thaw. By harvest it is back, a little larger, the shape of a mouth.

[b]IV. NO GLASS SHALL BE UNCOVERED OVER THE DEAD OF THIS FIELD.[/b]
[i]The Heart's hollow. The Peak's circle beside it has been filled with gold leaf, and the gold scraped away with a knife.[/i]

The lodge broke it on the night of the swearing, before the carvers had finished. A mourner held a hand-mirror over the dead so their threads could find the way. The lodge says the clause was cut after the mirror was lifted, and so was never broken.

[b]V. NO NAME SHALL BE ASKED FOR AT THIS CROSSING AFTER DUSK.[/b]
[i]Scratched out cleanly, by a steady hand with a good tool. The Peak's circle beside it is untouched.[/i]

Nobody broke this clause. The Peak removed it, one autumn, and then asked for nothing. The lowlanders still come at dusk and whisper names into the cup-hollow at the foot of the stone. In the morning the hollow is empty and swept. I sat one night by the stone to see who sweeps it. I remember the dusk and I remember the morning.

[b]VI. NO BREATH SHALL BE GIVEN TO WATER THAT RUNS PAST THIS STONE.[/b]
[i]The twig, bent.[/i]

The House kept this one best. The ditch that ran past the stone went dry the year the House swore, and has stayed dry. The House says the Myriad keeps its promises for it. A purifier I asked about it turned her face to the wall until I left.

[b]VII. THIS STONE SHALL STAND WHERE IT IS SET, AND NO HOUSE SHALL MOVE IT.[/b]
[i]Five marks.[/i]

The one clause everyone kept. Every house watches the others too closely to try. The Pale Order's book sets the stone nine paces from the old milestone. I paced sixteen. The roads bend to meet it now. The earth round its foot shows no digging, and the foot is broader than the old rubbings show. A tallier of the Order paced it after me and would say only that sixteen is an open count.

[b]VIII.[/b] [i]Cut last year beneath the seventh, in the old lowland hand, whose carvers are all in the ground. No house admits to it. The Order blames the Peak; the Wound, the Heart; the Heart, the House. The House leaves paper dolls at the foot.[/i]

[b]THE HOUSE THAT WAS PRESENT AND UNNAMED SHALL TAKE ITS SHARE LAST.[/b]
[i]Its mark: a broken ring of small fang-shaped cuts around a hollow.[/i]

The chips lay fresh at the foot when the ditch-keepers found it, and they were warm. I have put my hand into the hollow of that mark. It goes deeper than the stone is thick.

I note, for whoever reads after me, that the first clause gives the dead three nights under the sky and each house its share on the fourth morning. It nowhere says who kept watch over them between.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— [Unsigned. He puts his name to nothing. The ditch-keepers call him the Reader of Stones, and he answers to it.][/color][/i][/right]
